title: Fathom Ledger
text:
Overview
This deck is built on the set’s surveil cluster: a small number of repeatable surveil sources feed a payoff suite that all triggers off the words “scry or surveil”. The whole deck is really one engine with several outlets, plus a graveyard that grows every turn as a side effect.
The engine is Chandra, Chill of Compliance and Eye of Jace. Chandra’s first loyalty ability surveils one and, crucially, returns a noncreature, nonland card from that surveil to your hand, so she is card-neutral or better every turn while stocking the graveyard. Eye of Jace surveils on every upkeep for one mana, and once seven cards sit in the graveyard it sacrifices itself for two damage to each opponent. Matoya, Archon Elder converts each of those triggers into a card; Saheeli, Consul of Oversight converts them into Thopters; Diviner of Victory and Prudent Fateseer convert them into power.
The kill is a flying swarm that grows faster than most Standard boards can block. Saheeli is a 4/4 flier that makes a 1/1 Thopter on the first surveil of each turn, and Prudent Fateseer pumps the whole team on the same trigger. Peer Review, the back face of three prepared creatures in the deck, adds 2/2 Cadets while surveilling, which loops back into the same payoffs.
The second act is the graveyard itself. By the time six or seven lands are in play the yard is usually ten or more cards deep, and Return to the Light Realms returns every nonland permanent card from it — creatures, Saheeli, Chandra, Matoya — for one sorcery. That is not a value play, it is usually a lethal rebuild, and it is why the deck can afford to trade bodies early.

title: Fathom Ledger
text:
Approach
Plan by phases:

Turns 1 and 2: deploy surveil bodies, not payoffs. Diviner of Victory on one, Dark Matter Manipulator or Eye of Jace follows. Diviner is the best one-drop in the deck because it grows on every surveil and its prepared back face, Unwind History, is a bounce spell with surveil attached.
Turns 2 and 3: land the engine. Chandra on three is the priority play; Proft, Consulting Detective and Matoya, Archon Elder convert the first surveil triggers into cards. Proft costs two mana per trigger, so only pay when you have spare mana or need the card.
Turn 4 and later: close with the swarm. Saheeli, Prudent Fateseer and Desperate Futurescribe all want the same thing — a surveil every turn — and once two of them are down, each turn is a Thopter, a Cadet, and two or three points of extra power on the attack.
Long game: Return to the Light Realms. Cast it only when the graveyard holds at least two planeswalkers or four creatures, and ideally after an opponent has spent their sweeper.

title: Fathom Ledger
text:
Gameplay strategy
Early game. Lead on Diviner of Victory or Dark Matter Manipulator. Both attack the same resource — the graveyard — from different angles: Diviner grows off surveil triggers, Manipulator mills three and then scales with the yard. Trade freely with Theorix Charm and Your Fate Ends Here; every card you put in the graveyard is fuel.
Mid game. Chandra is the pivot. Her first ability surveils and returns a noncreature card, so she draws a card every turn as long as the surveil finds an instant or sorcery; her second ability pays for Theorix Charm and Rewrite Regrets; her minus ability taps a blocker and puts stun counters on it, which is how the deck survives a resolved large creature. Matoya plus Eye of Jace is a two-card draw engine: upkeep surveil, draw a card, every single turn.
The combo turn. With Saheeli and Prudent Fateseer on the battlefield, sequence the surveil last: cast whatever sets up the trigger (a Peer Review from a prepared creature, or activate Chandra), then attack. Saheeli makes a Thopter on the first surveil of the turn, Prudent Fateseer gives the team +1/+0 on the same trigger, and Desperate Futurescribe converts its combat trigger into a +1/+1 counter because you have surveilled. A typical turn four is two 1/1 Thopters, a 2/2 Cadet, and six or seven points of flying damage.
Win condition 2. Return to the Light Realms. The deck surveils and mills itself constantly, so the graveyard holds the engine by turn six. Nine mana is real, but Chandra pays part of it and the deck plays 25 lands; the usual line is to cast it on the turn after a sweeper, returning Saheeli, Chandra, Matoya and every creature, then attack for lethal with a fresh board and an empty-handed opponent.
Mulligan guide. Keep hands with two or three lands and at least one one-drop plus one engine card (Chandra, Eye of Jace, Proft). Six-card hands are fine if they contain Chandra. Ship hands with no surveil source at all — the deck’s payoffs are blank without one. Do not keep hands that need double white early; the only white cards you want on curve are Enlightened Confidant and Desperate Futurescribe, and both can wait.
Key interactions and edge cases.

Diviner of Victory enters prepared, so Unwind History is available immediately. Casting it unprepares Diviner, and the surveil it causes pumps Diviner — the two halves feed each other.
Chandra’s surveil-return only works on noncreature, nonland cards. Creature cards stay in the yard for Return to the Light Realms; that is the correct outcome, not a loss.
Eye of Jace triggers on upkeep, before you draw. Order it first so you know what you are drawing into before you choose your land drop.
Saheeli and Prudent Fateseer both say “triggers only once each turn”. Multiple surveils in one turn do not multiply them; spread the triggers across turns instead of dumping them.
Rewrite Regrets returns a creature or planeswalker with mana value six or less — Saheeli, Desperate Futurescribe, Semester Foreseer and Chandra are all valid, and it empowers Jace on the way out.
Hall of Echoes copies until end of turn only, and the copy is a land, not a creature. Copy Saheeli for a second 4/4 flier and a second Thopter trigger, or copy a large Dark Matter Manipulator to attack.

Matchups. Against aggro, lean on Enlightened Confidant’s lifelink, Theorix Charm and Chandra’s stun counters, and win with a single big Return to the Light Realms. Against control, do not over-commit: keep one engine piece in hand, force the sweeper, then reanimate. Against midrange, the flying swarm is usually faster than their ground board — attack in the air and use Unwind History to clear the one blocker that matters.

title: Palimpsest
text:
Overview
Palimpsest is a four-color Standard deck built on the fusion of two mechanics. Discover does the digging: it exiles cards from the library until it finds a nonland card cheap enough, then lets you cast it for free from exile. Flashback does the recycling: it lets the deck cast its cheap spells a second time out of the graveyard, so every card spent early is still a card later.
The two halves meet on one card: Quintorius Kand. Its static ability reads “Whenever you cast a spell from exile, Quintorius Kand deals 2 damage to each opponent and you gain 2 life.” Discover, by rule, casts the found card out of exile, so every discover trigger is two points of damage to the opponent plus two life. Flashback is what keeps the deck long enough to fire those triggers over and over, and Archmage’s Newt turns any graveyard instant or sorcery into a free recast.
The result is a deck that never truly runs out of cards: dead spells are re-cast at flashback cost, discovers replace themselves for free, and the graveyard is a second hand.

title: Palimpsest
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Lead on lands and hold interaction. Duel Tactics and Lightning Strike trade one mana for one mana against small attackers; Get Lost answers anything larger. Archmage’s Newt is the best turn-two play because it attacks for two, and its combat damage turns a graveyard Duel Tactics or Bulk Up into a fresh spell. Do not rush an Appraiser into open mana if a cheaper discover source is coming: Etali’s Favor at three mana is the safest engine piece because the aura replaces itself through discover 3.


The combo turn
The deck’s “combo turn” is any turn where two or more discover triggers resolve while Quintorius Kand is on the battlefield.

Land Quintorius Kand first, plus one point of loyalty.
Cast Geological Appraiser: it discovers 3, exiling until a card with mana value three or less appears, and casts it for free from exile. Kand deals 2 to the opponent.
Attack with Caparocti Sunborn, tap two creatures or artifacts, and discover 3 again for another free spell and another 2 damage.
At the end of the turn, use Buried Treasure’s graveyard ability, five mana plus exile, for a discover 5 and a fourth trigger.

Four triggers in a turn is 8 damage to the opponent, 8 life gained, and four free spells. Two such turns usually end the game, because Lightning Strike and Tome Blast add reach on top.


Win condition 2
When the burn route stalls, the deck just attacks. Trumpeting Carnosaur is a 7/6 with trample that already discovered 5 on the way in, and Etali’s Favor gives any creature plus one plus one and trample. Bulk Up doubles a creature’s power for one mana, so a Carnosaur that connects through Rogue’s Passage hits for fourteen. Quintorius Kand’s plus one makes a 3/2 Spirit every turn as a second attacker, and the Hidden Cave lands keep the pressure on after the graveyard runs dry.


Mulligan guide







Keep
Ship




Two to four lands including at least one red source, plus one engine piece (Appraiser or Etali’s Favor) and one two-mana play
Zero or one land, or four-plus lands with no engine and no interaction


One-land hands with only a Duel Tactics, if two of the next three cards are lands
Hands with only six-drops and no discover worth casting early



The deck’s low curve means functional five-card and six-card hands often win; flooding is the real loss condition.


Key interactions and edge cases

Discover casts the found card from exile, so it triggers Quintorius Kand even when the spell was free.
Anything the discover whiffs on goes to the bottom of the library, not the graveyard, so discover does not feed flashback. Resentful Revelation and flashback itself are what put cards into the graveyard.
Archmage’s Newt’s granted flashback uses the card’s mana cost. Saddling the Newt, three power of other creatures, upgrades the same ability to flashback zero, which makes Duel Tactics a free spell every attack.
Bulk Up doubles power after the plus one plus one from Etali’s Favor, so the order matters: pump first, then double.
Rogue’s Passage costs four mana to activate, so plan the turn around it if the opponent has a blocker that matters.
Buried Treasure’s discover 5 is sorcery speed and needs five mana, but it is one of the few engines that works from the graveyard.
Hidden Cave lands enter tapped: they are the slowest cards in the deck, so sacrifice them once the mana is no longer needed.



Matchups







Opponent type
Plan




Aggro
Get Lost and Lightning Strike early, trade Duel Tactics for their best one-drop, then stabilize behind two discover triggers per turn and win the race with reach


Midrange
The deck wins the long game: flashback gives every spell a second use and Carnosaur outclasses most bodies in combat


Control
Do not overextend into a board wipe; keep Lands and Buried Treasure in reserve so the discover plan works from an empty hand


Combo
Get Lost is the main answer, and the deck can win as early as turn five or six with a pumped trampler if the opponent spends their turn assembling

title: Grave Team Six
text:
Overview
Grave Team Six fuses two mechanics into one engine: Fathomless descent (your graveyard’s permanent count X makes creatures huge and spells brutal) and Teamwork (tap creatures with total power N to unlock the second mode of a spell). The bridge between the two is Souls of the Lost — its power literally equals the number of permanent cards in your graveyard, which makes it the perfect creature to tap for Teamwork costs, over and over again.
Every fetchland, surveil land, looting artifact, and mill spell in the deck doubles as fuel: each permanent in the graveyard makes Souls bigger, makes Terror Tide and Chupacabra Echo wipe harder, lets Squirming Emergence reanimate bigger things, and turns Matzalantli’s back face — the land The Core — into a mana engine. Teamwork spells then convert that giant board presence into reanimation, removal, counterspells, and a 6/5 hexproof Leviathan.

title: Grave Team Six
text:
Approach

Game plan phases

Dig (turns 1-3). Play fetchlands and crack them, surveil with Undercity Sewers / Hedge Maze / Underground Mortuary, cast Cache Grab or Song of Stupefaction to mill, and loot with Matzalantli, the Great Door. Every permanent that hits the graveyard counts.
Grow (turns 3-5). Souls of the Lost becomes a 5/6 or 6/7. Tap it (and Solemn Simulacrum or Chupacabra Echo) to pay Teamwork costs: Too Evil to Stay Dead reanimates anything, Cruel Alliance exiles any creature and gains life, We Say Thee Nay! hard-counters, Go Nuts! fights and pumps.
Win (turn 5+). Reanimate with Squirming Emergence and Earth’s Mightiest Heroes, clear the board with Terror Tide (Souls survives as X+1 toughness), then kill with Rogue’s Passage plus a giant Souls, Season of Loss draining for your creature count, or the hexproof Leviathan.

Curve and mana
Average CMC is about 3.1. The deck is black-heavy with green support and a light blue touch, matching the mana base: five UB lands, five UG lands, three BG surveil lands, seven fetchlands, and five basics. Fetchlands thin the deck and always count as a permanent in the graveyard after cracking.

title: Grave Team Six
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Prioritize a fetchland or surveil land on turn one. Turn two, either Souls of the Lost (discard a redundant land) or Song of Stupefaction / Cache Grab to start the graveyard. Do not hold back graveyard fuel — X grows fast, and every point matters for Souls, Terror Tide, and Squirming Emergence.


Mid game
With four or five permanents in the graveyard, Souls is a real threat and Teamwork costs are trivial to pay. Reanimate a Solemn Simulacrum to ramp and draw, or loop Matzalantli for card selection. Use Cruel Alliance and Chupacabra Echo to keep the opponent’s board small while your graveyard grows.


The combo turn

Graveyard has 10+ permanents: Souls of the Lost is an 11/12.
Tap Souls plus one other creature to cast Too Evil to Stay Dead with Teamwork — return the best creature card in your graveyard (often another Souls or Solemn).
Cast Squirming Emergence (X = 10+): return Matzalantli or a creature.
Attack: activate Rogue’s Passage on Souls. 11+ unblockable damage, often lethal. If they survive, Terror Tide next turn clears everything while Souls survives as X+1 toughness.



Win condition 2: Season of Loss and the Leviathan
Season of Loss with {P}{P}{P} makes each opponent lose life equal to the number of creature cards in your graveyard — commonly 8 to 12. The {P} mode forces sacrifices to clear blockers, and {P}{P} refills your hand if creatures died this turn. Atlantis Attacks (cast with Teamwork) creates a 6/5 hexproof Leviathan and bounces two permanents — a resilient finisher that dodges spot removal. Restless Reef and Restless Vinestalk close out games when the opponent is low.


Mulligan guide
Keep: two to three lands, plus any of Souls of the Lost, Cache Grab, Song of Stupefaction, Matzalantli, or a reanimation spell. A hand with no graveyard fuel and no two-drop is a mulligan. Ship hands full of six- and seven-mana spells. Lands that surveil or fetch count as fuel, so land-heavy hands are better here than in most decks.


Key interactions and edge cases

Souls of the Lost survives your own Terror Tide: toughness is X+1, so a board wipe leaves your biggest creature standing.
Matzalantli transforms with four or more permanent types (artifact, creature, enchantment, land, planeswalker, battle) in the graveyard — the deck naturally has artifact (Matzalantli, fetchlands), creature, land, and enchantment types.
Teamwork taps as an additional cost: tap creatures before the spell resolves, so removal in response does not stop the second mode.
Cache Grab mills four and returns a permanent card to hand — instant speed, and it is both fuel and recursion in one card.
Insidious Roots: every reanimation makes a Plant, then pumps all Plants; Plants also tap for mana, creating a late-game army that pays Teamwork costs.
Graveyard hate (exile effects) is the deck’s main weakness: fetchlands and mill still work, but keep Cache Grab and draw spells for resilience.



Matchups

Aggro: Terror Tide, Chupacabra Echo, and Cruel Alliance keep the board clear; Souls blocks well. Prioritize graveyard count over speed.
Midrange: win the value war — reanimation loops out-grind most midrange decks; Solemn Simulacrum and Squirming Emergence provide card advantage.
Control: We Say Thee Nay! protects key spells; Atlantis Attacks and recursion from the graveyard are hard for control to answer permanently. Rogue’s Passage turns any surviving creature into a clock.

title: Spiderweb Landslide
text:
Overview
Spiderweb Landslide is the tenth dedicated daily Hobbit combo deck. Nine earlier builds claimed the set’s headline engines — the goblin amass raid, the dwarven companies, the elvenking’s court, Smaug’s hoard, the wilderland pack, the Lake-town recruits, the mountain musicians, the crooked thieves and the Mirkwood menagerie — leaving exactly four Hobbit cards unused, and this deck plays all four of them: Old Fat Spider, Mirkwood Meditator, Eagle’s Rescue and Front Porch Sentries. The remaining usable Hobbit pool is only four cards, so the deck is fused around the mechanic those leftovers share — Landfall — and filled with Standard support that turns that mechanic into a burn combo.
The engine is a chain of landfall triggers. Mirkwood Meditator swings as a 4/2 every time a land enters; Spitfire Lagac pings each opponent for 1; Tatyova, Benthic Druid turns every land drop into a card; Genemorph Imago turns any creature into a 6/6; Felidar Retreat makes cats or anthems. Springbloom Druid and Arid Archway generate extra land drops per turn, and Twinflame Tyrant doubles every point of damage the engine produces. The second, fully independent win is voltron: Old Fat Spider — a 6/7 with reach that can’t be blocked by power 2 or less and draws a card whenever an opponent targets it — carries Eagle’s Rescue, With Great Power . . ., Ethereal Armor, Angelic Destiny and friends into a flying, first-strike, hexproof kill, again doubled by the Tyrant.

Springbloom Druid ramps and double-triggers landfall immediately (sacrifice a land, put two basics in tapped).
Catch the draft (turns 3–5). Spitfire Lagac on turn 4 turns every land drop into damage; Tatyova, Benthic Druid turns every land drop into a card; Felidar Retreat turns land drops into cats or counters. Arid Archway loops a land back to hand for a bonus trigger each turn.
Landslide (turns 5+). Twinflame Tyrant doubles everything. Each land drop now pings for 2; each cat token hits for 4; Old Fat Spider attacks for 24+. Niv-Mizzet, Visionary turns every ping into a card so the loop keeps finding lands.

title: Spiderweb Landslide
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Mirkwood Meditator on turn 2 is the ideal start — a 2/4 that blocks everything in the format’s early game and becomes a 4/2 on your first landfall. Front Porch Sentries trades and shrinks a blocker on the way out. Ethereal Armor on the Meditator makes a 3/4 first-striker that only grows. Play your basics first; the tapped duals enter on later turns when the tempo cost is smaller.


Mid game
Resolve landfall engines in order: Spitfire Lagac (damage), then Tatyova (cards), then Felidar Retreat (board). Each land drop from here on produces damage, a card, and a body simultaneously. Arid Archway adds a free extra trigger every turn: let it bounce a basic, then replay the basic. Genemorph Imago turns the 1/1 Springbloom Druid or a cat token into a 6/6 to attack through.


The combo turn

Board: Spitfire Lagac + Twinflame Tyrant (+ Niv-Mizzet, Visionary ideally).
Chain: play Springbloom Druid — sacrifice a land, two basics enter, two landfall triggers: 4 damage (doubled), two cards from Niv, two life from Tatyova.
Loop: Arid Archway enters, bounces a land, {C}{C}; replay the land: another 2 damage, another card.
Convert: every card Niv draws is another chance to find lands; Genemorph makes a 6/6; Felidar Retreat’s cats are 2/2s that hit for 4 with the Tyrant. A six-land turn ends the game.



Win condition 2 — the giant Spider
Suit up Old Fat Spider: Eagle’s Rescue (+2/+2 flying), With Great Power . . . (+2/+2 per aura), Ethereal Armor (+1/+1 per enchantment, first strike), Angelic Destiny (+4/+4 flying first strike), Fae Flight (hexproof on entry), Fungal Fortitude (recurrence). At five auras the Spider attacks as a 16/17 flying first-striker; Twinflame Tyrant doubles the damage to 32. Its own text makes it a nightmare to answer: it can’t be blocked by power 2 or less, and any opponent spell or ability that targets it draws you a card. With Great Power . . . also redirects all damage to it, and Angelic Destiny + Eagle’s Rescue + Fungal Fortitude recur the whole package from the graveyard.


Mulligan guide

Keep: 2–3 lands including a green source, a two-drop, and ideally Mirkwood Meditator or Springbloom Druid.
Ship: one-landers, six-land hands, and hands with the double-red Tyrant or double-white Angelic Destiny but no matching source.
Prefer hands with an engine (Lagac, Tatyova, Felidar Retreat) on a playable curve.
An opening of three ETB-tapped duals is a mulligan — you need basics early.



Key interactions and edge cases

Twinflame Tyrant doubles damage from any source you control — landfall pings, cat-token triggers, and Old Fat Spider’s combat damage all double. It does not double life loss.
Genemorph Imago sets base P/T, so it overrides Mirkwood Meditator’s 4/2 landfall option — target the Meditator only when you want 6/6, and don’t expect the 4/2 to stick.
Eagle’s Rescue recurs onto power 1 or less creatures — the natural target is Springbloom Druid (1/1), giving you a 3/3 flying ramp druid.
Fungal Fortitude returns the creature tapped — the Spider comes back tapped, so activate it before combat or accept the delay; the aura stays attached.
Fae Flight’s hexproof is until end of turn — cast it in response to removal, not preemptively.
Angelic Destiny returns to hand, not the battlefield — when the Spider dies, the Destiny goes back to hand while Fungal Fortitude brings the Spider back; both layers of protection work together.
Arid Archway’s bounce is mandatory — always bounce a basic you can replay; if you bounced a Desert (Arid Archway itself or another), you surveil 1.
Maelstrom’s colored mana only casts Dragon or Omen spells — use it for Twinflame Tyrant and Niv-Mizzet, Visionary; don’t hold it for Lagac.
Niv-Mizzet, Visionary draws per point of noncombat damage — a doubled 2-damage ping draws 2 cards; the draw triggers after the damage resolves.



Matchups

Aggro: Meditator’s 2/4 and the Sentries’ death-shrink hold the ground; Ethereal Armor turns any blocker into a first-strike wall; Tatyova’s life-gain and the life-gain duals buy the turn needed for the combo.
Midrange: the landfall engine out-values them — every land drop is damage, cards and bodies; Genemorph 6/6s and cat tokens go wide; the auras make the Spider bigger than anything they deploy.
Control: Niv-Mizzet and Tatyova refill after sweepers; Fae Flight and Fungal Fortitude blank spot removal; the Spider draws a card per targeting, so removal is a losing trade; the landfall burn kills through a clear board since lands can’t be countered.

title: Leaf and Landfall
text:
Curve and mana
The deck curves 1 / 11 / 12 / 9 / 0 / 3 across one through six mana (36 nonlands, average nonland cost 3.14), with 24 of the 36 costing three or less. The curve is deliberately flat: the two-mana slot holds Guardian of the Halls, Belladonna Took, Troop of Ponies and Plunder the Trollshaws, and the three-mana slot holds Wood Elves, Mirkwood Pathmaker, Mirkwood Meditator and Roll-Roll-Roll-Roll, so the deck always has something to do on two and on three that advances the land plan.
Counting sources, the mana base gives seventeen green, thirteen blue and nine white. Green is the base colour and every nonland card that costs a single coloured mana is green; blue carries the three-drops and the flashback on Plunder the Trollshaws; white is a light splash for Belladonna Took only. Because white is needed on turn two at the earliest and only for a two-drop, nine sources is comfortable, and both white duals gain a life on entry to blunt the cost of the tapped lands elsewhere.

title: Leaf and Landfall
text:
Early game
Turns one and two are about untapped mana and a cheap Elf, not about the payoff. Lead with Botanical Sanctum, then a shock land if you have a two-drop in hand, and hold the Tranquil Cove and Blossoming Sands for turns when the tempo does not matter. Guardian of the Halls is the best turn-two play because it is an Elf, so it switches on Thranduil’s Company’s extra land drop the turn the Company arrives. Belladonna Took is the best turn-two play when your hand has two or more token-makers, because she starts counting from the very next turn.
Do not trade the early Elf away casually. Every Elf in play upgrades Thranduil’s Company from a vanilla 3/4 into an extra land drop every turn, and the extra land drop is worth roughly one Elf token, two counters and a +2/+2 trigger every single turn thereafter.

title: Leaf and Landfall
text:
Mid game
Turn three is where the deck starts compounding. Wood Elves fetches a Forest onto the battlefield, which is a landfall trigger, which is already an Elf token if Thranduil has landed. Mirkwood Pathmaker comes down as a three-mana creature that is as large as your land count, so on turn three it is a 4/4 and by turn six it is a 7/7 that no common blocker can stop.
Turn four is Thranduil, Sindarin Liege or Thranduil’s Company, and the correct order is Company first if you can only afford one. The Company’s extra land drop is what turns a single land per turn into two, and two landfall triggers per turn is the difference between a slow board and a lethal one. Once both are in play, playing two lands in one turn produces two Elf tokens, four +1/+1 counters and two +2/+2 triggers for Boughside Wanderers.

title: Leaf and Landfall
text:
The combo turn
The deck’s engine turn is a sequence rather than a single card. With Thranduil, Sindarin Liege and Thranduil’s Company on the battlefield and Roll-Roll-Roll-Roll at two or more lore counters, you attack for the turn, then at the end step the Saga returns the land it exiled earlier. That is a free landfall trigger: a 1/1 Elf token from Thranduil, two +1/+1 counters from the Company, +2/+2 on Boughside Wanderers, and a third Belladonna Took trigger that pumps the whole team. Because the Saga cycles the same land every turn, the loop is repeatable without drawing anything.
The best single turn in the deck is the adventure line. Cast Silvan Rally for {1}{G/U}{G/U} first: mill four, take up to two lands into hand. Then cast Thranduil, Sindarin Liege from exile, play both lands — the Company’s extra drop means you can — and end the turn with Thranduil, two 1/1 Elf tokens that are 2/2 thanks to his lord ability, four counters placed wherever they matter, and a hand that now holds the rest of the deck’s lands.

title: Leaf and Landfall
text:
Win condition 2
When the ground is stalled, the deck wins with one attacker rather than six. Mirkwood Pathmaker’s power and toughness are each equal to the number of lands you control, so a normal game has it at 7/7 or 8/8 by turn six without any investment. Rogue’s Passage turns {4} and a tap into an unblockable attack, and Boughside Wanderers’ landfall pump adds +2/+2 per land in the same turn you go for it. Six to eight mana committed on the turn before the attack sets up a twelve-to-sixteen damage swing that ignores blockers entirely.
The wide plan and the tall plan use the same cards, so the deck does not have to choose. Thranduil’s landfall tokens and the Company’s counters build the swarm while the lands that produce them simultaneously build the Pathmaker.

title: Leaf and Landfall
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep two or three lands, one card that costs two or less, and at least one landfall payoff. A hand of Botanical Sanctum, a shock land, Guardian of the Halls, Thranduil’s Company and two more lands is the ideal keep: it curves two into four and turns on the extra land drop immediately. Ship one-land hands even with a perfect curve, because the deck needs to hit four lands on turn four to activate Rogue’s Passage and cast Boughside Wanderers. Ship hands with no landfall payoff at all — three Elves and no Company, no Thranduil and no Pathmaker is a pile of small bodies. A hand that is only lands and Belladonna Took is also a ship, because nothing in it makes a token.

title: Leaf and Landfall
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Landfall triggers on any land entering the battlefield, not just on a land played from hand. Wood Elves’ Forest, Troop of Ponies, Silvan Reveler’s discarded land, Roll-Roll-Roll-Roll’s returned land and Silvan Rally’s milled lands all trigger Thranduil, the Company and Boughside Wanderers.
Roll-Roll-Roll-Roll can also protect a creature: exiling a Thranduil or a Mirkwood Pathmaker and returning it at the end step dodges a sorcery-speed removal spell, and the returned permanent re-triggers any enters-the-battlefield ability.
Thranduil’s Company’s counters are placed on a target creature, so aim them at Mirkwood Pathmaker on the turn you intend to attack, and at a token on turns when you are building wide.
Thranduil, Sindarin Liege’s tokens are Elves, so they receive his own +1/+1 and they satisfy the Company’s requirement that you control another Elf.
Belladonna Took counts tokens per turn, not per source, so a single landfall token plus a Silvan Reveler land is already the second trigger and draws a card.
Silvan Reveler returns itself from the graveyard for {1}{G}{U} on any landfall, which makes it a repeatable three-mana enters-the-battlefield trigger as long as you keep playing lands.
Mirkwood Pathmaker’s size is a static characteristic, so it changes the moment a land enters — it does not need to be pumped, and it shrinks if a land is destroyed.
Botanical Sanctum enters untapped only while you control two or fewer other lands, so it is a turn-one or turn-two land; drawn late it is just a tapped dual.
Key to the Side-Door’s second ability needs a legendary card in hand with the same name as a legendary permanent you control, so a spare Thranduil, Sindarin Liege is two cards rather than a dead duplicate.
Troop of Ponies puts one land onto the battlefield and one into your hand, which is a landfall trigger now and a land drop next turn; sacrifice it before casting Boughside Wanderers so the land is already counted.
Plunder the Trollshaws is a fine turn-two play and a better flashback later: casting it from the graveyard draws two cards, which is the cheapest way to dig for the extra land drop.

title: Clachan Stampede
text:
Overview
Clachan Stampede fuses three mechanics into one board: Behold supplies the cheap Kithkin engine, Mount supplies the token bodies and the evasive finishers, and Morbid turns every chump block and sacrifice into permanent +1/+1 counters.
The engine runs on creature entry. Kinsbaile Aspirant is a one-mana Kithkin that gains +1/+1 every time another creature enters, and Thoughtweft Lieutenant hands out +1/+1 and trample whenever a Kithkin arrives. Clachan Festival makes two Kithkin tokens on entry and can keep making them for {4}{W}. Behold matters because these Kithkin feed Champion of the Clachan (behold a Kithkin, exile it, and every other Kithkin gets +1/+1) and Celestial Reunion (choose Kithkin, behold two, and tutor any cheap creature straight onto the battlefield).
Mounts convert that wide board into damage. Saddle taps spare bodies, so tokens are never wasted, and every saddled attack creates more material: Bridled Bighorn makes 1/1 Sheep, Seraphic Steed makes 3/3 flying Angels, and Ornery Tumblewagg doubles the counters you have been collecting.
Morbid is the back end. Because the deck trades tokens constantly and Bulwark Ox can sacrifice itself, creatures die almost every turn. That turns on Needletooth Pack (two +1/+1 counters on a target every end step), Cackling Prowler (grows every end step) and Slumbering Cerberus (untaps every end step), so a stalled board still grows.

title: Clachan Stampede

Game plan phases

Turns 1 to 3 — establish the engine. Land Kinsbaile Aspirant, District Mascot, Thoughtweft Lieutenant and Seraphic Steed. Trade nothing yet; just build a board that grows for free.
Turns 3 to 5 — go wide and saddle. Clachan Festival and Brigid’s Command flood the board with Kithkin, then tap them to saddle Bridled Bighorn, Congregation Gryff and Seraphic Steed. Every saddled attack adds a token or a counter.
Turns 5 to 7 — convert. Needletooth Pack and Abandoned Air Temple turn the accumulated board into an unrecoverable +1/+1 lead; Congregation Gryff closes through the air.

title: Clachan Stampede
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Open on Kinsbaile Aspirant or District Mascot and keep adding bodies. Do not attack into blocks you lose in the first three turns; the deck wins by compounding, not by racing. Thoughtweft Lieutenant is the best turn-two play when you already have a Kithkin, because the trample it hands out is what makes the later swarm unblockable.


Mid game and the combo turn
The “combo turn” is any turn where you can attack, saddle, and cash in on entry triggers:

Tap two spare bodies to saddle Bridled Bighorn — it makes a Sheep while attacking.
Saddle Seraphic Steed for a 3/3 flying Angel, or Congregation Gryff to pump it by the number of Mounts you control.
Cast Clachan Festival or Brigid’s Command so Aspirant, Lieutenant and Champion of the Clachan all trigger at once.
Spend the leftover mana on Abandoned Air Temple to put a counter on every creature.

Because saddling only taps creatures you are not attacking with, the tokens you make each turn are exactly the fuel the next turn needs.


Win condition two
Congregation Gryff is a flying lifelinker that gets +X/+X where X is the number of Mounts you control. With Seraphic Steed, Bridled Bighorn, District Mascot, Bulwark Ox and Ornery Tumblewagg all on the board it swings for a large evasive chunk and gains the life back. Secret Tunnel removes the last blocker by making two Kithkin unblockable, and Abandoned Air Temple finishes stalled games one counter at a time.


Mulligan guide

Keep any hand with a one-drop plus two lands, or with a Temple plus a basic.
Keep hands with Clachan Festival and a two-drop: the tokens carry the early game by themselves.
Mulligan hands that are all four- and five-drops with one land, and hands with all three colors but no cheap creature.
A single red source is not needed early; treat the red cards as late-game removal.



Key interactions and edge cases

Behold costs are optional or payable. Kinsbaile Aspirant reads “behold a Kithkin or pay {2}”, so you never lose tempo when you have no Kithkin. Champion of the Clachan and Celestial Reunion require the Kithkin, so cast them only when you have a token or a spare Kithkin to exile.
Champion of the Clachan exiles a Kithkin and returns it when it leaves. Exiling a token is fine; exiling a real Kithkin gives it back later.
Celestial Reunion puts the card onto the battlefield when the beheld creature is the chosen type, so choosing Kithkin and tutoring Seraphic Steed still nets a free body when the cost is paid with two Kithkin.
Morbid checks “a creature died this turn” at the end step. Chump-block with a token or sacrifice Bulwark Ox on the second main phase to turn it on every turn.
Bulwark Ox’s sacrifice ability gives every creature with a counter hexproof and indestructible, which protects the Ornery Tumblewagg and Needletooth Pack payoffs from a sweeper.



Matchups

Against aggro: the tokens are fine blockers and Slumbering Cerberus comes back every turn after a trade. Osseous Exhale kills an attacker for two mana.
Against control: do not over-extend into a sweeper. Build with Clachan Festival and Abandoned Air Temple, hold a Kithkin in hand for Champion of the Clachan, and win with the flying Gryff.
Against midrange: Molten Exhale plus Brigid’s Command fight a big creature; the token swarm out-sizes most ground boards.

Curve and mana
Average mana value across the 36 nonland cards is 3.44, spread as two mana: 11, three mana: 12, four mana: 5, five mana: 4, six mana: 2, seven mana: 2. The deck plays 24 lands with 14 red, 10 black and 9 green sources, so the early turns are always red or black and green arrives through Wastewood Verge or a Forest. Treasures pay for anything, which is what makes a three-colour deck with a seven-drop castable: Rapacious Dragon and Desolation of Smaug both hand back mana in the same turn they are played.

title: Hoardfire
text:
Early game
Lead with lands and a two-drop that banks a Treasure. Noggle Robber is the best turn-three play when there is nothing on board, because it is a 3/3 that leaves a Treasure behind on either side of the board. Bejeweled Warg wants to attack immediately — trample damage to a player is what turns it into a Treasure. Hold Pinecone Strike and Bilbo’s Deadly Slice for the first threat that would otherwise block Smaug; the deck wins by keeping its attacker’s lane clear, not by trading.

title: Hoardfire
text:
Mid game
Smaug the Magnificent on turn four is the pivot. If he lands with three or more Treasures, the attack is already a third of the opponent’s life total and the upkeep trigger makes the next one larger. From there the hoard is read twice per turn: Smaug’s attack uses it, Smaug, Wicked Worm converts spent Treasure mana into cards. Cast with Treasure mana whenever possible — Wicked Worm’s draw triggers on spent Treasure mana, not on the Treasure being sacrificed, so a spell paid with a Treasure and one land still triggers it.

title: Hoardfire
text:
The combo turn
The kill turn is Smaug the Magnificent plus a hoard of five or more Treasures. Attack, and the trigger deals five-plus damage to any target — face for the win, or a blocker that would otherwise trade. Because the damage is dealt by the attack trigger and not by combat damage, Smaug does not need to connect: an unblocked Smaug, a chump-blocked Smaug and a Smaug attacking into a bigger flyer all deal the same damage. Desert Were-Worm on the following turn is usually lethal, since attacking with 12 or more total power untaps the attackers and grants a second combat phase.

title: Hoardfire
text:
Win condition 2
The Misty Mountains Cold is the independent plan. Chapters one through three add a Treasure each; if you control four or more Treasures when a chapter resolves, the saga sacrifices itself and leaves a 6/6 red Dragon with flying. With two Treasures already banked the saga pays off on its second chapter — turn five on a normal curve — and the card is never dead, because the Treasures it makes are exactly what Smaug and Desolation of Smaug want. Rapacious Dragon and Smaug, the Great Calamity are the air force behind it, and Last Light of Durin’s Day can put a Dragon straight onto the battlefield once six Mountains have entered.

title: Hoardfire
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep any hand with two or three lands, one of them red, and a two- or three-mana Treasure source (Bejeweled Warg, Noggle Robber, Dori, Treasure Dredger or The Sackville-Bagginses). Keep a hand with The Misty Mountains Cold and four lands even if the rest is filler — the saga is a self-contained clock. Ship hands that need both black and green before turn four with only one land of either, and ship one-land hands even with a two-drop, because the deck has no one-mana play. Hobbit Hole is not a mana source: never count it as one of the two lands you need to keep.

title: Hoardfire
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Smaug the Magnificent’s trigger counts Treasures at the moment of attack. Sacrificing Treasures for mana during the attack step shrinks the trigger, so crack them after damage or in the second main phase.
The Misty Mountains Cold checks the Treasure count as each chapter resolves. Order matters if you are playing a Treasure-maker in the same turn: play the maker first, then let the chapter resolve.
Desolation of Smaug deals 3 to each non-Dragon, including your own Bejeweled Warg and Noggle Robber. Cast it after Smaug is out, or accept the trade when your Dragons are still lethal through the air.
Orcrist, Goblin-cleaver’s Treasure count is per creature you control of the chosen type. Naming Rogue or Warrior in a board of Rogues and Warriors is usually more Treasures than naming Dragon.
The Lonely Mountain enters tapped unless an Equipment is on the battlefield, and Orcrist is the only Equipment in the deck — deploy Orcrist before the Mountain if the untapped land matters.
Treasure Dredger, Treasure Dredger and similar activated abilities can be used at instant speed, which means you can hold a Treasure back and activate it in response to a removal spell that targets Smaug, then swing for the larger count.

title: Hoardfire
text:
Matchups
Against aggro, the plan is to trade early and let Smaug’s attack trigger act as removal; Pinecone Strike and Desolation of Smaug carry the mid-game, and The Lonely Mountain’s Dwarf tokens are free blockers. Against midrange, bank Treasures and hold removal for the turn Smaug attacks — a five-Treasure trigger plus a 4/3 flyer ends games in two swings. Against control, lead with The Sackville-Bagginses and Treasure Dredger to force interaction, keep Smaug for a turn where the opponent is tapped out, and remember that the saga and Rapacious Dragon are a second, independent clock that does not need the commander-style payoff to survive.

Galion, Elvenking’s Butler adds a free 4/4: on attack, the smallest Elf’s base power and toughness become Galion’s 4/4 until end of turn, which turns a 1/1 landfall token into a 4/4 attacker with no additional investment.
The third route is the win-condition land itself: Restless Vinestalk becomes a 5/5 green and blue Plant with trample for {3}{G}{U} and stays a land, so it is a threat that survives creature sweepers, and its attack trigger sets up a trade by making another creature’s base power and toughness 3/3. Between Pathmaker, Vinestalk, Galion’s copies, Thranduil’s Company counters and The Arkenstone’s team anthem, the deck has lethal combat damage available in any game where the drain plan is one Elf short.

title: Evergreen Requiem
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep any hand with two to four lands plus a two- or three-drop Elf, and keep a hand with one of Thranduil, the Elvenking or Thranduil’s Company plus a green source and a black or blue source. Ship hands with fewer than two lands, hands with no green source (the deck’s mana base leans green: sixteen of twenty-four lands produce green), and five-land hands where the only spells cost four or more — the deck needs landfall triggers, not a flooded draw. A two-land hand with Silvan Rally or Down in the Valley is a keep: both find the third and fourth land.

title: Evergreen Requiem
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Thranduil copies activated abilities only. Elvenking’s Harper’s unblockable ability, Llanowar Elves’ mana ability, Woodland Weavemaster’s scaling mana ability, Elrond’s blink and Lathril’s drain all count; Down in the Valley and The Arkenstone are not Elf cards and grant nothing.
The drain ability’s cost is tapping ten untapped Elves, not sacrificing them. An Elf with vigilance, or one that has already attacked without tapping (Thranduil’s Company grants vigilance), can be used for the drain in the same turn it attacked.
Thranduil, Sindarin Liege and Thranduil, the Elvenking are both legendary; the extra copies are not dead, because discarding a duplicate legendary Elf is exactly the graveyard-filling play the deck wants.
Silvan Reveler’s landfall trigger returns it from the graveyard to your hand for {1}{G}{U}, which is a repeatable body and a repeatable loot if you have the mana; it is the deck’s most resilient engine piece.
Mirkwood Nurturer returns a permanent you control to its hand — target your own land or a Silvan Reveler, then replay it for a landfall trigger. Do not target the permanent you are about to sacrifice to Elvenking’s Halls in the same turn.
Elven Passage’s behold clause lets you untap the fetched land if you control or reveal an Elf, which is the difference between a two-mana turn and a full turn; hold it until you have an Elf in hand or in play.
Dreamroot Cascade and Deathcap Glade enter untapped only if you already control two or more other lands, so play basics and Watery Grave first and let the check lands follow.
The Arkenstone’s end step draw is a free card every turn, and it makes the whole team +1/+1 — with ten Elves it is also ten extra power on the drain turn’s follow-up attack.
Confusticate and Bebother’s discard half is a real engine play, not just a fallback: discarding Lathril, Elrond or a duplicate legendary Elf is often better than drawing two.
Menace on Lathril means it cannot be blocked by a single creature, which matters for the token plan but not for the drain; keep Lathril attacking only when the tokens are worth more than the drain turn’s timing.

title: Bedrock Uprising
text:
Overview
Earthbend animates one of your own lands: it becomes a 0/0 land creature with haste, gets N +1/+1 counters, and when it dies or is exiled it returns to the battlefield tapped. That last clause is the whole deck. Every earthbend is a permanent threat that cannot be traded away permanently — the land comes back, and because it is still a land it also keeps tapping for mana.
Bedrock Uprising is built so that a single earthbend feeds three separate payoffs. Toph, the Blind Bandit sizes her power off the total +1/+1 counters on your lands, so every animated Forest makes her bigger whether she is on the board or not. Wildwood Scourge and Knight of Wundagore each grow a counter whenever counters land on another creature you control, which means they grow off every earthbend in the deck, including the ones from Ba Sing Se and Rockalanche. And Dai Li Agents converts the resulting board of counter-carrying land creatures straight into life loss for the opponent, so the deck does not need to connect with every attacker to close a game.
Nothing in the deck asks for a rare dual-land package. Great Divide Guide gives every land and every Ally you control the ability to tap for any color, which turns the eight Forests, three Swamps and two Mountains into a functional three-color mana base, and Ba Sing Se plus Crawling Barrens do double duty as both mana and win conditions.

Black is a light splash for Fatal Fissure and the two black-green finishers, red is a lighter splash for Bitter Work and Savage Mansion. Great Divide Guide upgrades all of it, so do not be shy about leading on a Forest and following with a Guide.

title: Bedrock Uprising
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Lead with a two-drop. Haru, Hidden Talent is the best turn-two because every Ally afterwards (Toph, Earth Kingdom General, Great Divide Guide) triggers him for a free animated land. Great Divide Guide is the right play when your hand is colour-hungry or when you want the Ally trigger plus fixing in one card. Wildwood Scourge on one is a fine investment: it starts as a 1/1 and never stops growing, since every earthbend in the deck puts counters on another creature you control.


Mid game and the burst turn
The deck’s big turn is a turn where you stack two or more earthbends. Rockalanche and Earthbending Lesson both put four-plus counters on a single land, Toph adds two when she lands, and Ba Sing Se can add two more on the same turn as a sorcery. Because animated lands have haste, a turn that starts with four mana can end with a fresh 4/4 and a 6/6 swinging at the opponent. Do not spread earthbends across turns for value when you can concentrate them: Toph counts total counters on lands, so a single enormous land creature is worth more than three small ones, and Dai Li Agents counts creatures with counters on them, so three of them is worth more when you attack.


Win condition 2
Dai Li Agents is the deck’s non-combat kill. Whenever it attacks, each opponent loses X life and you gain X life, where X is the number of creatures you control with +1/+1 counters. Animated lands are creatures with +1/+1 counters, so a Ba Sing Se activation plus Toph plus one dormant Crawling Barrens can push X to four or five. Unlike Toph, Dai Li Agents does not need toughness or evasion, so it is the answer against decks that gum up the ground.


Mulligan guide
Keep any two-land hand with a two-drop and a three-drop. Keep hands with Great Divide Guide plus a colour-hungry spell package, because the Guide fixes everything. Go to six on one-land hands and on hands with no earthbend source at all. Never keep a hand that is only payoffs: Toph, Wildwood Scourge and Knight of Wundagore are all blank without an earthbend to feed them, so a hand of three payoffs and no engine is a mulligan even at seven cards.


Key interactions and edge cases
Animated land creatures keep their land type, so they still tap for mana, still count as lands for Toph, and still return tapped when they die instead of going to the graveyard. Do not be afraid to attack a 4/4 land into a bigger blocker if the trade sets up Beifong’s Bounty Hunters, which earthbends for the dead creature’s power. Inspiring Call draws a card for each creature with a +1/+1 counter and makes them indestructible, which is the cleanest way to protect a board of animated lands from a sweeper; remember that it counts land creatures too. Fatal Fissure is not a removal spell that earthbends later, it is an earthbend spell that also removes something: cast it on the creature you intend to kill this turn, then finish the job and take four counters. Ba Sing Se enters tapped unless you control a basic land, so it is a fine turn-one play only if you already know you want the green.


Matchups
Against aggro, Earth Kingdom General’s lifegain and Inspiring Call’s indestructible mode are the key cards; trade animated lands early and let the lands come back. Against control, hold Inspiring Call for their sweeper, and lean on Crawling Barrens and Ba Sing Se, which rebuild the board from lands rather than from the hand. Against other midrange decks, Dai Li Agents is the trump: it does not need to connect, and the drain races any ground stall. Explosive combo decks are the worst matchup; the deck has two removal spells and no counterspells, so the plan is to race with hasty lands and use Fatal Fissure to break up the combo turn.

title: Teeming Presence

Early game
Turns one to three are about mana that also builds a board. Simulacrum Shaper is the best turn-two play: it ramps, it blocks, and it replaces itself. Greenhouse Propagator is the follow-up, because it both taps for {G} and starts the life total that Germinate Recruits converts into Cadets. Do not trade Simulacrum Shaper for nothing. Its death trigger is the deck’s cheapest card draw, and chumping with it is often better than chumping with a token that Loot counts.

title: Teeming Presence

Mid game
The mid game is the creature count. Six creatures is the number to aim at, because six is where every three-drop and four-drop in hand becomes free. Jiang Yanggu puts two bodies on the board at once (and Mowu is a third distinct power for Loot), Germinate Recruits turns a Propagator-heavy board into three or four Cadets at instant speed, and Garruk’s -3 adds a 4/4 Beast that also draws a card off his static ability.
Garruk’s +2 is easy to underrate: untapping two lands with Loot in play is a second Loot activation, and untapping two lands with eight lands in play is half a turn of mana.

title: Teeming Presence
text:
The combo turn
Omnipresence is the turn the deck stops paying for spells:

Resolve Omnipresence with six or more creatures on the board. Check the count first: the free-cast clause uses the creature count at the moment you cast, not at the moment the enchantment resolved.
Cast everything in hand with mana value at or below that count, in the order that grows the board: Germinate Recruits and Jiang Yanggu first (more creatures), then Garruk, then Verdant Kraken.
Verdant Kraken makes a 3/3 Forest Tentacle at the beginning of each player’s upkeep, so the count grows on your opponent’s turn as well.
At seven or more creatures, Face Yourself is free. Target yourself: you get a hasty token copy of every creature you control, including the copies’ own power, and the whole board attacks.
With Garruk on the battlefield the copies are not sacrificed at the end step, because Face Yourself only demands a planeswalker. Without him they still attack once, which is usually enough.

Two Face Yourselfs in one turn is the ceiling: the first copy doubles the board, the second copies the doubled board.

Win condition 2
Emrakul is the second finish and it does not need Omnipresence. The card’s own exile ability costs {3}: exile it from hand, target a land, and that land taps for {C}{C} until Emrakul is cast from exile. On a 26-land manabase that is a two-mana land on turn four, which is the difference between a turn eight Emrakul and a turn eleven one. When it resolves, the cast trigger untaps every land you control, so the second main phase is fully funded.
Ghalta the Unstoppable is the cheaper version of the same plan: at 8 power on the board it costs {G}, and it gives every other creature trample, which is what makes a board of Cadets lethal through blockers.
Hall of Echoes is the third conversion. Five mana and the land becomes a copy of your best creature until end of turn, with the legend rule suspended, so it copies Emrakul next to the real Emrakul, or copies Verdant Kraken to double the token production. It taps for {C}, so it never pays a green pip; treat it as a spell that happens to be a land.

Mulligan guide
Keep: three or four lands with Simulacrum Shaper or Greenhouse Propagator; hands with Loot, the Nexus plus two cheap creatures (Loot is the deck’s mana); hands with Pia, Aether Ascetic and at least one enchantment payoff to find.
Mulligan: two-land hands where one land is Hall of Echoes or Roiling Canopy (both are effectively a land behind); hands with no green source; hands that are all five-drops and above with no ramp.
The deck mulligans more aggressively than a midrange deck because it needs both halves: a ramp creature and something to ramp into. A six-card hand with three lands, a Shaper and two payoffs is better than a seven-card hand of lands and expensive spells.

title: Teeming Presence
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Omnipresence only covers spells cast from hand. Flashback, adventure and graveyard casts are not free.
Casting for free means paying nothing, so an X spell cast off Omnipresence has X equal to zero. Germinate Recruits is therefore the one card in the deck that must be cast for its own {2}{W} before Omnipresence lands, not after.
Face Yourself copies are sacrificed at the beginning of the end step if you don’t control a planeswalker. Garruk is the only planeswalker in the deck, and he is worth holding until after the swing for exactly that reason.
Loot, the Nexus counts distinct power values, not creatures. Two 2/2 Cadets add one mana, not two; a 2/1 Loot, a 3/3 Mowu, a 4/4 Beast, a 6/6 Kraken and an 8/8 Ghalta add five.
Garruk’s static ability draws on creatures with power 4 or greater entering, which includes Face Yourself copies of Kraken, Invigorator, Ghalta and Emrakul.
Hexhaven Invigorator’s trigger is damage, not combat damage. A sweeper that deals three to it fetches three lands.
Roiling Canopy enters tapped and needs five other Forests to pump, so it is a late-game land, never a keep.
Hall of Echoes and Roiling Canopy both produce colourless or green only; the deck’s white and red cards are almost always cast for free.

title: Lifespark
text:
Overview
Lifespark fuses two build-around mechanics: Prowess (creatures grow whenever you cast a noncreature spell) and Infusion (Tarkir Dragonstorm bonuses that activate “if you gained life this turn”). The deck is a spell-slinger engine: gain a little life, then ride a chain of cheap instants and sorceries that pump every creature on the board while arming your Infusion payoffs.
The engine is Bria, Riptide Rogue: she grants prowess to every other creature you control, so even tokens, mana dorks, and animated manlands grow with each spell, and every noncreature spell also makes one of your creatures unblockable. Firebending Student turns power into red mana on attack, letting a big turn snowball: pump, attack for mana, cast more spells, pump again. Sokka, Tenacious Tactician turns each noncreature spell into a 1/1 Ally that itself has prowess, doubling the swarm. Life gain (gainlands, Lightning Helix, lifelink, Luminollusk) arms the green Infusion suite: Efflorescence becomes a +2/+2 trample-and-indestructible pump, and Lumaret’s Favor copies itself.

Eleven lands produce colored mana untapped early (checklands), six gainlands trade a tapped entry for the life gain that fuels the mechanic, and four basics support the singleton splash colors. Red and blue are the core; green supplies Infusion; white is a light splash for Sokka, Thor, Stoat, and Helix.

title: Lifespark
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Play a two-drop prowess creature on turn two (Emberheart Challenger, Firebending Student, Stormcatch Mentor, or Brightblade Stoat) or a gainland to pre-arm Infusion. Hold Lightning Strike for blockers or planeswalkers. If you have a gainland, sequence it before your first spell so Efflorescence and Lumaret’s Favor are infused.


Mid game
Resolve Bria as early as possible; she is the force multiplier. After that, every noncreature spell grows the entire team, so even a Lightning Helix pointed at a blocker grows your attackers. Sokka and Queen Brahne convert spells into board presence: Sokka’s Ally tokens have prowess twice over (Sokka’s aura plus Bria), and Brahne’s Wizards deal 1 to each opponent per spell, which doubles as reach.


The combo turn
With Bria and Firebending Student on board: attack with Student, adding red mana equal to its power (already boosted by previous spells). Use that mana plus Stormcatch Mentor’s discount to cast a chain of pump and burn spells. Each spell triggers every prowess creature, growing Student for more mana and making a creature unblockable via Bria. Finish by animating Restless Ridgeline (itself a prowess creature under Bria) and attacking with unblockable, infused, indestructible creatures.


Win condition 2: burn reach
When the board stalls, convert it into damage: sacrifice a prowess-pumped Heartfire Immolator for damage equal to its power; chain Lightning Strike and Lightning Helix (discounted by Mentor); let Queen Brahne tokens ping each opponent every time you cast a spell. Lightning Helix doubles as the life gain that keeps Infusion armed while burning.


Mulligan guide
Keep any hand with two to three lands (at least one red source and one blue or green source) and a two-drop prowess creature or Bria. Mulligan hands with four or more lands, no creatures, or no way to reach three mana by turn three. Bria plus any two spells is a strong keep.


Key interactions and edge cases

Infusion checks “if you gained life this turn” at resolution, so any life gain earlier in the turn works, including a gainland played that same turn.
Bria’s unblockable ability targets a creature each time you cast a noncreature spell; multiple spells can make multiple creatures unblockable.
Efflorescence’s indestructible saves a creature from the damage of your own Lightning Strike or from blockers, but not from sacrifice effects.
Firebending Student’s mana expires at end of combat; spend it in the second main phase.
Comforting Counsel counts every life gain event, including lifelink damage and each gainland.



Matchups

Aggro: The lifegain package (Stoat, Helix, Luminollusk, gainlands) buys time; infused Efflorescence creates an indestructible blocker; Withering-Curse-style sweeps are not needed if you race.
Control: Cavern of Souls protects Bria and Thor from counterspells; Emberheart Challenger and Mentor apply early pressure; Bria’s unblockable ability punches through removal-heavy boards.
Midrange: The combo turn outgrows most midrange boards; keep Lightning Strike for their must-answer creature and win the race.

title: Ride the Rot
text:
Curve and mana
24 lands: 4 Forest, 3 Swamp, 2 Island, 4 Deathcap Glade, 2 Hedge Maze, 1 Undercity Sewers, and the utility package of 2 Restless Cottage, 2 Fountainport, 2 Rogue's Passage and 2 Bucolic Ranch.
The mana is deliberately green-first because thirteen of the deck’s twenty-two creatures cost green, black is the second requirement (Bloodghast’s double black on turn two, The Gitrog at five), and blue is a light splash for Archmage's Newt. The split is 14 green sources, 10 black sources and 6 blue sources counting the lands that make both. Molt Tender and Bucolic Ranch smooth the rest: the Tender exiles a graveyard card for any colour, and the Ranch pays for Mounts in any colour.
The nonland curve is 8 ones, 20 twos, 6 threes and 2 fives — an average nonland mana value of 2.11. Fourteen cards cost one or two mana and do something the engine wants, so the deck is functional with two lands and dangerous with four.

title: Ride the Rot
text:
Early game (turns 1 to 3)

Turn 1: Scavenger's Talent if you expect a grind, otherwise Molt Tender to mill and fix. Both cost one.
Turn 2: Stubborn Burrowfiend is the default; Venomsac Lagac is the better choice against an aggressive start because deathtouch plus +0/+3 while saddled blocks almost anything. Bloodghast is fine when you have a land in hand to bring it back.
Turn 3: Drover Grizzly, or hold up Corrupted Conviction and sacrifice something the opponent spent a removal spell on anyway. Sacrificing a body you were going to lose is the deck’s cheapest card advantage.
Start saddling as soon as you have two power available: Stubborn Burrowfiend’s saddled trigger mills two cards, and every one of those cards is either graveyard fuel for itself, reanimation material for Squirming Emergence, or a Plant token from Insidious Roots.

title: Ride the Rot
text:
Mid game (turns 4 to 6)

Sequence Scavenger's Talent levels before committing bodies. At level 2 every sacrifice mills someone two cards; at level 3 the end step starts returning creatures.
Squirming Emergence at three mana almost always has a legal target: by turn four your yard typically holds four or more permanent cards from mills, trades and sacrifices. Getting back Stubborn Burrowfiend or Drover Grizzly restarts the whole engine.
Insidious Roots turns every Bloodghast return into a Plant token and a +1/+1 counter on every Plant you already have. A stalled board of Plants is still a growing board, and the Plants tap for any colour to keep paying costs.
Worthy Cost is your answer to anything that outclasses your board, and it is at its best when the sacrificed creature was going to be reanimated or was a token.

title: Ride the Rot
text:
The combo turn

Have a big body. Stubborn Burrowfiend after two saddled attacks with a stocked yard is usually 6/6 or larger; Bloodghast and Plants can also saddle.
Cast The Gitrog, Ravenous Ride. It has haste, so it can attack the turn it lands.
Saddle it with the biggest creature (Saddle 1 only needs one power, so any body qualifies).
Before combat, activate Rogue's Passage if a blocker would stop the 6/5 — trample usually gets there, but unblockable guarantees the trigger. Drover Grizzly is the cheaper option: saddle the Grizzly first and the whole team has trample.
Gitrog deals combat damage, you sacrifice the creature that saddled it, and you draw X cards and put up to X lands from your hand onto the battlefield tapped, where X is that creature’s power.
Each of those lands triggers Bloodghast out of the graveyard, triggers Insidious Roots, and untaps nothing — so plan the order: resolve landfall first, then use the returned bodies to saddle again next turn.
Rebuy The Gitrog with Squirming Emergence (five mana value, so you need five permanent cards in the yard) and do it again.

title: Ride the Rot
section: Win condition 2: the Scavenger’s Talent loop
text:
Win condition 2: the Scavenger’s Talent loop
Scavenger's Talent at level 3 reads: at the beginning of your end step you may sacrifice three other nonland permanents, and if you do, return a creature card from your graveyard to the battlefield with a finality counter on it. The deck feeds that cost without spending real cards — Food tokens from Vinereap Mentor and from Talent’s own level 1 trigger, Map tokens from Fanatical Offering, Plants from Insidious Roots, and returned Bloodghasts. Level 2’s mill keeps filling the yard that Squirming Emergence and the Talent both draw from. You trade a handful of trinkets each turn for one real creature, and the trinkets regenerate from the deaths, the sacrifices and the landfalls.

title: Ride the Rot
text:
Mulligan guide

Keep: two or three lands with green plus one of black or blue, at least one sacrifice outlet or graveyard filler, and a two-drop that saddles.
Keep aggressively: any hand with Stubborn Burrowfiend and a mill source, because the Burrowfiend is both the engine and a clock.
Trim: one-land hands, hands with no green source, and five-land hands without a two-drop.
The deck is fine discarding or sacrificing its own cards; card quality matters far more than card count, so do not keep a hand just because it has seven cards.

title: Ride the Rot
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Saddle is a sorcery-speed activation and tapping is the cost. Tapping a Bloodghast to saddle does not remove its landfall trigger — the trigger only cares about the land entering, so a saddled and tapped Bloodghast still returns the next time a land drops.
Stubborn Burrowfiend triggers only on the first time it becomes saddled each turn, but it can be saddled again for combat and combat only cares that it is saddled at the moment it attacks.
Saddle 2 and Saddle 3 are power-based, not creature-count-based. One 3-power creature saddles Saddle 3 by itself; three 1-power Plants do it too.
The Gitrog sacrifices a creature that saddled it this turn — not any creature. If you saddle it with a token and then sacrifice that token, the draw is small. Saddle it with the Burrowfiend if you want the big draw.
Gitrog puts lands from your hand onto the battlefield tapped. If your hand has no lands, the ride only draws. Keep lands in hand when a ride is coming.
Squirming Emergence needs permanent cards in the graveyard, not cards. Milled instants and sorceries do not count, which is why Molt Tender’s exile-for-mana ability is worth using on a spare sorcery.
Insidious Roots triggers on creature cards leaving the graveyard, in either direction. A reanimated creature counts; so does one exiled by Molt Tender.
Archmage's Newt gives flashback to instants and sorceries, and flashback {0} while it is saddled. With a Newt saddled, a Fanatical Offering or Corrupted Conviction in the graveyard can be recast for free, which is another two cards and another sacrifice.
Restless Cottage exiles a card from any graveyard when it attacks. Use it on an opponent’s reanimation target or on your own key card if an opponent is exiling your yard.
Finality counters matter. Creatures returned by Scavenger's Talent cannot be returned again after they die, so reanimate a body you intend to keep, not one you intend to sacrifice.

title: Ride the Rot
text:
Matchups

Aggro: Venomsac Lagac’s deathtouch and +0/+3 while saddled is the wall, Restless Cottage’s Foods buy life, and Worthy Cost removes the biggest threat for one mana plus a spare body. Trade early and let the graveyard grow from the trades.
Control: the deck is resilient because nothing important stays dead. Bloodghast and Squirming Emergence ignore a single sweeper, Restless Cottage attacks under sorcery-speed removal, and Fountainport plus Fanatical Offering keep the hand full. Do not over-commit into a wipe; hold one reanimation in hand.
Graveyard hate: the deck’s one soft spot. Against exile effects, lean on the board instead: the Mounts are still real creatures, Drover Grizzly still gives trample, and Scavenger's Talent still makes Foods. Keep a Worthy Cost for their hate permanent.
Ramp and midrange: go under them with saddled Mounts. Drover Grizzly plus Stubborn Burrowfiend is often ten trample damage by turn five, and Rogue's Passage removes the blocker that would have saved them.
Mirror: whoever saddles first usually wins the race. Hold Worthy Cost for their Burrowfiend rather than using it on a token.

Turn 3: Start the sacrifice loop. Feed a milled creature or a Robot token to the Cauldron, then cast the Void card you have been holding — Hymn of the Faller, Decode Transmissions or Elegy Acolyte. Order matters: sacrifice first, cast second.

Lich-Knights' Conquest is the biggest turn available: sacrifice Food, Clue and Robot tokens plus any spare creatures, then put that many creature cards back onto the battlefield. Return Elegy Acolyte and Seedship Broodtender first when the sacrifice outlets are already down.

Confirm an outlet is untapped: Cauldron of Essence or Vampiric Rites.

Cast the plotted payload for free — Rise of the Varmints for a Varmint for every creature card in your graveyard, or Pitiless Carnage to sacrifice the whole board and redraw it.
If the board is real, attack with Alpharael, Stonechosen to halve the defending player’s life. Use Rogue's Passage ({4}, tap) to make it unblockable when the ground is clogged.
Repeat next turn. Void triggers are checked at end step, so the sacrifice only has to happen once per turn cycle to keep the Robots and the growth coming.

Cauldron of Essence drains each opponent for 1 every time a creature you control dies, and the deck generates disposable bodies deliberately — Robot tokens from Elegy Acolyte, Food from Restless Cottage, Clues from Tolls of War, Allies from Tolls of War’s sacrifice trigger, and Varmints from Rise of the Varmints. Sacrifice them for value and the drain adds up without ever attacking. Treacherous Greed adds a six-point life swing plus three cards, and Decode Transmissions drains 2 from each opponent while replacing itself. Against a deck that can block forever, this is the real clock.

Mulligan guide

Keep: two or three lands with a green or black source plus a two-mana engine piece (Cauldron of Essence, Seedship Broodtender) or a sacrifice outlet, and at least one card that does something with the graveyard.
Keep on five or six: any hand with Cauldron of Essence plus two lands. The engine is redundant enough to run on a small hand.
Trim: one-land hands; hands with no black or green source; hands that are all five-drops (Alpharael, Stonechosen, Lich-Knights' Conquest) with no early engine.
Plot cards make mediocre hands keepable. If you can plot on turn two and three, the hand is effectively cheaper than it looks.

title: Plot Hole

Key interactions and edge cases

Void checks once, at end step. The trigger condition is “a nonland permanent left the battlefield this turn or a spell was warped this turn”. A single sacrifice enables every Void card in the same turn, so batch your plays.
Cauldron of Essence reanimation is sorcery speed. Sacrifice first, then activate the Cauldron before your combat step if you want the returned creature to attack.
Pitiless Carnage counts permanents, not creatures. Sacrifice lands in a flood and you still draw the cards; there is no requirement that the permanents be creatures.
Lich-Knights’ Conquest wants artifacts and enchantments too. Food from Restless Cottage, Clues from Tolls of War, and the Robots from Elegy Acolyte are all valid fodder, and they return creature cards from the graveyard one for one.
Rise of the Varmints counts creature cards only. Noncreature mill (instants, sorceries) does nothing for it; prioritise creature-heavy milling when you are setting up the swarm.
Restless Cottage exiles a graveyard card on attack. It says “up to one”, so decline it — your own graveyard is the resource Rise of the Varmints measures.
Treacherous Greed needs a creature that dealt damage this turn. Attack first, then cast it in the post-combat main phase.
Tolls of War triggers once per turn. One sacrifice per turn keeps the Ally tokens coming; extra sacrifices still drain through the Cauldron.

Aggro: the Cauldron’s drain and Elegy Acolyte’s lifelink make races winnable. Tragic Trajectory at -10/-10 is a one-mana answer to any threat the turn after you sacrifice something. Trade Robot tokens freely; they come back.
Control: plot the payoffs, then cast them on a turn the opponent taps out for a sweeper. Lich-Knights' Conquest rebuilds from the graveyard after a wipe, and Slickshot Lockpicker giving flashback to a discarded Pitiless Carnage turns a dead card into a restock.
Graveyard hate: the deck is soft to heavy exile, but every threat has a non-graveyard path. Alpharael, Stonechosen halves a life total with an empty yard, and the drain plan is entirely board-based.
Other midrange: the deck wins long games. Cauldron of Essence is a free engine that never stops draining, and Rise of the Varmints gets bigger every turn the game goes on.

Mid game and the combo turn
The combo turn is any turn where you have a Valiant creature, two or more blink effects and enough mana to use them. The correct order:

Target the Valiant creature with the cheapest blink (Daydream first, since flashback makes it two uses).
The creature returns as a new object with a +1/+1 counter and its Valiant is “fresh” again.
Target the same creature with the next blink. Valiant triggers a second time this turn.
If Kykar, Zephyr Awakener is out, each of those spells also triggers Kykar, which blinks a second creature - a third and fourth Valiant trigger.
With Abuelo, Ancestral Echo, convert leftover mana {1}{W}{U} into another blink each turn without spending a card.

That sequence is why the deck can chain: Seedglaive Mentor gains two or three counters in one turn, Emberheart Challenger exiles two or three cards to play, and Whiskerquill Scribe filters into the next enabler.

title: Target Practice
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Blink resets Valiant. Valiant reads “for the first time each turn” per object. A blinked creature is a new object, so a second blink in the same turn triggers it again. This is the deck’s core loop and the reason to fire blink spells at already-targeted creatures.
Blink your own creature in response to removal. Personify, Getaway Glamer and Abuelo all exile and return, which blanks a kill spell and still produces the Valiant trigger.
Go Ninja Go and Getaway Glamer are modal, not dead. Their damage and destroy modes answer a blocker without spending a blink.
Torch the Tower bargains with a token. Personify’s shapeshifter, a Kykar Spirit, or a Flowerfoot offspring token pays the bargain cost for the extra damage and scry.
Ennis, Debate Moderator blinks on entry and grows at end of turn if anything was exiled that turn, which the entire deck does. Blinking Ennis is a repeatable source of +1/+1 counters.
Cragflame’s equip is a Valiant trigger. Equipping is an ability you control that targets, so the Mentor can grow during your precombat main phase before attacking.
Whiskervale Forerunner only puts the creature onto the battlefield on your turn. On an opponent’s turn the trigger still digs, but the creature goes to hand.
Abuelo returns at the beginning of the next end step - the creature is gone for the whole combat, so do not blink an attacker you need this turn.

Aggro: you are faster on the play and your blinks blank their removal. Block with the Mentor, blink it, and let Arabella’s lifegain swing the race. Bring in the Torch the Tower count.
Control: do not overextend into sweepers. Hold one Valiant creature and one blink, force them to spend removal, then rebuild with Personify. Emberheart Challenger and Whiskerquill Scribe are your card advantage engines, so protect them and let Restless lands chip in.
Midrange: the Mentor plus Cragflame plus Rogue’s Passage line is the answer - they cannot block it and cannot race a giant with vigilance. Trade early creatures for tempo, then commit to the voltron turn.
Ramp: race. Arabella’s drain does not care about their board, and Go Ninja Go’s damage mode clears a mana dork without spending a blink.

Pizza Face, Gastromancer animates non-creature artifacts into 0/0 Mutants, so animate a Food or a Map you were never going to sacrifice.

title: Terracotta Charge
text:
Overview
Earthbend animates one of your own lands: it becomes a 0/0 land creature with haste, it receives N +1/+1 counters, and if it dies or is exiled the land returns to the battlefield tapped. Because the permanent is still a land, it keeps tapping for mana, it keeps counting for landfall, and it never truly leaves. That is the engine half of this deck.
The other half is the attack step. Terracotta Charge is built so that every earthbend is also an attacker, and every attacker is also a payoff. Earthbend is a sorcery-speed threat only in the sense that you cast the spell — the land arrives with haste, so the turn you animate it is the turn it hits. From there the deck stacks attack triggers: Bumi, Unleashed untaps all your lands on combat damage and gives you a second combat phase in which only land creatures may attack, which is the same as saying “swing with the entire earthbent board again”. The Earth King converts any attack by a power-4-or-greater creature into a stack of basic lands entering tapped, which is mana, landfall and fresh earthbend targets in one trigger. Earth Rumble Wrestlers gets +1/+0 and trample simply for controlling a land creature or having played a land this turn, which in this deck is always true.
The fusion is the point: attack payoffs here do not want normal creatures, they want lands that are creatures. The deck therefore gets to run a land count worthy of a midrange deck, a creature count worthy of aggro, and a wipe-resistant threat base: sweepers that kill the animated lands return those lands to play tapped, ready to be animated again.
