title: Terracotta Charge
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Two-drops first. Rebellious Captives is the cleanest turn two: a 2/2 Ally that later, with six mana spare, turns into two +1/+1 counters plus an earthbend 2. Earth King’s Lieutenant is the better card when you have more Allies behind it — it arrives, hands a counter to each other Ally, and grows a counter of its own every time another Ally appears, so Suki’s tokens and the Captives keep growing it. Keep Origin of Metalbending in hand until it does something: the destroy mode answers an equipment or enchantment, and the counter-plus-indestructible mode is how a 4/4 land creature survives a fight it should lose.


Midgame and the combo turn
The burst turn is any turn where two earthbends point at the same land. Earthbend sets the land’s base to 0/0 and then adds counters, so repeated earthbends stack on one permanent: a land that gets earthbend 2 from Earthbender Ascension, then earthbend 4 from Earthbending Lesson, is an 8/8 that attacked the moment each spell resolved. With Toph, Hardheaded Teacher in play, every spell you cast afterwards adds another counter to a land for free, so a sequence like Captives, Origin of Metalbending, Earthbending Lesson can hand out three separate animations on one turn. Then attack, and let Bumi, Unleashed start the second combat: Bumi untaps all lands when it connects, and the extra phase only allows land creatures, which is exactly the board you have built.


Win condition 2
Dai Li Agents is the non-combat kill. Whenever it attacks, each opponent loses X life and you gain X, where X is the number of creatures you control with +1/+1 counters. In this deck that is nearly the whole board, because animated lands carry counters and the Ally line piles counters onto itself. A typical board of an animated land, an earthbent Ba Sing Se creature, a Lieutenant and a Suki token is X = 4, and Bumi’s extra combat doubles it in one turn. Against a ground stall the drain does not care about blockers at all.


Mulligan guide
Keep any hand with two or three lands and a creature or an earthbend source. Keep hands that contain Earthbender Ascension: it is the only card that both animates a land and finds a land, so it fixes the deck’s two failure modes at once. Go to six on one-land hands, on hands with no two-drop, and on hands that are only payoffs (The Earth King, Ouroboroid and Badgermole do nothing without either a land creature or a power-4 attacker). Never keep a hand whose only green source is Fabled Passage plus a Ba Sing Se that will enter tapped.


Key interactions and edge cases
An earthbent land is a land in every zone: it still taps for mana while it is a creature, it triggers landfall when it enters or returns, and it triggers Suki, Courageous Rescuer when it dies during your turn, because “leaves the battlefield” is satisfied before the land comes back tapped. Earthbend targets a land you control, not a land that must be untapped, so Ba Sing Se can animate a Forest you already tapped for mana that turn — the new creature has haste and can attack immediately. The Earth King’s trigger looks at creatures with power 4 or greater that are attacking, so it counts the Bear token, Bumi, Badgermole, Earth Rumble Wrestlers with its land-creature bonus, and any land carrying four or more counters; the lands it finds arrive tapped, which does not stop them from being attacked with next turn or animated the same turn by a spell. Restless Bivouac’s counter trigger happens when it attacks, so it grows another attacker even in Bumi’s land-only second combat. Ouroboroid’s trigger is a beginning-of-combat counter placement, which means it also grows animated lands and the game’s mana base if those lands are creatures.


Matchups
Against aggro, the deck races well but wants to trade animated lands early: they come back tapped, so a chump block costs tempo rather than a card. Origin of Metalbending’s indestructible mode and Suki’s token generation are the stabilisers, and Dai Li Agents’ lifegain swing is the race-flipper. Against control, the important resource is the land count, not the hand: Ba Sing Se, Restless Bivouac and Earthbender Ascension rebuild after a sweeper, and the earthbent lands return to play tapped, so a wipe usually leaves you with mana and a fresh animation on the next turn. Against other midrange decks, The Earth King is the trump: attacking with two power-4 creatures fetches two lands a turn, which both ramps and arms the next wave of animates. Against fast combo, the deck has almost no interaction beyond Origin of Metalbending’s artifact and enchantment mode, so the plan is to race with haste land creatures and aim the second combat phase at the combo turn.

Curve and mana
Twenty-four lands: 18 basics (6 Forest, 5 Plains, 4 Mountain, 2 Swamp, 1 Island), 2 Great Divide Guide-fuelled utility lands (Jasmine Dragon Tea Shop, Ba Sing Se) and 2 Rogue’s Passage. Thirty-six nonlands — 2 one-drops, 15 twos, 9 threes, 6 fours, 4 fives — average mana value 2.86.
Five colors on a basics manabase sounds greedy, and it would be without Great Divide Guide: two copies make every land in the deck produce any color, so the basic count is a curve decision rather than a color decision. Green is deepest (Haru, the Guide, the Ascension, Elfsworn Giant, The Boulder), white carries the token half, red carries the landfall burn, and black and blue are single-card splashes: Dai Li Agents, Embalmed Ascendant, Far Fortune, End Boss and Glitch Ghost Surveyor. Jasmine Dragon Tea Shop casts every Ally in the deck and makes tokens late; Ba Sing Se earthbends on its own.

Early game (turns 1-3)

Turn 1: Earth Kingdom Protectors or hold up Invasion Reinforcements’ flash. A one-mana Ally is a one-mana earthbend once Haru is down.
Turn 2: Haru, Hidden Talent first, then keep chaining Allies. Sabotender, Walking Sarcophagus and Rebellious Captives are the other two-drops; Sabotender starts the clock the opponent cannot answer.
Turn 3: Tannuk, Memorial Ensign or Earthbender Ascension. Ascension fetches a basic tapped, which both fixes your colors and adds one more landfall trigger.
Earthbend targets basics early. Land creatures with a single counter are fragile, so keep them back as blockers until they can trade or attack profitably.

Deploy wide: Kyoshi Warriors, The Boulder, Ready to Rumble and Dai Li Agents. Dai Li Agents earthbends twice on entry, which usually converts two spare lands into 1/1 and 2/2 creatures with counters.
Watch the second Tannuk trigger. Two land entries in one turn (an earthbend return, an Ascension fetch, a Ba Sing Se activation) turns Tannuk into a card engine.
Attack with the land creatures before combat tricks matter. They have haste, they count for Dai Li Agents’ drain, and if they die they return tapped — which is exactly what the landfall cards want.
Great Divide Guide converts the manabase the moment it lands: from then on every land and every Ally taps for any color, so the black and blue splashes stop being awkward.

The combo turn

Have Haru (or any Ally-entry engine) plus a token source: Invasion Reinforcements, Kyoshi Warriors, Elfsworn Giant’s landfall Elves, Howlsquad Heavy’s Goblin, Jasmine Dragon Tea Shop at five mana.
Every token is an Ally entering, so Haru earthbends 1. Spread the earthbends across two lands rather than stacking one, unless you need a single big blocker.
The land creatures attack the turn they are made. Dai Li Agents’ attack trigger counts each of them for the drain, and each point drained raises speed by 1 the next turn.
Land creatures that trade return to the battlefield tapped, re-triggering Sabotender, Tannuk and Spitfire Lagac, and making an Elf Warrior if Elfsworn Giant is out. The loop costs no cards.

Mulligan guide

Keep: two or three lands with green and a white or red source, one Haru or one landfall clock (Sabotender, Tannuk), and at least one Ally that makes a token.
Keep (no Haru): any hand with two lands, Great Divide Guide and a two-drop. The Guide fixes the rest.
Trim: five-land hands with no engine; hands with Dai Li Agents, Elfsworn Giant and Far Fortune and no early play; hands that need both black and blue with neither a Guide nor Jasmine Dragon Tea Shop.
One land plus Guide is a real keep if the rest of the hand is two-drops — the deck’s curve starts at one.

title: Break Ground
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Earthbend targets are chosen on resolution. With Haru in play and two Allies entering, choose different lands so a single removal spell does not erase all your board.
Returning lands trigger landfall. An earthbent land that dies in combat comes back tapped, which is another land entry for Sabotender, Tannuk, Spitfire Lagac, Elfsworn Giant and Earthbender Ascension. Blocking with land creatures is often a value play.
Rebellious Captives’ exhaust is a late-game earthbend. Six mana buys two counters on a body plus a fresh land creature; each exhaust ability can be activated only once per game.
Earth Kingdom Protectors can save a land creature by sacrificing itself, granting another Ally indestructible. It is the deck’s only protection, so keep the one white mana up when a key land creature attacks into open mana.
Dai Li Agents counts every creature with a +1/+1 counter, not just land creatures. Earthbent lands, Rebellious Captives after its exhaust and anything grown by Earthbender Ascension all count.
Start your engines! needs opponent life loss. Speed rises only while your opponent is losing life on your turn, so landfall pings and Dai Li Agents are what switch the max-speed payoffs on. Do not trade away the burn creatures.
Embalmed Ascendant’s max-speed trigger watches your creatures dying, which includes earthbent lands returning to the battlefield. It is both the drain and the reason blocking is good.
Rogue’s Passage costs {4} to activate and produces colorless mana, so it is a real tempo cost. Land it on a turn where the attack is lethal rather than as a fourth land.

title: Break Ground
text:
Matchups

Aggro: the deck trades well — its attackers are expendable lands and its blockers come back. Earth Kingdom Protectors protects the relevant bodies and Dai Li Agents’ drain is often the difference in a close race.
Control: landfall burn ignores sweepers, because every returning earthbent land is another trigger. Rebuild with Howlsquad Heavy’s Goblin and Jasmine Dragon Tea Shop’s token after a wipe.
Ramp and big mana: the burn clock is the plan; Rogue’s Passage plus a large earthbent land beats a stalled ground, and speed 4 with Far Fortune closes before a slower deck stabilises.
Mirror: whoever resolves Haru and Tannuk first usually leads. Kill Haru on sight — the Ally chains are the engine, not the win conditions.

title: Death by Committee
text:
Overview
Death by Committee fuses the two rolled mechanics — Sacrifice and Teamwork — into one engine: the committee is the sacrifice fodder. Forsaken Miner, Reassembling Skeleton and Bloodghast refuse to stay dead, so every turn the deck has a fresh set of bodies: tap them to pay Teamwork costs, sacrifice them to draw cards and exile threats, and let their death triggers refill the hand. The Teamwork payoff spells from the Spider-Man set turn that rotating cast of characters into removal, burn and reanimation that does double duty.
The engine loop: a skeleton dies to Fanatical Offering (draw two) or Worthy Cost (exile a threat), the death triggers draw more cards (Midnight Reaper) or make Food (Restless Cottage attacks), the skeleton recurs (crime triggers, {1}{B}, landfall), and the rebuilt board — plus 4/4 Restless Cottage manlands — taps for Teamwork 2 or 4 to cast Cruel Alliance, Repulsor Blast or HULK SMASH! in their doubled modes. The graveyard fills as a side effect, and Too Evil to Stay Dead turns it into a reanimation spell: with Teamwork paid it resurrects any creature card, no mana-value limit.
The finish line is three-pronged. Rune-Scarred Demon and Bloodthirsty Conqueror come back as flying beaters and tutors. Conqueror plus Enduring Tenacity plus any Food sacrifice is a true infinite loop — each life gain drains the opponent, each drain gains life. And the lands themselves kill: Restless Cottage is a 4/4 Horror that makes Food on attack, and Rogue’s Passage makes it unblockable, with Team Tactics doubling the damage.

title: Death by Committee
text:
Approach

Game plan by phase

Dig the graves (turns 1–3). Turn 1 Forsaken Miner or Worthy Cost (sacrificing a skeleton); turn 2 Reassembling Skeleton, Bloodghast or Fanatical Offering. Every removal spell is a “crime”, which recurs Forsaken Miner for {B} — the first two skeletons become an endless stream.
Hold the committee meeting (turns 3–5). Corpseberry Cultivator grows on every forage; Midnight Reaper converts each death into a card; Restless Cottage wakes up as a 4/4 to tap for Teamwork 4 and attack for Food. Cast Too Evil to Stay Dead, Cruel Alliance, HULK SMASH! or Repulsor Blast with their doubled modes.
The vote passes (turns 5+). Too Evil to Stay Dead (Teamwork) reanimates the big two: Rune-Scarred Demon tutors the missing combo piece, Bloodthirsty Conqueror starts the drain. Close with the infinite Food loop, or send an unblockable, double-striking Restless Cottage over the top.

Curve and mana
Seventeen creatures, seventeen spells, twenty-six lands. The nonland curve averages about 2.4 mana: nine one- and two-drop recursion bodies, eight three-drops, four four-drops and three reanimation-only finishers (mana value 5 to 7, almost never hard-cast). Black is the spine (roughly twenty sources), green supports it (seventeen), and red is a splash of six cards (five to six sources). title: Death by Committee
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Prioritize a black source and a one-drop: Forsaken Miner on turn 1 threatens a free 2/2 every time you later cast removal, which is a crime. Reassembling Skeleton on turn 2 blocks the format’s early attackers and sets up turn 3 Fanatical Offering. Do not hold skeletons — they are meant to die; the whole deck is built around them coming back. Sequence the untapped fast lands early and the tapped duals (Mortuary, Commercial District, Overgrown Tomb) later.


Mid game
Start sacrificing on your own terms. Fanatical Offering turns any skeleton into two cards and a Map token; Worthy Cost answers a planeswalker or creature for one mana plus a body that was going to die anyway. Every nontoken death triggers Midnight Reaper, so a single Reassembling Skeleton recursion loop is a repeatable draw spell. Corpseberry Cultivator forages at every combat — exile three graveyard cards (or sacrifice a Food from a Cottage attack) to grow it into a credible Teamwork contributor.


The combo turn
The board is a committee of 2-power skeletons and a Restless Cottage. Tap total power 4 (two 2/2 Miners, or Miner + Bloodghast, or the 4/4 Cottage) to pay Teamwork on Too Evil to Stay Dead and reanimate two of Bloodthirsty Conqueror, Rune-Scarred Demon and Enduring Tenacity from the graveyard you have been filling all game. Demon tutors the missing piece; then the drain loop closes:

Attack with Restless Cottage — it creates a Food token.
Sacrifice the Food: gain 3 life.
Enduring Tenacity: target opponent loses 3 life.
Bloodthirsty Conqueror: you gain 3 life — loop back to step 3. The opponent dies.

The loop needs only Conqueror + Tenacity + any lifegain, and both halves are reanimation targets, so the graveyard is the hand. If the loop is disrupted, the reanimated pair still attacks for 10-11 flying damage with the Demon’s tutor finding whatever is missing.


Win condition 2
The lands kill. Activate Restless Cottage ({2}{B}{G}) into a 4/4, cast Team Tactics tapping any creature (Teamwork 1 is nearly free) for double strike and trample, then activate Rogue’s Passage ({4}, {T}) — 8 unblockable damage from a land. In long games the Cottage also grinds: attack, make Food, exile a graveyard card (shutting down opposing reanimation), then sacrifice the Food to grow Corpseberry Cultivator or to feed the drain loop.


Mulligan guide
Keep any hand with two or three lands and a one- or two-drop — the deck functions on skeletons alone. Ship hands with no black source or with only tapped lands and no early play. Keep Too Evil to Stay Dead plus a sacrifice spell plus a body; the reanimation plan only needs a graveyard, which sacrifice provides. Against aggressive decks, favor removal (Worthy Cost, HULK SMASH!) over the Teamwork spells.


Key interactions and edge cases

Crime recursion: Worthy Cost, Cruel Alliance, Repulsor Blast and HULK SMASH!’s fight mode all target opponents or their permanents, so each one recurs Forsaken Miner for {B} — sequence removal before combat to rebuild the board for Teamwork.
Teamwork is optional: every Teamwork spell can be cast without tapping — a doubled mode is a bonus, not a requirement; tap only when the payoff is worth the tapped creatures.
Enduring Tenacity returns as an enchantment when it dies as a creature — it stops being sacrifice fodder but keeps draining, so the combo survives a board wipe.
Too Evil to Stay Dead without Teamwork is still a two-for-one enabler at mana value 4 or less — Solemn Simulacrum is the ideal cheap target (ramps, then draws on death).
Fountainport tokens count: a 1/1 Fish is a creature for Teamwork 1 and a sacrifice for Fanatical Offering, and sacrificing it draws a card.
Don’t over-sacrifice: the team is also the Teamwork payment; keep at least one body untapped to pay Teamwork 2/4 next turn.



Matchups

Aggro: the skeletons block forever and Worthy Cost / HULK SMASH! / Cruel Alliance clear the path; Conqueror’s lifegain ends the race.
Midrange: grind them out — every sacrifice replaces itself with cards (Fanatical Offering, Midnight Reaper) while Too Evil reanimates bigger creatures than they can answer.
Control: spread threats (manlands, Fountainport Fish) so sweepers never fully reset; the graveyard is a second hand, so wraths that don’t exile are meaningless. Rogue’s Passage closes through blockers.
Graveyard hate: the deck still plays a fair midrange game — skeletons and removal — but mulligan aggressively for Cottage plus Team Tactics to win on the land plan instead.

title: Paid in Blood
text:
Overview
Paid in Blood is a five-color engine that turns dying into damage. Every creature that dies pays the opponent: Vein Ripper drains 2 on any creature death anywhere, Cauldron of Essence drains 1 and gains 1 on each of your deaths, and the life gained feeds Marauding Blight-Priest, which drains 1 more per trigger. Scavenger’s Talent converts deaths into Food tokens, Demand Answers and Eaten Alive spend those tokens on cards and removal, and Ruthless Lawbringer trades any creature for any nonland permanent.
The fodder never runs out. Bonebind Orator and Unstoppable Slasher return from the graveyard, Cauldron of Essence reanimates one creature per activation, Raise the Past floods back every 2-mana-value creature, and Hop to It, Kambal (token copies via Three Steps Ahead) and Great Arashin City keep tokens flowing. Bloodletter of Aclazotz doubles the entire drain package on your turn, turning a modest loop into a kill.

title: Paid in Blood
text:
Approach
Game plan phases

title: Paid in Blood
text:
Gameplay strategy
Early game. Prioritize a two-drop over a tapped land when the colors allow. Play Scoured Barrens early for the life-gain trigger. Spend Eaten Alive freely on aggressive starts; the sacrifice cost feeds the engine either way.
Mid game. Assemble Cauldron of Essence plus one drain payoff before grinding. Sacrifice Food tokens to Demand Answers rather than creatures, and let Ruthless Lawbringer convert expendable creatures into premium removal. The Gitrog wants a saddle creature ready when it attacks.
The combo turn. With Cauldron of Essence and Vein Ripper on the battlefield, each sacrifice drains 3 and gains 3 (1 from Cauldron, 2 from Vein Ripper). Recur Bonebind Orator or Unstoppable Slasher and repeat every turn. Bloodletter of Aclazotz doubles the drain to 6 per sacrifice. A single Food token becomes 3 life and 3 damage per cycle.
Win condition 2. Attack with Bloodthirsty Conqueror, Vein Ripper and Vampire Nighthawk over the top. Amonkhet Raceway grants haste at max speed, which the drain package reaches quickly. Soulstone Sanctuary and Crawling Barrens are repeatable attackers, and Raise the Past turns a board wipe into a swarm.
Mulligan guide. Keep any hand with two or three lands including early black or white. A two-drop plus removal is a strong keep. Mulligan hands with mostly tapped lands or no early plays. Scavenger’s Talent plus a sacrifice outlet is the best opener.
Key interactions and edge cases.

Cauldron of Essence reanimation is sorcery-speed only; plan the recursion around your main phase.
Vein Ripper’s ward cost is a sacrifice, so it protects itself from removal by draining the opponent.
Eaten Alive exiles, which bypasses opposing death triggers but still triggers your own via the sacrifice cost.
Unstoppable Slasher returns tapped with stun counters, so it is a slow but repeatable clock.
The Gitrog only draws when it deals combat damage while saddled; do not attack it into obvious blockers without a trick.
Three Steps Ahead can copy any of your creatures into a token, which then triggers Kambal and feeds the sacrifice engine.

Matchups. Against aggro, early removal and the life-gain drain package stabilize and out-race. Against control, Three Steps Ahead protects key pieces and the recursion engine grinds through sweepers. Against other midrange decks, the drain clock is faster than conventional damage because it ignores blockers.

Denzilore Fatehold is the pivot. Cast it at flash speed on the opponent’s end step when you can, so it survives a turn and attacks immediately. The turn after Denzilore lands, add Yoshimaru: from that point each surveil is two counters on every creature, and the board grows without further investment. title: Sphinxwake

The combo turn
The engine turn is a stack of small surveil events. With Denzilore and Yoshimaru on the battlefield:

Eye of Jace’s upkeep trigger: +2/+2 to every creature.
Proctor of Potential returning from the graveyard, or any creature entering: another +2/+2.
Surveillance Phantasm’s {3}{U} activation: another +2/+2.
Guiding Hydra’s beginning-of-combat trigger: one counter on it becomes two on each other creature.

Four triggers in a turn is +8/+8 to the whole team for {3}{U}{W}{U} plus the upkeep trigger. Attack with Denzilore, Phantasm and Phoenix in the air; the ground creatures are only there to be big blockers or to be copied by Hall of Echoes.

title: Sphinxwake
text:
Win condition 2
Hall of Echoes is the second finish and the reason the deck satisfies the “land as part of the win” requirement. Once a creature is carrying eight or more counters, {5} plus the land makes a copy of it until end of turn, with the legend rule suspended — so a second Denzilore, or a second copy of the biggest Hydra-fed creature, attacks in the same combat. The land is not a creature spell and cannot be countered as one; it is an uncounterable extra attacker.
Eye of Jace is the third, quieter finish: once the graveyard has seven or more cards — trivial with a surveil engine and a Phoenix that keeps dying — it sacrifices itself for two damage to each opponent and two life. That is the last two points after a stalled board, and it costs no mana.

title: Sphinxwake

Mulligan guide
Keep: two or three lands plus Eye of Jace or Proctor of Potential; any hand with Denzilore and a white source; hands with Eye of Jace plus two removal spells against a fast deck.

title: Sphinxwake
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Denzilore triggers once per scry or surveil event, not once per card, so a Surveil 2 is still a single trigger.
Yoshimaru’s replacement effect applies to every counter placed on your creatures, including the counters Guiding Hydra moves at combat and the +1/+1 counter Generous Revival adds — the revived creature enters with two.
Guiding Hydra’s trigger is optional; with a single counter on it, removing that counter kills it, so only use it when the counter is not the last one, or when you want the death for Darklight Phoenix.
Proctor of Potential’s recursion needs a scry or surveil earlier in the same turn. Eye of Jace’s upkeep trigger covers this automatically; without Eye of Jace, surveil first with Phantasm or Refute Destiny, then recur.
Prophesied End gives the controller a card when the target was not attacking. Use it on attackers, or on a creature whose death is worth the card — a two-for-one against a blocking creature is usually fine.
Darklight Phoenix returns at the beginning of combat only if two or more creatures died this turn. Combat trades count, and so does sacrificing to your own removal; plan the second death before combat.
Hall of Echoes produces {C}, which cannot pay for Denzilore or Phantasm. Do not keep a two-land hand that is Hall of Echoes plus one coloured source.
Generous Revival’s flashback is {4}{W}; it is a late-game card, not a turn-three plan.

title: Tap Dance
text:
Overview
Tap Dance is built on one exchange rate: creatures become mana, and mana becomes creatures again.
Convoke lets you tap your board to pay for spells, so every body you own is a discount. Blink spells buy those bodies back — the same Silvergill Mentor or Merrow Skyswimmer enters again and again, each time making another Merfolk token that can be tapped for the next spell. Pestered Wellguard closes the loop from the other side: the instant it is tapped to help pay a convoke cost, it hands you a 1/1 Faerie with flying, so even paying for spells leaves you further ahead.
Nothing in the list is decorative. The creatures are all enter-the-battlefield payoffs worth flickering, the spells are either flicker effects or convoke payoffs, and the lands tap for coloured mana and then turn into attackers. The deck plays as a midrange value engine that can suddenly go wide and kill with one or two attack steps.

title: Tap Dance
text:
Approach

Game plan phases
Turns 1–2 — seed the board. Drop cheap bodies that pay off later. Silvergill Mentor and Charming Prince cost two, and both leave value behind: a 1/1 Merfolk token, or a scry, or a flicker. Casting Kykar is the real turn two or three goal, because from then on every noncreature spell you cast is also a token or a flicker.
Turns 3–5 — turn on the engine. This is where the deck separates from a normal token deck. Personify and Daydream re-trigger your best enters-the-battlefield creature, and the tokens they leave behind pay for Merrow Skyswimmer and The Wandering Rescuer ahead of curve. Pestered Wellguard and Kykar both convert spells into extra bodies, so the board grows twice per spell.
Turns 5+ — cash out. With six or more creatures the convoke spells are effectively free. Web of Life and Destiny starts putting a creature onto the battlefield every combat, Harmonized Crescendo refills your hand, and Winnowing clears the opponent’s side. From there, two or three attack steps with Restless Prairie in play end the game.

title: Tap Dance
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Lead with the cheapest body that does something when it arrives. Silvergill Mentor is the default turn-two play: you usually have a Merfolk to behold (Merrow Skyswimmer in hand counts), so the extra {2} is rarely paid, and you get a 1/1 Merfolk immediately. Hold Personify for a turn where it doubles as a token; a two-mana spell that blinks a creature and adds a body is the best rate in the deck.
Do not be afraid to trade creatures early. Your bodies are ammunition as much as attackers, and anything that dies is one less blocker to worry about when you go wide later.


Mid game
Kykar is the pivot. Once it is in play, every noncreature spell you cast is a second spell: choose the Spirit token when you want board width, and choose the flicker when you want a repeat enters-the-battlefield trigger. Pestered Wellguard does the same job without needing a spell at all — simply tap it to convoke something and the Faerie arrives anyway.
Start using convoke aggressively from here. Tapping out to cast Merrow Skyswimmer on turn three is often better than holding up mana, because the Swimmer replaces one of the creatures you tapped and adds a flying vigilance body.


The combo turn
The deck’s big turn looks like this: you have Kykar plus one or two two-mana flicker spells and a board of tokens.

Cast Personify targeting your best enters-the-battlefield creature (Silvergill Mentor or Merrow Skyswimmer). That creature re-enters and makes a Merfolk token, and Personify leaves a 1/1 changeling token. Kykar triggers — take the Spirit.
Cast Daydream on the same creature. Another trigger, another counter, another Kykar choice. With flashback, Daydream can be cast a second time later in the game.
Now convoke. Every token you just made pays for the next spell. Web of Life and Destiny at eight mana is realistically castable on turn five or six by tapping five or six creatures, and from then on it puts a free creature onto the battlefield at the start of every combat.



Win condition 2
The Wandering Rescuer is a four-mana (with convoke, often two) 3/4 with flash and double strike that gives every other tapped creature you control hexproof. Attack with it alongside tokens, and the tokens are untargetable while they are attacking. Restless Prairie adds another +1/+1 to the whole team on the same attack, and Sandstorm Salvager’s activated ability puts a counter and trample on each token. Two attack steps like that usually end the game.


Mulligan guide

Keep two to four lands, at least one of which is untapped.
Keep any hand with a two-drop enters-the-battlefield creature (Silvergill Mentor, Ennis, Charming Prince) and a flicker spell (Personify or Daydream).
Keep hands with Kykar and at least three lands.
Mulligan all-split-land hands with no basic land, since the verge lands need a basic to unlock their second colour.
Mulligan hands with no creature at all, however many spells they hold — the engine needs bodies to tap.



Key interactions and edge cases

Pestered Wellguard and convoke. Tapping it to pay a convoke cost counts as it becoming tapped, so a single convoke spell can leave a Faerie behind. This is the deck’s cheapest source of repeatable board width.
Personify’s changeling token is every creature type. That single token makes Winnowing one-sided: choose your changeling token as the creature you control, and every other creature you own shares a type with it and survives, while the opponent loses everything except their chosen creature.
Harmonized Crescendo counts changelings. If your changeling token is on the battlefield, choosing almost any creature type counts it, so the draw spell rarely misses.
Kykar and flash. The Wandering Rescuer has flash, so it can be cast at the end of an opponent’s turn, triggering Kykar’s flicker or Spirit ability before your own turn.
Silvergill Mentor’s additional cost. Behold a Merfolk or pay {2}. A Merfolk token, Merrow Skyswimmer or Pestered Wellguard satisfies the behold, so the extra mana is usually avoidable.
Splash Portal draws on Kykar. Kykar is a Bird, so blinking it with Splash Portal replaces the card.
Ennis and Charming Prince flicker at the next end step, not immediately. Their value shows up on the following turn, so play them before you need the trigger.
Daydream has flashback. Casting it twice from hand and graveyard is a real card-advantage loop with a creature worth blinking.



Matchups

Aggro. Your tokens chump and trade, Pestered Wellguard grows the board while blocking, and Winnowing plus Vote Out take out the biggest threats. Restless Cottage’s Food token is a small but real life buffer.
Control. Kykar and Pestered Wellguard make bodies that survive a single sweeper, and The Wandering Rescuer’s hexproof protects tapped attackers. Hold Personify for after a wipe — rebuilding from one creature is what the deck does best.
Midrange. You win the long game with Web of Life and Destiny and repeatable enters-the-battlefield triggers, provided you keep at least one creature on the battlefield to keep flickering.
Other token decks. Winnowing is at its best here, and Restless Prairie tips creature-to-creature combat in your favour.

Early game
Turn one is not a real turn for this deck, so plan for turn two and three. Attercop into Thranduil, Sindarin Liege is the strongest opening the deck has: the Spider trades with anything, and the Liege turns the third land into a token while making the Spider a 3/2 on the attack. Wood Elves is the deck’s best three-drop and it looks unremarkable: a 1/1 for {2}{G} that fetches a Forest. What it actually does is put a land onto the battlefield, which is a landfall trigger for the Liege, the Company and Attercop, and it does it without using the land drop you still have in hand. title: Loam and Legend

The combo turn
The doubled landfall turn is assembled from four pieces: Thranduil’s Company on the battlefield, another Elf to unlock its extra land drop, a landfall token maker, and Bard, King of Dale. With all four, a single turn plays two lands, each of which makes two Elf tokens and puts two counters on a creature, and each of which grows the Weavemaster and Attercop as it arrives.
The sequence matters. Play the land you have held for the extra drop first, let the triggers resolve, then play the second land. Put the Company’s two counters on the creature that is already blocked or already unblocked rather than on the newest token, and remember that the counters and the vigilance last until end of turn — the swung-in Elf that received them untaps. Down in the Valley adds a third and fourth trigger by giving itself landfall at chapter two, and Roll-Roll-Roll-Roll adds one more by exiling a land you already control and returning it at the end step, tapping it for mana in between.

Curve and mana
Twenty-five lands: thirteen basics (5 Mountain, 4 Swamp, 4 Forest) plus twelve fixing and engine lands. Red is the engine color — Smaug, the saga and the big Dragons want double-red by turn four — so red sources are deepest. Black feeds Smaug, Wicked Worm and removal; green is a light splash for Jolene, Savage Ventmaw and the verges. The curve runs heavy on fours and fives; a two- or three-drop Treasure maker bridges to turn-four Smaug or Dracosaur, and Fomori Vault keeps the top of the deck honest.

Early game
Play a Treasure maker and hold the ground: Charming Scoundrel on two (loot a redundant Dragon away or bank a Treasure), Dori or the saga on three. Do not overcommit into sweepers — one engine plus removal is enough until Smaug arrives. Against aggro, Hell to Pay and Scorching Shot trade one-for-one while the saga banks gold.

Resolve Smaug: he has haste, so he attacks the turn he lands for your Treasure count — a saga at three chapters plus an upkeep Treasure is already four to six damage before the body. Every Dragon cast the same turn triggers Terror for doubled damage, every spell pings through Firespitter Whelp, and Jolene converts spare Treasures into doubled 2-point pings. The Misty Mountains Cold finishes independently too: a 6/6 Dragon plus Dwarf tokens from The Lonely Mountain is a wide, evasive clock.

title: Wyrmgold

title: Wyrmgold

Key interactions and edge cases

Smaug’s trigger counts Treasures as it resolves — Jolene’s attack Treasure and Goldvein Pick’s combat Treasure arrive in time for the next swing, not the current one.
Twinflame Tyrant doubles damage from your sources to opponents and their permanents: Smaug’s burn, Terror triggers, Whelp pings, and Hell to Pay’s damage — more excess damage means more Treasures.
Desolation of Smaug damages your own non-Dragons: Dori, Jolene and Charming Scoundrel are casualties; every other creature is a Dragon or Dinosaur Dragon and survives.
Smaug, Wicked Worm counts artifacts opponents control on entry — Equipment, Treasures and artifact creatures feed the burst; Treasure-paid spells draw at 1 life.
Bonehoard Dracosaur’s exiles can be played as lands, but a land still uses your land drop.
The Lonely Mountain enters tapped unless you control an Equipment; with two Goldvein Picks its token costs {2}{R} instead of {4}{R}. Last Light of Durin’s Day counts every Mountain that enters and at six counters puts a Dragon onto the battlefield; Fomori Vault digs X cards where X is your artifact count.

Midrange (counters, landfall): Smaug’s haste burn races their board; Dracosaur and Dragonhawk out-value their topdecks.
Control: grind with Dracosaur and Dragonhawk, hold Treasures until Twinflame resolves, and end through Rogue’s Passage.
Combo and big mana: the deck is the aggressor; speed up the Smaug clock and point removal at their pieces.

title: Exhaust Manifold
text:
Curve and mana
The 37 non-land cards are three one-drops, twenty-eight two-drops, five three-drops and one four-drop, for an average CMC of 2.1. Twenty-seven of the thirty-one creatures cost exactly two mana, which is the point: the deck wants to spend its early turns making two threats, and The Water Crystal is the only card that costs more than three.
The mana base is eighteen shocklands, two Restless Reef and Rogue’s Passage plus one Island and one Forest. Twenty-two of the twenty-three lands produce at least one of the four colours and every colour has at least eight sources: eleven blue, eleven black, ten green, eight red. The shocks are the fix: paying 2 life to bring one in untapped means a hand with Breeding Pool and Blood Crypt casts any green, blue, black or red card on turn two. The cost is real against aggro — expect to pay four to eight life over a game — but Master’s Councillors and Scarblade Scout’s lifelink usually buy it back.

title: Exhaust Manifold
text:
Early game
Turns one to three are two-drop turns: the deck has no one-drop plan beyond Greasewrench Goblin, and every other creature costs two. Prioritise by what the opponent is doing. Against aggro, Scarblade Scout first (lifelink plus mill) so the ground holds. Against control, Volatile Wanderglyph and Prowcatcher Specialist first, because a two-power clock backed by haste is how you punish a slow start. Riverchurn Monument can come down on turn two over a creature if the hand is removal-light.
Play shocklands untapped for the first four or five turns. The deck’s own lifelink and Master’s Councillors’ growth make the life payment an investment; a two-colour hand that comes in tapped is how this deck loses a turn it cannot spare.

title: Exhaust Manifold
text:
Mid game
Turns four to six are when the engine assembles. The Water Crystal is the highest-impact card in the deck: with it out, Scarblade Scout’s entry mills six, Master’s Councillors’ second-draw trigger mills seven, Restless Reef’s attack mills eight and Riverchurn Monument’s exhaust tacks four onto every target. Play it before spending any exhaust abilities.
The tap triggers are the deck’s card advantage. Volatile Wanderglyph turns every Teamwork cost into a free loot, and the discard feeds Afterburner Expert into the graveyard. Greasewrench Goblin’s exhaust is a second draw, which turns Master’s Councillors into a mill engine on its own: exhaust the Goblin (discard, draw two), and the second card drawn fires Councillors’ trigger.
Do not attack into open blocks with the small bodies once the mill clock is online. The deck wins with its library plan far more often than it wins with damage, and every creature that dies is one fewer body to pay Teamwork costs with.

title: Exhaust Manifold
text:
The combo turn
The mill kill is a chained exhaust, not an infinite loop:

Get The Water Crystal onto the battlefield, then let Riverchurn Monument’s {1}, {T} ability put two cards into every graveyard until each player has seven or more.
Activate Riverchurn Monument’s exhaust ({2}{U}{U}, {T}): every targeted player mills cards equal to the number already in their graveyard, plus four from The Water Crystal. A graveyard of ten becomes fourteen.
Next turn, activate that same exhaust again while Elvish Refueler is untapped and nothing else has been exhausted that turn: Refueler lets you activate exhaust abilities as though they had never been used, so the sixteen-card graveyard becomes twenty.
Each turn the number roughly doubles, and The Water Crystal’s own tap ability adds hand-size-plus-four per turn in between. Against a deck that fills its own graveyard, this closes out the game in three turns.

A representative turn: The Water Crystal and Elvish Refueler out, four cards in hand. Tap Crystal for eight to the opponent, exhaust Riverchurn Monument for their graveyard plus four, attack with Restless Reef for another eight. Thirty-plus cards off a library in one turn.

title: Exhaust Manifold
text:
Win condition 2
When milling is too slow or a single large threat has to die, the deck attacks. Prowcatcher Specialist with two counters is a 4/1, Greenbelt Guardian with three is a 5/5 trampler, and Sita Varma’s exhaust is the finisher: with four mana invested, X equals four counters and every other creature’s base power and toughness becomes five or more for the turn. Attack with everything, hold Rogue’s Passage’s {4}, {T} activation for the biggest creature, and the board that was milling for three a turn suddenly swings for twenty.
Afterburner Expert is the second route: because it returns from the graveyard whenever you activate an exhaust ability, a 4/2 that dies in combat comes back for free the turn you activate Greasewrench Goblin’s or Greenbelt Guardian’s exhaust, and Too Evil to Stay Dead with teamwork brings back anything else.

title: Exhaust Manifold
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep any hand with two to four lands, at least two two-drops, and at least one of each colour pair you need for the cards in hand. A hand with Riverchurn Monument plus The Water Crystal is an automatic keep despite having little board presence: that pair is the game plan. Ship hands that need two specific colours and have only shocklands of a third, and ship hands with no creatures — the deck cannot pay Teamwork costs without a board, and its mill engine needs a blocker to survive to turn five.

title: Exhaust Manifold
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

The Water Crystal’s plus four applies to every opponent mill, including its own tap ability: with five cards in hand that ability mills nine, not five.
Elvish Refueler’s permission works only while you have not activated an exhaust ability this turn, so sequence it first: re-use Riverchurn Monument’s exhaust before touching Greasewrench Goblin or Greenbelt Guardian.
Every exhaust activation returns Afterburner Expert from the graveyard to the battlefield, not just your own exhaust abilities’ costs — any activation triggers it, and it can only be answered by exile.
Sita Varma’s exhaust sets base power and toughness, not counters: Veteran Ice Climber becomes a large unblockable creature that mills its new power when it attacks.
Master’s Councillors counts every graveyard with seven or more cards, including yours: after a couple of Riverchurn Monument activations it is a 5/3 for two.

Detail




Storied never turns off

Hone counters live on the Equipment
A hone counter from Dwalin, Weaponmaster is placed on the Equipment, so it moves with the Equipment when you re-equip and it survives the equipped creature dying. A Mattock with two hone counters is +4/+2


Dáin Ironfoot’s double strike is an attack trigger

They are artifacts that count for Storied, they can be re-equipped to a different creature, and Fíli’s tokens get nothing from them until equipped


Bombur needs an enduring story to untap

Kíli draws only once each turn
His trigger is once per turn, so ordering matters: play the artifact and the Dwarf in the same turn and draw one card, not two. The first equip each turn being free is separate and always available


Bilbo carries Equipment because he cannot be blocked
An unblockable 1/1 with a Mattock is a 3/3 ward {1} that cannot be blocked, which is the cleanest way to use Dáin Ironfoot’s double strike through a stall


Spirebluff Canal is untapped only early
It enters tapped unless you control two or fewer other lands, so it is a turn-one to turn-three land. Do not count it as a fourth or fifth land for a double-strike turn

title: Quill Cadence
text:
Overview
The deck is a burn engine disguised as an aggro deck. Ingris Stingerquill is the whole idea: a three-mana 1/4 flier whose trigger reads “whenever a creature you control attacks, that creature deals 1 damage to each opponent”. That is not a combat-damage payoff, so it does not care about blocks, toughness, or whether the attacker survives. Four attacking one-drops are four damage to each opponent even if all four are blocked.
Everything else exists to put bodies on the board and make them attack the turn they arrive. Samut, Hazoret’s Champion grants the team haste for two mana. Gallia, the Merrymaker is a hasty two-drop who gives haste to every creature carrying a +1/+1 counter and hands a counter to anything that entered this turn. Emergency Phytomedic and Vigorbloom Vanguard enter prepared, so they hand you a free Seed Suture — a +1/+1 counter and a life — the exact counter Gallia and Vanguard’s vigilance static want.
The second engine is the Way cycle. Way of the Warlord and Way of the Pyromancer each empower Jace on entry, which means they arrive as a five-loyalty or two-loyalty Jace token. Warlord gives every planeswalker you control a drain ability; Pyromancer gives them a mana ability. Repurposed Enforcer attacks for empower X equal to your board, Campus Crier empowers from the graveyard, and Arcane Amphisbaena empowers on entry, so the loyalty count keeps climbing without spending cards.
The last piece is a land. Hall of Echoes copies a creature for five mana and ignores the legend rule that turn, so it becomes a second Ingris: five attackers then deal ten damage per opponent per attack step.

title: Quill Cadence
text:
Approach
Plan by phases:

Turns 1 and 2: land a prepared body and a haste enabler. Emergency Phytomedic on one is the ideal opener because the free Seed Suture immediately makes your next attacker bigger. Samut or Gallia on two is the follow-up that makes the deck function.
Turn 3: Ingris Stingerquill. From this point every attack step converts bodies into damage regardless of blocks. If Ingris is answered, Repurposed Enforcer plus Way of the Warlord is the pivot to the planeswalker plan.
Turns 4 and 5: stack the board and get paid. Cast Seed Suture copies before combat, put counters on the creatures that will attack, and hold Gallia’s activated ability for anything that entered this turn.
Closing: Hall of Echoes on five mana copying Ingris, or a Way of the Warlord on a fat Jace token to finish through a stalled board.

Curve and mana
Twenty-six of the thirty-six spells cost two, four cost one (Emergency Phytomedic), and six cost three (Ingris and Way of the Warlord). Nothing costs four or more. The land count is 24: ten conditional duals, twelve basics and Hall of Echoes.
Twenty-four lands with twelve unconditional sources is deliberate: the duals carry the four-color manabase, but the deck never wants to miss its third land, because Ingris on three is the turn the deck starts winning. Black comes from seven sources (Stingerquill Annex, Formidable Commons, Swamp) and is only needed for Ingris, so a single black source is enough. Red sits at nine sources (Mountain, Stingerquill Annex, Dedicated Commons) because Samut, Gallia, both Ways and Ingris all want it; white and green also sit at nine, which is why the deck can afford one colorless land.

title: Quill Cadence
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Lead with Emergency Phytomedic over Vigorbloom Vanguard when a two-drop follows: the free Seed Suture grows the creature that will actually attack, so put the counter there, not on the Phytomedic. Against one-toughness blockers, Arcane Amphisbaena is the better two-drop — deathtouch trades up and it still empowers on entry. Play basics first; a dual only arrives untapped once a Jace token exists.


Mid game and the combo turn
The deck’s “combo turn” is any turn where a haste enabler and three or more bodies are on the board. Order of operations:

Seed Suture copies first, counters on the creatures with the best combat math.
Samut or Gallia, then attack with everything.
Ingris’s trigger resolves per attacker, so even a chump attack with a 1/1 is a point to each opponent.
Post-combat, Repurposed Enforcer’s attack trigger has already empowered Jace for your board size; spend that loyalty on Way of the Warlord’s drain in the following turns.

With Gallia in play, remember her activated ability targets a creature that entered this turn, so a Cadet made by Ingris’s {4} activation can attack immediately and still carry a counter.


Win condition two
Way of the Warlord arrives as a five-loyalty Jace token and gives every planeswalker you control “-4: this planeswalker deals 2 damage to up to one target creature or planeswalker and 2 damage to target player” — two points a turn per planeswalker, through blockers. Way of the Pyromancer pays for those activations with “+1: Add {R}”, and Campus Crier’s graveyard empower tops the loyalty back up. Slower than the Sphinx, but it beats a board stall.


Mulligan guide
Keep hands with two or three lands, at least one unconditional colored source, and a two-drop. Samut or Gallia plus any two creatures is a keep. A hand of only conditional duals with no one- or two-drop is a mulligan even at four lands, because every dual enters tapped and the deck falls a full turn behind. Ingris is not a reason to keep a bad hand.


Key interactions and edge cases

Prepared is one-shot here. Neither prepared creature re-prepares, so treat Seed Suture as a single free spell per body. Do not hold the creature back hoping for a second copy.
Vigorbloom Vanguard’s vigilance static and Gallia’s haste static both key off +1/+1 counters, which makes Seed Suture and Gallia’s activated ability double-duty.
Ingris is a 1/4 flier: it blocks well and attacks badly. Its {4} activation is the way it contributes to the attack step, by making a Cadet and hasting the team.
Hall of Echoes copies until end of turn and waives the legend rule only for that turn, so the second Ingris disappears at end of turn. Use the copy turn to attack, not to set up.
Hall of Echoes produces only colorless mana; it cannot pay for Ingris’s black or red pips.
Jace tokens die at zero loyalty. Way of the Warlord’s drain costs four, so do not spend the token below four loyalty on the surveil ability unless the card is worth more than the drain.



Matchups

Sweeper control: do not commit four creatures into untapped four mana. Keep Campus Crier in the graveyard and pivot to the Way of the Warlord drain, which needs no board.
Spot-removal midrange: expect Ingris to die. Repurposed Enforcer and the Cadet tokens keep the attack triggers relevant, and Hall of Echoes copies whichever creature survived.
Faster aggro or combo: Amphisbaena’s deathtouch and Vanguard’s vigilance trade profitably, Seed Suture’s life gain buys a turn, and every attacker is worth a point even when blocked.

title: Boneyard Bloom
text:
Overview
Renew is an activated ability that lives in the graveyard: pay the cost, exile the card, put counters on a creature, “activate only as a sorcery.” The mechanic is a one-shot resource, so the deck is built to (a) put Renew creatures into the graveyard early and (b) convert those buried cards into a single overwhelming attacker.
Two cards turn that conversion into real card flow rather than a one-for-one trade. Kheru Goldkeeper makes a Treasure every time one or more cards leave your graveyard during your turn, and Kishla Skimmer draws a card the same way (once per turn). Every Renew activation, and every Molt Tender mana activation, therefore leaves a Treasure or a card behind. The deck digs its own engine out of the graveyard, then finishes with evasion plus a land that makes the attacker unblockable.

title: Boneyard Bloom
text:
Approach

Game plan phases
Turns 1-3 — stock the boneyard. Molt Tender on turn one mills and later fixes mana by exiling graveyard cards. Alchemist’s Assistant and Rot-Curse Rakshasa put early points of damage on the table (the Rakshasa is a 5/5 trampler for two mana, decayed, so it is a one-shot attacker that leaves a Renew card in the graveyard). Sage of the Fang and Champion of Dusan arrive on turn three as bodies that later become ammunition.
Turns 4-6 — build the pile. Lasyd Prowler mills a chunk of the library on entry, which both fills the graveyard with Renew creatures and loads lands into the graveyard for its own Renew count. Bitter Triumph and Long Goodbye keep the board manageable while Bitter Triumph’s discard cost drops the first Renew creature into the graveyard for free.
The combo turn — pre-combat main phase. Pick one attacker (Kheru Goldkeeper or Qarsi Revenant for natural evasion), then chain Renew activations in the correct order: everything that adds counters first, Sage of the Fang last so its “double the number of +1/+1 counters” multiplies the finished total. Every activation triggers Kheru Goldkeeper (Treasure) and one of them triggers Kishla Skimmer (draw). Then attack.

title: Boneyard Bloom
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Lead with Molt Tender when you have it; milling a Renew creature into the graveyard is worth more than the 1/1 body. Rot-Curse Rakshasa is the fastest pressure in the deck and a perfectly acceptable turn-two play, because it is never meant to survive: attack, trade or sacrifice it, and the Renew ability is online in the graveyard. Hold Bitter Triumph until it can also bin a stuck Renew creature as its additional cost.


Mid game
Deploy two or three bodies and stop over-committing. Lasyd Prowler’s entry mill is the biggest single graveyard-filling play in the deck, and everything it mills makes its own later Renew bigger. Kishla Skimmer is the priority land beyond the first few turns: it converts the exile costs you are already paying into cards. Kheru Goldkeeper is the one four-drop worth tapping out for, because the Treasure it makes pays the next Renew activation.


The combo turn
Sequence matters. In your pre-combat main phase:

Confirm the target. Kheru Goldkeeper, Qarsi Revenant or a Rakshasa with a counter already on it are the best homes.
Activate the keyword Renews first: Alchemist’s Assistant ({1}{B}, lifelink counter), Champion of Dusan ({1}{G}, +1/+1 and trample counters), Qarsi Revenant ({2}{B}, flying plus deathtouch plus lifelink counters).
Activate Kheru Goldkeeper’s Renew ({2}{B}{G}{U}) for two +1/+1 counters and a flying counter if you have the mana.
Activate Sage of the Fang’s Renew ({3}{G}) last: one more counter, then double the total.
Activate Rogue’s Passage ({4}, {T}) on the same creature, then attack. Deathtouch plus trample plus unblockable plus a doubled counter total is the kill; lifelink buys the turn back if the attack is not lethal.

Each activation exiles a card from the graveyard, so Kheru Goldkeeper adds a Treasure and Kishla Skimmer adds a card on the way through.


Win condition 2 — the copy turn
Naga Fleshcrafter enters as a copy of any creature on the battlefield, then its Renew ({2}{U}) puts a +1/+1 counter on a target nonlegendary creature you control and makes every other creature you control a copy of that creature until end of turn. Pick a fat printed body — Lasyd Prowler (5/5) or Rot-Curse Rakshasa (5/5 trample) — and attack with the whole board as copies of it. The copies get the printed body, not the counters, so choose the target for its base stats. Copies of the Rakshasa are decayed and will be sacrificed at end of combat, which is irrelevant when the swing is lethal.


Mulligan guide
Keep any hand with three lands and a two-drop, or two lands that include Molt Tender. Ideal keeps have 3-4 lands, one or two Renew creatures, and one engine card (Kishla Skimmer, Lasyd Prowler or Kheru Goldkeeper). Send back hands that are all four-drops, hands with no black source and no Molt Tender, and one-land hands. Do not keep a hand that needs to reach four mana and has no way to get there.


Key interactions and edge cases

Sage of the Fang’s doubling is a multiplier, so it must be the last activation of the chain. Doubling before adding the other counters wastes the effect.
Renew is sorcery speed only, meaning pre-combat main phase is the whole window. Plan the whole chain before activating the first ability.
Every Renew activation exiles a card, so the abilities are finite. Count the graveyard before starting a chain and keep one activation in reserve if the attack might not be lethal.
Rot-Curse Rakshasa’s Renew ({X}{B}{B}) puts decayed counters on any number of target creatures. Used on defending creatures it removes their ability to block for the rest of the game, and any that attack are sacrificed at end of combat. It is a legitimate way to clear the way for the alpha strike.
Molt Tender’s second ability exiles a card from the graveyard for mana, which also triggers Kheru Goldkeeper and Kishla Skimmer. It is a mana source that advances the engine.
Bitter Triumph’s discard cost is upside: discard a Renew creature that is stuck in hand to destroy a creature or planeswalker.
Maximum Overdrive grants indestructible, so it doubles as protection for the stacked attacker in response to removal, and it adds a counter that Sage of the Fang can later double.
Naga Fleshcrafter’s copy is not a triggered ability you can chain for value: the copies lose the copied creature’s counters, so it is a one-turn finisher rather than a value engine.



Matchups
Aggro. Alchemist’s Assistant and the lifelink counters from the Renew package are the stabilisers, and Bitter Triumph and Long Goodbye trade up. Racing is viable because Rot-Curse Rakshasa attacks for five on turn two.
Control. Long Goodbye cannot be countered, and Kishla Skimmer plus Kheru Goldkeeper grind card advantage out of graveyard exiles. Do not spend the whole graveyard into a sweeper: keep two Renew creatures in reserve and rebuild.
Midrange. Counter stacking wins the creature fight. Sage of the Fang’s doubling outscales anything fair, and Rogue’s Passage walks past the biggest blocker.
Combo. There is no stack interaction, so the plan is speed plus discard: Bitter Triumph to rip a piece and Rot-Curse Rakshasa’s decayed counters to stop the creatures that matter.

title: Vanish on Cue
text:
Overview
The deck is built on a single clockwork: every turn you want to do two things — cast a prepared spell for free, and lose a permanent you control. Those two actions are not separate plans, they are the same plan. Prepared creatures produce the free spells; the free spells produce artifacts; the artifacts get sacrificed to removal, to Ice Cream Kitty, or to a Disappear payoff that hands you a Rat, an Insect, a card, or three +1/+1 counters. Disappear is worded “if a permanent left the battlefield under your control this turn,” so a token dying is currency, and the deck manufactures that currency on demand.
The failure mode this deck avoids is the usual one for these mechanics: Disappear cards with nothing to sacrifice, or Prepared creatures whose spell does nothing but cantrip. Here the two halves feed each other. Woodwork Prodigy re-prepares itself every upkeep and its Soul Tether spell makes a Heartwood artifact token, which is exactly the permanent you want to lose. Pizza Face turns those leftovers into a threat. Codie, Ravenous Codex doubles every prepared spell, so a single upkeep can produce two Heartwoods, or mill six, or deal two points of free noncombat damage.
Nothing in the deck needs a two-card infinite. It wins on accumulated value, one grown threat and a widening token board at a time, with enough removal to survive the early turns.

title: Vanish on Cue
text:
Approach

Game plan phases

Turns 1-2, deploy and enable. Stingerquill Voxmancer, Paradox Shaper, Rat King, or Bloodline Recollector. Rat King on turn two is the ideal opener — it starts paying you immediately if anything leaves.
Turns 3-4, build the loop. Woodwork Prodigy (Heartwood each upkeep, if you keep re-preparing it), Michelangelo, Codie. This is where you begin sacrificing for value every single turn: a Heartwood into Embrace Oblivion, a Food for 3 life, a Terramorphic Expanse for a land.
Turns 4-6, cash out. Pizza Face, Lord Dregg, and the second Rat King turn tokens into a board. Zhao converts each sacrifice into team damage.
Late, close. Grow one artifact into a 6/6 or larger Mutant and clear a path with Rogue’s Passage, or loop Rat Kings out of the graveyard and attack wide with the anthem up.

title: Vanish on Cue
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Lead with the cheapest Disappear payoff you have, not the cheapest Prepared creature. Rat King on turn two means every sacrifice from turn three onward is worth a Rat and a counter. If you have no payoff, play Paradox Shaper and start milling: Omit Variables fills the graveyard, and the threshold text on nothing in this deck matters, but the cards in the graveyard do — Rat King’s recursion and Bloodline Recollector both read the yard.
Do not crack Terramorphic Expanse on turn one out of habit. It is worth more as a Disappear trigger on the turn you need one, and the deck rarely needs the color that early.


Mid game
This is where the engine has to run every turn without exception. The checklist for each end step: did a permanent leave the battlefield under my control this turn? If not, find one — Food for {2}, a Heartwood into Embrace Oblivion, a Clue, a spare Rat.
Woodwork Prodigy is the quiet engine. Left alone, it becomes prepared every upkeep, and each Soul Tether makes a Heartwood artifact that taps for red or green. Those tokens ramp you into Pizza Face and Lord Dregg while also being the sacrifice fodder that keeps Disappear live. With Codie out, one upkeep makes two Heartwoods.
Against creature decks, hold Embrace Oblivion and Stir Up Trouble as instant-speed Disappear triggers rather than as pure removal. Killing their attacker and turning on your own end-step payoffs in the same action is the whole point of the fusion.


The combo turn
There is no single explosive turn, but the closest thing is an upkeep stack:

Upkeep: Paradox Shaper becomes prepared, Woodwork Prodigy becomes prepared, Stingerquill Voxmancer becomes prepared.
Cast Omit Variables (mill three), Soul Tether (Heartwood token), Vicious Verse (one damage to the opponent). Codie copies each one if it is on the battlefield.
Sacrifice a Heartwood to Ice Cream Kitty ({2}) or to Embrace Oblivion while killing a creature.
End step: Rat King makes a Rat and grows; Lord Dregg makes a flier; Pizza Face puts three counters on the second Heartwood and animates it into a 3/3 Mutant; Michelangelo grows; Zhao has already pumped the team.

That is four or five permanents gained and one lost, every turn, without spending a card from hand.


Win condition two
Rat King, Verminister is the deck’s real comeback engine. Its last ability reads: tap, sacrifice three Rats, return target creature card and all other cards with the same name as that card from your graveyard to the battlefield tapped. With four Rat Kings in the deck, sacrificing three Rat tokens can return two or three Rat Kings at once — each of which then makes another Rat at end of turn. Zhao turns the resulting swarm into a lethal alpha strike, and Rogue’s Passage makes the biggest one unblockable.


Mulligan guide
Keep hands with one Disappear payoff (Rat King, Pizza Face, Lord Dregg) and two or three lands, plus at least one cheap enabler. A hand of only Prepared creatures and no sacrifice outlet is a mulligan: the creatures will each produce one free spell and then sit there. Six-card hands are acceptable if they contain Rat King plus two lands. Never keep a one-land hand, even with Terramorphic Expanse — the deck needs to reach four mana to function.


Key interactions and edge cases

Codie’s activated ability is unreachable. It costs {W}{U}{B}{R}{G} and this deck has no white source. Codie is played purely for the passive that copies prepared spells; do not count on the mass-prepare mode.
Prepared spells are cast, then unprepare the creature. You can hold the copy for the opponent’s turn if the spell is an instant (none of the prepare spells here are), so in practice cast them on your own turn and re-prepare through the upkeep or Hexhaven.
Sacrificing a land counts. Terramorphic Expanse satisfies Disappear on its own. Cracking a fetch is a legal way to turn the team on.
Food’s own ability is a free trigger. {2}, tap, sacrifice: gain 3 life. It is the cheapest way to guarantee a Disappear check with no card spent.
Pizza Face animates artifacts, so target the right one. A Heartwood becomes a 0/0 Mutant with three counters, which is a 3/3 that keeps growing. Do not target a Food you intend to eat this turn.
Rat King’s recursion needs matching names. Returning Rat King returns only other Rat Kings; it will not return a Lord Dregg. Plan the graveyard accordingly.
Zhao triggers on every sacrifice, including costs. Embrace Oblivion’s additional cost pumps the team before damage.



Matchups







Opponent
Plan




Aggro
Trade early with Embrace Oblivion and Savor, land Rat King and block with Rats, stabilise behind Ice Cream Kitty lifegain and Lord Dregg fliers.


Control
Do not overextend into sweepers. Keep Codie and one Prepared engine back, force them to answer a stream of tokens, and win with an animated artifact plus Rogue’s Passage rather than a wide board.


Ramp / big mana
Race with Zhao-pumped Rats, save Stir Up Trouble for their payoff, and use Rogue’s Passage to make the damage unblockable.


Combo
The deck has no counterspells; the plan is speed, mulligan toward the fastest Rat King start and use Stir Up Trouble on their engine piece.

title: Hoardwake
text:
Early game
Turns one and two are about getting the hoard started and getting the first non-Treasure artifact on the board. Bilbo, Thief in the Night on two is the strongest opening: he is a 2/2 that can be attacking on turn three and, from then on, every attack lets you recast an artifact or a removal spell out of the graveyard. The Sackville-Bagginses on two is the value alternative — hold them until you have a Treasure or a spare body, because eating one on entry is a card and a Treasure at the same time.
Turn three is Dori, Bearer of Friends or The Misty Mountains Cold. Dori is the faster body (3/2 trample plus a Treasure), the saga is the better long game (a Treasure every chapter and a Dragon at four). Long-Bodied Grey Dog is the third option and the one to play at instant speed when the opponent attacks — a flash 2/2 with reach that makes a Treasure is a clean two-for-one against a flier.
If you have a Fateful Discovery in hand, play it before the next Treasure rather than after: a Treasure made with Discovery on the battlefield is a card, and the sequencing is the difference between a two-card turn and a three-card turn.

title: Hoardwake
text:
Mid game
Smaug the Magnificent on four is the pivot. He has haste, so he attacks the turn he lands, and he is only worth attacking with once the hoard is real — count the Treasures before combat, not after, because the trigger reads the board at the moment it resolves. A typical turn four with two Treasures in play is 4 damage in the air plus 2 damage to any target, and the upkeep Treasure means the number only goes up.
Glóin the Mighty on three is the turn that makes five-drops early: {R}{R} at the beginning of your first main phase each turn pays for Smaug, Wicked Worm or Fateful Discovery a turn ahead of schedule, and his adventure Easy Pickings deals 1 damage to each creature your opponents control, which is the answer to a board of one-toughness tokens.
From the middle of the game the deck is playing with spare artifacts, and that is when the sacrifice outlets become live. Stone-Giant of High Pass makes a 3/1 artifact Wall on entry and on every attack, so it always has food. Sacrificing a Treasure, a spent Getaway Barrel or a Stone Boulder to the Giant is 4 damage, and if The Sackville-Bagginses are in play that same sacrifice is also 1 life off an opponent.

title: Hoardwake
text:
The combo turn
The engine turn is: a Treasure producer, Fateful Discovery or The Arkenstone on the board, and either Smaug the Magnificent or a saga with three counters of lore.

Start the turn with the producers already in play, so the upkeep Treasure from Smaug and the chapter Treasure from The Misty Mountains Cold have both resolved.
Cast Long-Bodied Grey Dog or Dori, Bearer of Friends for another Treasure; Fateful Discovery draws a card for each of those Treasures as they enter.
Attack with Smaug the Magnificent. His trigger deals damage equal to the number of Treasures you control — with four Treasures that is 4 damage to a creature or to the opponent, on top of 4 in the air.
If the hoard has four or more Treasures and a saga is at any chapter, the saga sacrifices itself for a 6/6 red Dragon token with flying. Doing this on the same turn as the Smaug attack is usually the turn the game ends.
Spend the leftover mana on The Lonely Mountain for a 2/2 Dwarf, or on Stone-Giant of High Pass for 4 damage, whichever the board needs.

A realistic turn five: three Treasures plus a Treasure made by Dori, Fateful Discovery drawing twice, Smaug landing for 4 damage plus 4 in the air, and the saga flipping into a 6/6 Dragon on the following upkeep.

title: Hoardwake
text:
Win condition 2
The Dragons do not need Smaug the Magnificent. The Misty Mountains Cold is a four-chapter saga that turns itself into a 6/6 red flying Dragon token, and multiple copies are cumulative: a second copy starts a new Treasure every chapter and can flip as soon as the hoard is at four. Smaug, Wicked Worm is a 5/5 flying Dragon that pays you a card every time you cast a spell with Treasure mana and arrives with tapped Treasures equal to the artifacts your opponents control, which makes it a strong follow-up against artifact decks. Smaug, the Great Calamity is the top end: a 5/5 flying Dragon with five damage of removal stapled to its adventure.
The third, quiet win condition is burn. Stone-Giant of High Pass converts a spare artifact into 4 damage to any target, Getaway Barrel makes that sacrifice a free creature off the top thirteen cards, and the Sackville-Bagginses add 1 life per token sacrificed. Two Giants, a few Stone Boulders and a stocked hoard is 12 to 16 damage that never has to attack.

title: Hoardwake
text:
Key interactions and edge cases







Interaction
Ruling detail




The Misty Mountains Cold counts the Treasure it just made
The chapter creates a Treasure token and then checks whether you control four or more Treasures. The token from the same chapter counts, so with three Treasures in play the saga flips into a 6/6 Dragon on that chapter, and it can flip on chapter one if the hoard is already large


The saga is sacrificed whether or not it flips
The four-or-more check sacrifices the saga, and only if it sacrifices do you get the Dragon. If the hoard is at four and the saga has already sacrificed itself, a second copy is the way to get a second Dragon


Smaug the Magnificent’s trigger reads the board when it resolves
“Damage equal to the number of Treasures you control” is checked at resolution, not at attack declaration, so sacrificing Treasures for Stone-Giant damage before the trigger resolves shrinks it. Order the sacrifices after combat if the damage is going at the opponent


Smaug, Wicked Worm counts the opponent’s artifacts
Its entry trigger creates X tapped Treasures where X is the number of artifacts your opponents control, not yours. Against an artifact-light opponent it is a 5/5 flying Dragon for {3}{B}{R} and nothing more, which is still a fine body in a deck with this much reach


The Wicked Worm’s draw needs Treasure mana actually spent
The card draw only triggers if mana from a Treasure was spent on the spell. Casting a spell with lands alone is fine, it just does not draw


Desolation of Smaug kills your own non-Dragons
It deals 3 damage to each non-Dragon creature, including Dori, the Sackville-Bagginses, the Dog, Bilbo and Glóin. Cast it when your board is Dragons, Treasures and Stone Boulders, or when the opponent’s board is worth more than yours; the four extra mana can only be spent on Dragon spells


Orcrist, Goblin-cleaver chooses one creature type per hit
The trigger creates one Treasure for each creature you control of the chosen type. With Dragons in play, choosing Dragon is usually the biggest number; with a token board, choose whatever type is most numerous


The Arkenstone is played as an artifact in this list
The front face is a legendary artifact for {5} that gives your creatures +1/+1 and draws a card at every end step. Its adventure, Seek the Heart, costs {2}{W}, and this manabase produces no white, so treat the card as an artifact only


Fateful Discovery draws on every Treasure
A Treasure token is an artifact, so it triggers Fateful Discovery. Two Treasure producers in one turn with a Discovery out is three cards, which is how a deck this mana-hungry keeps hitting its land drops


Long-Bodied Grey Dog’s Treasure enters tapped
The token comes in tapped, so it cannot pay for a spell the turn it is made, but it still triggers Fateful Discovery and still counts for Smaug the Magnificent the same turn


Bilbo, Thief in the Night recasts artifacts from the graveyard
When he attacks you may cast an artifact, instant or sorcery from your graveyard. Getaway Barrel and Desolation of Smaug are the two best targets, and Bilbo’s cost reduction also applies to spells cast this way


Stone-Giant of High Pass eats artifacts only
The {2}{R} sacrifice requires an artifact: a Treasure token, a Stone Boulder, a Getaway Barrel or The Arkenstone. It cannot eat a creature, which is why the Sackville-Bagginses matter as the other outlet


The Lonely Mountain enters tapped without an Equipment
The land enters untapped only while you control an Equipment, and Orcrist is the only Equipment in the list. On the first three turns it is a tapped Mountain; from the turn Orcrist lands it is a normal Mountain that also makes 2/2 Dwarves with spare mana


Rogue’s Passage has no timing restriction
{4}, {T} can be activated in the declare-blockers step, after blockers are chosen. It pays for itself in any colour and is how a 6/6 Dragon token or a charged Smaug gets through a stalled board

title: Vanishing Act

Game plan phases
Turns 1 to 2 — set the table. Land, then either Deduce or Toxin Analysis. Both Investigate, so you trade a card for a card and leave a Clue behind. A first-turn Scene of the Crime is also fine: it enters tapped but it is a Clue that later cashes in for a card, a poison counter pair, and a Disappear trigger all at once.
Turns 3 to 4 — establish pressure. Turncoat Kunoichi, Oroku Saki, Shredder Rising and Michelangelo, Game Master are the three-mana core. Turns 4 to 6 — start the Sneak loop. Every attack step is now a decision: if a Ninja goes unblocked, return it to hand during declare blockers and pay a sneak cost. That is a rebate, a Disappear trigger and often lethal damage in the same moment. Lord Dregg and Putrid Pals convert that online Disappear into tokens and counters once the turn ends.
