title: Vanishing Act
text:
Early game
Spend the first two turns on cards that do not cost you anything: Deduce and Toxin Analysis both draw a card and leave a Clue, so the deck starts ahead on material. Do not attack into a bad block just to look busy. Against faster decks, hold Toxin Analysis to give a blocker deathtouch and lifelink; a Putrid Pals or Foot Mystic with deathtouch and lifelink blanks most ground assaults.

title: Vanishing Act
section: Mid game and the combo turn
text:
Mid game and the combo turn
The pattern that wins is always the same, and it happens inside one combat step:

Before combat, cast your draw spells and leave Clue tokens on the battlefield.
Attack with everything that can get through. Turtle Lair or Rogue’s Passage guarantees at least one unblocked attacker.
During declare blockers, return an unblocked attacker to your hand to pay a sneak cost. Cast Elektra for one and two black to kill a blocker and add a tapped, attacking 3/3; cast Oroku Saki for one and one black to keep the pressure and draw; cast Michelangelo, Improviser for two and two green to add a 4/4 that rewards connecting.
After combat, sacrifice each Clue you do not need (two mana each). Every sacrifice draws a card, turns Disappear on and, if a Persuasive Interrogators is on the battlefield, hands an opponent two poison counters.
At the end step, collect: Michelangelo, Game Master gets a counter, Lord Dregg makes a 1/1 flying Insect Warrior, and Putrid Pals arrives with two +1/+1 counters on any turn where something already left your battlefield.

Note that Turncoat Kunoichi exiles a creature only until it leaves the battlefield, so bouncing Turncoat to hand to pay a sneak cost returns that creature to its owner — pay the sneak cost instead when you want the exile to be permanent.

title: Vanishing Act
text:
Win condition two: poison
Persuasive Interrogators turns every sacrificed Clue into two poison counters, and a player with ten or more poison counters loses regardless of life total. Clues come from Deduce, Toxin Analysis, the Interrogators’ own enters-the-battlefield trigger and Scene of the Crime, so five Clue sacrifices finish the game. This is the route to take when the opponent clogs the ground with bigger creatures: keep two mana open, crack a Clue every turn, and let the poison accumulate while your Ninjas hold the board.

title: Vanishing Act
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep hands with two or three lands, at least one black source, and a play on turns two and three. A hand of six or seven lands is a mulligan. Since the mana base fetches basics, a one-land hand with an Evolving Wilds and a two-drop is playable; a one-land hand with only utility lands is not. Do not keep a hand that has no creature at all — this deck wins by attacking.

title: Vanishing Act
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Sleight of hand and Sneak: you pay a sneak cost only “if you also return an unblocked attacker you control to hand during the declare blockers step”. The attacker must actually be unblocked, so unblockable effects (Turtle Lair, Rogue’s Passage, Escape-style effects) are what make the mechanic reliable.
The bounced creature is not lost: casting it again later re-triggers its enters-the-battlefield ability, so returning Turncoat Kunoichi or Oroku Saki is rarely a real cost.
Shark Shredder, Killer Clone has first strike and steals a creature card from the defending player’s graveyard whenever it connects, and that creature enters tapped and attacking that player. Trade early, then take their best dead creature.
Shredder, Unrelenting gives another creature deathtouch when it enters and whenever it attacks. Pair it with first strike damage (Shark Shredder) or trample from a pumped Michelangelo, Game Master to make blocks hopeless.
Michelangelo, Improviser puts a creature card and a land card from hand onto the battlefield when it connects — free acceleration, and the land entering is not a sacrifice, so Disappear still needs a Clue or a bounce.
Fetch lands are Disappear triggers: cracking an Evolving Wilds in your second main phase switches Disappear on for the end step even if you never sacrificed a Clue that turn.
Clue sacrifices cost two mana each. Sequence them into spare mana rather than tapping out for a big creature and leaving three Clues unused.

title: Vanishing Act
text:
Matchups
Against aggro. You have more interaction than it looks: Elektra kills a small attacker on entry, Turncoat Kunoichi exiles one, Shredder’s Technique kills anything, and Toxin Analysis turns a blocker into a deathtouch lifelink wall. Foot Ninjas gains three life. Stabilise, then race with Lord Dregg’s fliers.
Against control. Sneak costs make your threats cheap enough to double-spell, Oroku Saki and Deduce keep your hand full, and the Disappear tokens rebuild a board after a sweeper. Persuasive Interrogators is the trump: poison ignores their life total.
Against midrange. Shark Shredder and Shredder, Unrelenting outclass most four- and five-drop blockers, and their graveyards become your resources. Use Rogue’s Passage to make the biggest deathtouch threat unblockable rather than fighting on the ground.

title: Face Value
text:
Overview
Everything in this deck is cast one of two ways: as itself for coloured mana, or face down as a 2/2 with ward {2} for a flat {3}. That second option is the whole reason a three-colour deck works here. Thirteen cards in the list have disguise, so a hand of blue lands and red spells can still put two bodies on the board on turn two and turn three. Ward {2} means the cheap spot removal that would otherwise punish a deck this small mostly cannot touch those bodies at all.
Pyrotechnic Performer converts every one of those flips into a trigger: the creature that turns face up deals damage equal to its power to each opponent. A face-down 2/2 flipping is two damage to both opponents for one or two mana. Bubble Smuggler flipping is six. With two Performers out those numbers double.
The investigate package is the fuel line rather than the win condition. Deduce, Gleaming Geardrake, Detective’s Satchel and a flipped Mistway Spy all hand you Clues, and Clues turn into cards at two mana each. Cards find more face-down creatures, more flips, and more Heroes for Human Torch. Torch turns every one of those Clue-draws into a point to the opponent’s face, and once you have another Hero in play he is a flying clock that the power-up ability can grow by three counters in a single activation.

title: Face Value
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Lead with a one-drop you do not mind trading: Mistway Spy face down is often better than face up, because the flip is what makes it a Clue engine. Hold Deduce until you have something to do with the card it draws, or use it end of turn as a two for one. Quicksilver from the opening hand is the fastest start available and costs nothing, so keep him in every seven that has two lands.


Mid game and the combo turn
The burst turn is: Pyrotechnic Performer already in play, two or three face-down creatures, five or six mana. Flip them one at a time. Each flip resolves its own enter-face-up trigger, and each one is a separate Pyrotechnic Performer trigger, so removal pointed at the Performer mid-sequence does not retroactively cancel the damage already dealt. Bubble Smuggler is the biggest single flip at six damage to each opponent; two Performers turn that into twelve.
Note the ordering on Mistway Spy: flip it first in a turn where you intend to connect, because the investigate rider applies to all combat damage that turn, not just the Spy’s. Two attacking bodies with the rider up is two Clues for one flip.


Win condition 2
Human Torch needs one other Hero. Brave Brawler at two mana is the cheapest reliable one, Quicksilver the fastest. Once both are down, every Clue sacrificed to draw is one damage to the opponent, and a Detective’s Satchel activation is two Clues and therefore two damage on top of the cards. Torch’s power-up costs {6}{R}, reduced by {2}{R} if he entered this turn, so the realistic line is Torch plus Brave Brawler on six mana, then a four mana power-up for a 5/5 flier.


Mulligan guide
Keep any seven with two or three lands and at least two cards that can be cast face down. Ship hands with no blue or red source and no generic three available by turn three. A hand of five lands and Pyrotechnic Performer is a mulligan: the deck needs bodies, not payoffs. Do not ship a hand with Quicksilver, two lands and a Deduce just because it has no red source.


Key interactions and edge cases

Case of the Filched Falcon solves at your end step once you control three artifacts. Clues, the Satchel itself and Thopters all count. Solving then sacrificing for {2}{U} makes a 4/4 flier out of a Clue token that still has the sacrifice-for-a-card ability.
Detective’s Satchel’s Thopter activation requires that you have sacrificed an artifact this turn. In practice you crack a Clue first, then tap the Satchel.
Gleaming Geardrake grows on every artifact sacrifice, including Clue cracks and the Satchel’s own activation cost. It is a legitimate secondary threat at four or five power with flying.
Unyielding Gatekeeper on your own permanent exiles it and returns it tapped, which is a way to blank a removal spell or re-trigger an enters ability. On an opponent’s permanent it gifts them a 2/2 Detective, so only use it that way when the exile matters more than the token.
Torch the Witness with X equal to half the target’s toughness plus one is the efficient way to both kill the creature and get the Clue.
Fugitive Codebreaker discards your hand when it flips. Flip it after you have emptied your hand of lands and cheap spells, not before.



Matchups
Against aggressive red and white decks the plan is to trade early and stabilise on Brave Brawler lifelink plus Torch the Witness, then win the long game with Clue cards. Against control, face-down bodies dodge sorcery speed sweepers only partially, so hold a flip and a Clue in reserve and force them to spend answers on 2/2s; ward {2} makes their cheap interaction very expensive. Against midrange green decks, Rogue’s Passage plus the 6/6 Smuggler is usually the cleanest path, because their blockers are big but slow.

Sanctum Lurker’s second ability is a continuous effect, not a trigger. A planeswalker at zero loyalty stays on the battlefield and can be activated again as long as you can add loyalty to it, which is what the empower effects are for.

title: Prep Rally
text:
Overview
Prep Rally is built entirely around Reality Fracture’s flagship mechanic. A creature that is prepared lets you cast a copy of its spell once; doing so unprepares it. Every nonland card here is either a prepared creature with a spell worth casting, a card that prepares a creature again, or a payoff that turns those free spells into damage.
The engine is the small re-prepare loop. Stingerquill Voxmancer and Paradox Shaper prepare themselves during your upkeep, so each turn they hand you a free spell: Vicious Verse for 1 damage to the opponent, or Omit Variables to mill three. Skycoach Waypoint (3 generic, tap: target creature becomes prepared) and Hexhaven Dueling Arena (2 generic, tap: target creature that attacked this turn becomes prepared) extend that loop to every other prepared creature in the deck, including the bigger bodies such as Variable Chaser and Pyre Rhymer. Codie, Ravenous Codex then copies each prepared spell you cast, which doubles the per-turn payload for as long as it lives.
The payoffs convert that trickle into a clock. Tomik, Izzet Sparkmage raises each noncombat damage instance by 1, so a single Vicious Verse copy hits for 2 (4 with Codie out). Master of Barbs turns any noncombat damage into a team-wide +1/+0, and Whiplash Wordsmith gains flying and haste on the same condition, so the drain and the beatdown plan feed each other.

title: Prep Rally
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Lead on cheap prepared creatures rather than pure attackers. Diviner of Victory and Stingerquill Voxmancer both cost one mana and both hand you a spell: Unwind History clears a small blocker and surveils, Vicious Verse starts the drain. Pompous Battlemage is a prowess body that comes with Improvised Act attached, which filters a land into a real card. Trading early is fine: Bloodline Recollector re-prepares itself at the end step whenever three or more creatures died that turn.


Mid game
Turn three and four are about payoffs, not bodies. Tomik, Izzet Sparkmage and Master of Barbs turn every free spell into progress, and Variable Chaser plus Pyre Rhymer give the deck a real clock while it grinds. Paradox Shaper’s upkeep Omit Variables quietly fills the graveyard, which makes Cruel Calculations a two-mana draw spell that scales with the number of mills you stacked that turn. Once Skycoach Waypoint or Hexhaven Dueling Arena is untapped, every creature with a prepare spell becomes a repeatable resource, and Semester Foreseer and Prudent Fateseer add Cadets to the board while doing it.


The combo turn
The deck’s best turn follows a fixed shape: start with one or more creatures left prepared from the previous upkeep, cast the cheap prepared spells first (Vicious Verse, Improvised Act) to trigger prowess and to switch Whiplash Wordsmith to flying and haste, then attack, then activate Hexhaven Dueling Arena in the second main phase to re-prepare the attacker you want next turn. With Codie out every prepared spell happens twice, so a board of four or five prepared creatures represents eight to ten spell effects, most of them damage. Tomik turns each Vicious Verse copy into 2 damage and each Ancestral Craving into 4, and Master of Barbs converts the whole sequence into a lethal attack step.


Win condition two
The second win is plain evasive damage. Variable Chaser is a 2/3 flier with prowess, Pyre Rhymer is a 3/3 with prowess, Whiplash Wordsmith is a 3/3 that gains flying and haste after any noncombat damage, and Peer Review supplies 2/2 Cadets. Master of Barbs stacks +1/+0 on the team for every turn you dealt noncombat damage, so the drain plan actively builds the combat plan. Codie’s second ability (one of each colour for each creature you control to become prepared) is a late-game dream this manabase cannot actually pay, so treat the copy clause as its real job.


Mulligan guide
Keep hands with one or two cheap prepared creatures plus a re-prepare engine or a payoff. Two or three lands with at least one black and one red source is the sweet spot. Six-card hands are fine when they contain Stingerquill Voxmancer plus any payoff; the deck snowballs from small boards. Ship hands that are all four-drops, hands with only colourless lands, and hands with no way to prepare anything past the first spell.


Key interactions and edge cases

Casting a prepared spell unprepares that creature, so time the copies. If Skycoach Waypoint is untapped, casting a copy this turn costs you nothing.
Prepared spells are real spells, so they trigger prowess on Pompous Battlemage, Variable Chaser, Pyre Rhymer and Tomik, and Codie copies them. Cast the cheap ones first.
Prudent Fateseer’s pump triggers only once each turn, so surveil before combat to make the attack step count.
Diviner of Victory grows on scry or surveil only. Omit Variables is a mill, not a surveil, but Unwind History, Peer Review and Thundering Falls all trigger it.
Cruel Calculations counts cards put into a graveyard from a library this turn, so cast it after Omit Variables (and after Codie has copied it).
Ancestral Craving is a drain: aim it at the opponent, who draws three and loses 3 life. With Tomik that is 4. With Codie, twice.
Bloodline Recollector only re-prepares when three or more creatures died in the turn, so use it after combat trades or a board wipe.



Matchups
The deck races rather than answers. Against aggro it wins the damage race with drain plus fliers, but it has almost no removal, so Diviner of Victory’s Unwind History and good blocks are the only interaction. Against grindy midrange it out-values most opponents: each upkeep re-prepares a creature and Codie doubles the payoff. Against combo it must be the aggressor, converting Vicious Verse copies and Whiplash Wordsmith’s haste into a fast clock. Against control it leans on Codie’s copy clause, Bloodline Recollector’s free card advantage and Arc of Fortune to rebuild after a wipe.

title: Twice-Told Tales

Curve and mana
Twenty-four lands: ten basics (5 Plains, 4 Mountain, 1 Island) plus fourteen colored and utility lands. White and red are the core — every Dwarf except Wizard’s Staff is {W}, {R}, or {R}{W} — so the verges and basics carry the early curve, while Cavern of Souls fixes any Dwarf spell and the blue sources (two Floodfarm, two Riverpyre, one Island) are enough for Wizard’s Staff’s single {U}.

The deck goldfishes four lands on turn four in roughly two games out of three and most wins are decided by turn six or seven — before that, ward {1} and the attack tax keep the growing army alive.

title: Twice-Told Tales

Early game
Lead with a two-drop legendary Dwarf — Thorin Oakenshield, Kíli the Resourceful, or Dáin, Lord of the Iron Hills are all fine openers, and Óin the Brave is the aggressive option. On turn two or three add Equipment: Dwarven Mattock enters attached to a Dwarf for +2/+2 and ward {1}, and Iron Hills Blacksmith’s Axe token brings the permanent count to three artifacts and legendaries. Once the story begins — usually turn three — everything downstream unlocks.

title: Twice-Told Tales
text:
Mid game
Fíli the Pathfinder is the priority four-drop: with the story live it anthems the whole team and starts converting every nontoken Dwarf into a 2/2 token. Dáin Ironfoot and Dwarven Shortsword both produce Equipment and tokens on entry, and each one of those entries draws a card through Kíli. Do not overextend into sweepers before Thorin’s ward is online; when it is, Day of Judgment-style answers cost extra and the story tax from Dáin discourages attacks entirely.

title: Twice-Told Tales
text:
The combo turn
The signature sequence: Fíli the Pathfinder equipped with Wizard’s Staff while Bifur is on the battlefield and the story endures. Cast or reanimate a nontoken Dwarf — Dwarven Shortsword makes one of its own — and Fíli’s trigger fires three times: once naturally, once from Bifur doubling a Dwarf’s triggered ability, once from the Staff doubling the equipped creature’s ability. One Dwarf in is three 2/2 tokens out, each draw through Kíli refilling the hand. Then The Lonely Mountain, discounted by every Equipment and Axe on the board, adds more 2/2s each activation, and the equipped attackers — double strike from Dáin Ironfoot, ward {1} from Thorin — attack for the game.

title: Twice-Told Tales
text:
Win condition 2
Balin, Loremaster is the wheel. With a hand of five or six cards, Balin’s own entry trigger (or any later Dwarf entering) discards the hand and draws exactly that many, and with the story told Balin deals that many damage to each opponent. The deck is built to refill: Kíli draws on Dwarf and Equipment entries, Óin loots, and the tokens keep the board growing while Balin’s triggers keep the life totals falling. A six-card wheel is 6 damage and a fresh hand; a second Dwarf in the same turn does it again.

title: Twice-Told Tales
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep any hand with two or three lands and a two-drop Dwarf. Hands with Fíli plus an Equipment or a Blacksmith are strong. Ship one-lander openers, hands full of four-plus drops, and hands without white and red available on turn two. Against aggressive decks, prioritize Thorin’s ward and Dáin’s tax over the doubling pieces; against control, Cavern of Souls and a cheap legendary are the keep.

title: Twice-Told Tales
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Storied counts artifacts, legendaries, and Sagas — every creature in the deck except Iron Hills Blacksmith is legendary, and every Equipment is an artifact, so three permanents is the story; the Blacksmith’s Axe tokens count.
Fíli’s token trigger only fires for nontoken Dwarves — tokens from The Lonely Mountain and Dwarven Shortsword do not chain into more tokens, but they do draw through Kíli and trigger Balin and Warleader-style effects.
Bifur doubles triggered abilities of Dwarves, and Wizard’s Staff doubles those of the equipped creature — when both are on Fíli, the trigger fires three times; if the Staff equips Balin instead, his wheel also fires twice (be careful: the second wheel discards the hand drawn by the first).
Wizard’s Staff’s prowess and its trigger-doubling apply only while it remains attached.
Thorin’s ward {1} needs the story; before turn three the Dwarves are vulnerable — sequence Equipment before the key creature when racing removal.
Dáin Ironfoot grants double strike only to equipped attacking creatures — Axes from his own entry and the Blacksmith count.
The Lonely Mountain enters tapped unless you control an Equipment, and its token activation is sorcery-speed — activate as part of the main-phase alpha strike, not in combat.
Cavern of Souls mana can only pay for Dwarf creature spells — it can’t cast Wizard’s Staff, Vow to Erebor, or the instants; the blue splash still needs its own sources.
Iron Hills and its counter ability are sorcery-speed and sacrifice the land — a finisher pump, not a value engine.

title: Twice-Told Tales
text:
Matchups

Aggro (fliers, lifegain, cats): the low curve races; Thorin’s ward {1} taxes their removal, and Dáin, Lord of the Iron Hills ends their attacks entirely once the story is live. Burst Lightning clears an early threat.
Midrange (counters, landfall): the token count outpaces their removal — every nontoken Dwarf replaced by three 2/2s through the doubling layer; double strike plus trample ends through their biggest blocker.
Control: Cavern of Souls makes every Dwarf uncounterable, ward {1} taxes sweepers and spot removal, and Kíli’s draw keeps the hand full; Balin’s wheel punishes their card-advantage game and wins through an empty battlefield.
Combo and big mana: the deck is the aggressor — establish the story early, tax their development, and close with an equipped double-striking team before their engine comes online.

title: Haggle the Horizon
text:
Mulligan guide

Keep: two or three lands in the right colours, at least one one-drop explorer, and either a Map-maker (Spyglass Siren, Sentinel of the Nameless City) or a removal spell with a bargain outlet.
Keep aggressive: Cenote Scout plus Nicanzil, Current Conductor plus lands is a real hand; the deck wins off a wide, pumped board rather than a single haymaker.
Trim: hands with no turn-one or turn-two play; hands where all three colours are required before turn three; five-land hands with only Boommobile and Loot, the Pathfinder as action.

title: Haggle the Horizon
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

A Map token is both a Bargain cost and an explore. Bargain is paid as you cast the spell, before it resolves; the Map’s own explore ability costs {1} and a tap and can only be activated as a sorcery. Decide which one you need before you commit.
Nicanzil triggers off the explore, not the explorer. It sees any creature you control exploring, so a Map cracked on your best attacker still adds a land or a counter.
Jadelight Spelunker’s X is locked in on cast. It explores X times on entry; if a land shows up, it goes to hand and the next explore can find another.
Boommobile’s mana and Boom Scholar’s discount only pay for abilities. They cannot cast spells, so plan the exhaust turn rather than the spell turn.
Sita Varma sets base power and toughness. Counters and other bonuses on your other creatures are overwritten for the turn; put counters on Sita Varma instead, and attack with the Merfolk whose counters you cashed in on the previous turn.
Exhaust abilities can only be activated once each. With no repeat-enabler in the deck, spend each exhaust on the turn it actually wins or stabilises.
Torch the Tower exiles the permanent it kills. Do not expect to remove something and leave it in a graveyard.

Control: hold Map tokens to force Torch the Tower and Brave the Wilds through as two-for-ones, and use manlands and Bitter Work Earthbend so your threats are lands that sweepers miss. Loot, the Pathfinder’s exhaust draw three replaces a wiped board.
Midrange: your counters accumulate faster than theirs because explore triggers are free. Keep Over the Edge for an artifact or enchantment that matters and win the long game with Bitter Work card draw.
Combo: you rarely have interaction beyond Torch the Tower and Over the Edge, so apply pressure early and hold Boommobile mana to threaten an exhaust that ends the game first.

title: Heartwood Hatchlings
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Heartwood Crafter is the ideal one-drop: it enters prepared, blocks well enough as a 1/1, and its mana ability pays for the Soul Tether it is holding. Turn two is Konstrari Improviser, or a second Crafter plus Artifist Acumen to dig. The important discipline in the first three turns is not to fire Soul Tether into an empty board. A Heartwood token with nothing to convert is a 2/2-for-three rate; the same token on the turn Draconic Visitor lands is a 5/5 flier. Fire the tethers when the mana is otherwise going unused, or when a Tenured Tethermage or Woodwork Prodigy is about to make the board wide enough that the extra artifact count matters.


Mid game
Woodwork Prodigy is the engine’s centre. It re-prepares during every upkeep, so from turn three it offers a Soul Tether each turn without spending a card. With Geist of Saint Thalia out, that copy costs two mana total and can be paid with a Heartwood plus one land. Tenured Tethermage converts a spare land into two tapped Heartwoods, which is the fastest way to reach five mana for Draconic Visitor while keeping the board intact. Karn, Gilded Guardian is the mid-game refill: a Heartwood is two colours, so Karn usually draws two cards on entry and leaves a 5/5 vigilance trampler behind.


The combo turn
The deck’s best turn is the one where Draconic Visitor arrives on a board that already holds prepared bodies and artifacts. Order it like this: cast Draconic Visitor, then cast every Soul Tether you have queued. Each copy now creates a 5/5 red Dragon with flying instead of a Heartwood. Woodwork Prodigy re-prepares at the next upkeep, which is another Dragon. Saheeli, Jewel of Avishkar converts each of those noncreature spells into a Thopter that also arrives as a Dragon, and Puppet Crafting on the Echoverse Fulcrum gives the board a 5/5 Construct that survives a creature-only sweeper. Two prepared bodies plus Saheeli is three Dragons in one turn off six or seven mana.


Win condition two
When the air plan is answered, the deck wins on the ground with artifact bodies. Craftwork Crusher is a 7/5 trampler that removes a creature or planeswalker and draws a card when it enters, Hungering Puppetbeast eats spare Heartwoods for +1/+1 counters and a keyword of choice, and Aerid Konstrari pumps itself by the number of artifacts you control. Hall of Echoes is the land half of this plan: five mana turns it into a copy of the biggest creature on the board, so the Crusher attacks as two 7/5 tramplers and Draconic Visitor can be doubled for a second conversion effect in the same turn.


Mulligan guide
Keep two or three lands with at least one green source, one prepared creature, and one payoff — Draconic Visitor, Karn, Gilded Guardian or Craftwork Crusher. A hand of Heartwood Crafter into Konstrari Improviser with no five-drop is still a keep, because Woodwork Prodigy and Tenured Tethermage are common enough that the deck finds its converter by turn five. Ship hands with no green source, hands whose only lands are Hall of Echoes and Konstrari Annex, and hands with two or more Draconic Visitor and no early creature.


Key interactions and edge cases

Prepared only re-arms through the card’s own text or an outside effect. Heartwood Crafter and Konstrari Improviser enter prepared once; after their Soul Tether resolves they are vanilla bodies. Woodwork Prodigy is the only card here that re-prepares every turn, which is why it is a four-of.
Draconic Visitor replaces the creation, it does not copy the token. Soul Tether under the Visitor makes one 5/5 Dragon and no Heartwood, so the mana rock is gone. Sequence ramp first, conversion second.
Saheeli, Jewel of Avishkar triggers on casting, and Soul Tether copies are sorceries, so the Thopter arrives before the Soul Tether resolves. With the Visitor out that Thopter is a 5/5 Dragon.
Tenured Tethermage’s land sacrifice is optional and it is a real cost: only take it with four or more lands, or when the two Heartwoods immediately pay for a five-drop.
Karn, Gilded Guardian counts colours among other artifacts you control. A Heartwood is both red and green, so one Heartwood is already two cards; the deck has no other multicoloured artifact, so expect two, not five.
The Echoverse Fulcrum’s five-mana ability destroys all creatures, Dragons included. It is a reset button for the turn the opponent has committed more than you, not a removal spell.
Puppet Crafting can enchant any non-Aura artifact, so a Heartwood token is a legal target and stays a mana rock while it is a 5/5. Enchanting the Echoverse Fulcrum makes the sweeper body-safe.
Hall of Echoes taps for colourless only. Two copies are utility, not mana fixing; do not count them as green or red sources when keeping a hand.
Craftwork Crusher’s choose-two modes are picked on entry, and the damage mode can hit a planeswalker or clear a blocker before the trample damage is assigned.



Matchups
Against aggro the deck is soft: there is no removal spell in the list, so the plan is to trade Heartwood Crafter and Konstrari Improviser early, land Karn as a 5/5 blocker, and race with Dragons from turn five. Against midrange it is a favourite, because the token engine goes wider than most midrange boards and Craftwork Crusher answers their best creature on entry. Against control, hold Draconic Visitor until you can cast it with a Soul Tether or a Saheeli trigger behind it, and lean on Karn and the Echoverse Fulcrum to keep cards flowing; a single Visitor that resolves usually ends the game in two attacks. Against combo, the deck has no interaction beyond damage, so it must mulligan toward the fastest curve and count on flying Dragons closing before the opponent’s engine comes online.

Infusion checks the whole turn, not just combat. Bloodfell Caves and Illegitimate Business gain 1 life as they enter, so a spell cast in the first main phase of the turn a tapland lands is already doubled. Bogwater Lumaret does the same for every creature that follows it.

Teacher’s Pest and Moseo are a loop, not a one-shot. {B}{G} returns Teacher’s Pest tapped for another lifegain attack, and Moseo returns whatever the Pest traded with, so a stalled board still generates Infusion fuel every turn.

title: Bellow and Burn
text:
Curve and mana
Twenty-three lands: twelve basics (4 Swamp, 4 Mountain, 4 Forest) and eleven nonbasics (2 Goblin-town, 1 Rogue’s Passage, 1 Restless Vents, 2 Blood Crypt, 1 Blazemire Verge, 2 Overgrown Tomb, 1 Deathcap Glade, 1 Thornspire Verge). Every source that produces black also produces a second color (Blood Crypt, Blazemire Verge, Overgrown Tomb, Deathcap Glade, Goblin-town, Restless Vents), which is what keeps a three-color deck this consistent.
The spell curve is deliberately flat: eleven cards at two mana or less, six at three, and only three cards above four mana. The deck wants to be at four lands on turn four, then spend every mana on a counter event rather than on a big spell.

title: Bellow and Burn
text:
Win condition 2
The Great Goblin’s burn does not require combat. Counting the triggers in a typical game — four amass spells, two Beorn’s Hospitality landfalls, three combat-step counters from Innkeeper’s Talent, one Goblin-town activation, and a Misty Mountains Raider attack — thirteen counter events is 26 damage from one card. That is the plan against decks that can block forever: stop attacking, keep placing counters, and let the bellow finish. Great Ugly-Looking Goblin’s exile clause and The Great Goblin’s impulse draw keep the amass spells coming while the opponent’s blockers rot.

title: Bellow and Burn
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep any hand with two or three lands, a source of black, and a two-drop (Goblin-town Flunkies, Bothersome Noisemaker, Beorn’s Hospitality, Innkeeper’s Talent). Against fast aggro, prioritize Beorn’s Hospitality and Fearsome Goblin Pair, which block and convert into amass when they trade.

title: Bellow and Burn
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

The Great Goblin triggers once per “put one or more counters” event, not once per counter. A flashback Tidings of War (amass 3) is still a single 2-damage trigger — but it grows the Army three times as much.
Innkeeper’s Talent level 3 doubles the counters placed, not the number of Great Goblin triggers. Use it for Army size, not for extra burn.
Azog, Moria’s Ruin gives the counters to the controller of the destroyed creature. Kill a small creature, your own creature (you draw a card), or a token — do not casually destroy a large creature an opponent controls unless you can answer the Army it creates.
Bolg of the North’s sacrifice and Fearsome Goblin Pair’s death trigger both resolve in the same turn if you sacrifice the Pair: 4 counters from the death plus Bolg’s damage, with excess damage converting to even more counters.
Amass always targets the single Army you control. If the opponent kills the Army, every future amass makes a new 0/0 and starts again — which is why Warg Tactics’ hexproof and Innkeeper’s Talent’s ward matter more than they look.
Goblin-town enters tapped. Sequence it on a turn where the tapped source does not cost you a play, or keep it for the sacrifice activation in the late game.
Clap! Snap! is cast from exile, so Bothersome Noisemaker sees it as a noncreature spell and amasses on top of the adventure’s own amass 2.
Gnashing of Teeth’s first mode exiles the creature if it would die — useful against opponents recycling their own graveyard.

Ruling detail




Ferocious checks power four or greater
All five ferocious cards check for any creature you control with power four or greater when the ability triggers. Ordinary Bear (4/5), Beorn the Fierce (6/6) and Large Bear (5/5) get there on their own; a Bear token with counters or a Wolf under Beorn does too


Beorn’s combat trigger makes new Bears
The trample counter goes on up to one target creature you control and that creature becomes a Bear in addition to its other types. Point it at a Wargling or a Wolf token and the anthem begins applying to it, and it counts toward the three-Bear condition for the draw


Chief Warg’s Company needs two other Wolves
It is a Wolf itself, but the attack restriction counts only other Wolves. Two of Wargling, Ravening Warg, Nighthowl Pursuer, Wilderland Scrounger, The Chief Warg or a Wolf token satisfy it


Dancing from Dark to Dawn counts creature spells only
The counter trigger fires on casting a creature spell, so the activation uses the mana value of what you cast. Landfall tokens do not trigger it, but they do trigger on the land itself


Mirkwood is a sorcery-speed sacrifice
The two counters must be used at sorcery speed, and the land is gone afterwards. Activate it after tapping it for mana in the same turn


Little Bear’s untap
It untaps another target creature you control on entry; if that creature is a Bear it also gets a +1/+1 counter. Flashing it in during combat untaps an attacker you have already attacked with


Pinecone Strike is modal
Three damage to a creature, or destroying an artifact token, or both if you have two targets. It is the cleanest answer to Treasure and Map tokens


No reach in the red splash
Beyond Large Bear’s reach and Wilderland Scrounger’s size, the deck is soft to fliers. Quarrel and Pinecone Strike are the answers, and racing with trample is often better than trading

Counting the conditional Verge lands and Cavern of Souls for creature spells, the mana base offers roughly sixteen sources of black, twenty of green and four of red — green is the deepest because Beorn the Fierce and Dancing from Dark to Dawn both ask for double green, while red is a four-source splash for Pinecone Strike alone.

Turn three is where the deck stops being a tribal deck and starts being a machine. Chief Warg’s Company is the single most important card in this window: a 5/3 with trample turns on every ferocious trigger in your hand at once and adds a 2/2 Wolf every upkeep. Remember its restriction — it cannot attack unless you control two or more other Wolves, so pair it with Nighthowl Pursuer, Wargling, a Wolf token, or hold it back as the blocker that also makes attackers.
Once power four is present, sequence your attacks so the payoffs stack: Wargling first, because it grants trample to the whole team for the turn, then Nighthowl Pursuer’s +2/+2 and Wilderland Scrounger’s team counters, with The Chief Warg drawing you a card on the same swing. When the ground is stalled, the deck goes wide without ever casting a token spell. Chief Warg’s Company makes a 2/2 green Wolf every upkeep, Head of the Hunt turns every opposing creature that dies into a 2/2 green Wolf, and Dancing from Dark to Dawn makes a 2/2 green Bear token on every land drop. Beorn the Fierce then does double duty: each Bear token is a 4/4, and with three or more Bears on the battlefield you draw two cards at the start of combat.
The tokens are not just chaff. Rhovanion Rampager eats the smallest of them to grow itself equal to their power, Duskwatch Hunter walks past token blockers entirely, and Beorn the Fierce’s combat trigger can promote a Wolf token into a Bear to pick up the anthem. Against a board of 1/1s and 2/2s, this half of the deck wins by itself.

Mulligan guide
Keep hands with two or three lands, one one-drop or two-drop, and one card that puts counters on something. A hand with Beorn’s Hospitality plus four lands is a keep: the enchantment turns every land into a counter and the deck’s top end does not need a fast start. Ship hands that show only tapped lands and no action, and ship one-land hands even with a perfect curve, because the deck’s engine wants to see land four on schedule.

title: Wargwake
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Chief Warg’s Company counts other Wolves only: a 2/2 Wolf token from its own upkeep trigger is one of the two it needs to attack.
Wargling grants trample to every creature you control, not just Wolves, and the trigger only fires while a power-four creature is attacking.
Beorn the Fierce’s combat trigger makes the target a Bear in addition to its other types, so a Wolf can be an anthem target and still count for Mirkwood and Chief Warg’s Company.
Large Bear has haste: casting it on turn five with a Wolf token already attacking turns ferocious on in the same combat step.
Duskwatch Hunter’s entry trigger can put the counter on any creature, including itself or one of your tokens, and it cannot be blocked by tokens at all.
Rhovanion Rampager sacrifices before it grows: feed it a 2/2 Wolf token and it gains two counters, so a single Company token per turn turns it into a genuine threat.
Quarrel is one-way damage, not a fight — your creature deals damage equal to its power and takes none. Aim a 5/3 Company at a four-toughness blocker and the Company survives.
Gnashing of Teeth exiles instead of destroying, which is exactly what you want against graveyard decks, but it does not feed Head of the Hunt’s token trigger — use Quarrel or a Pinecone Strike when you specifically want the 2/2 Wolf.
Pinecone Strike can choose both modes, so it can kill an artifact creature token outright, and its damage also exiles the creature it kills.
Beorn’s Hospitality’s animation makes it a Bear creature whose power and toughness equal your land count, which also counts towards Beorn the Fierce’s three-Bear draw trigger.
Mirkwood enters tapped and can only be sacrificed at sorcery speed, so play it on a turn you are not holding up interaction, and sacrifice it in a second main phase after attackers are set.
Twenty-four lands is deliberate: the two landfall engines both convert land drops into board presence, so a flood is closer to a win than to a loss.
Name Wolf with Cavern of Souls: it covers nine creature cards in the deck, while Bear would only cover Large Bear and Beorn the Fierce.

Attack with Fire Lord Azula and Iroh (firebending 2 each), ideally with Sozin's Comet cast first (firebending 5 on everything) or Fire Nation Palace activated ({1}{R}, {T}) to grant firebending 4 — an Iroh with both printed firebending 2 and the Palace’s firebending 4 generates 6 red mana per attack.
With the combat mana banked, cast from the graveyard: Burst Lightning, Firebending Lesson, Traumatic Critique with X as high as the mana allows. Azula copies each spell; with Firebender Ascension at four quest counters, the copy trigger itself is copied.
Repeat each turn. Shimmercreep and Explosive Prodigy add on-entry damage, Ozai turns leftover mana red and becomes an indestructible flyer at six-plus unspent mana, and the loop outpaces any removal that isn’t graveyard hate.

title: Kindle the Archive
text:
Win condition 2: the Vivid beatdown
Burn is plan A; the board is plan B. Squawkroaster is a double striker whose power equals the number of colors among permanents you control — 5 or more in this deck, so it attacks as a 5/5 double strike minimum. Glister Bairn makes it +X/+X bigger every combat, and Prismabasher-style team pumps come from the same Vivid scaling. Self-Destruct turns a pumped Squawkroaster into a one-shot fireball (it deals damage equal to its power to any target), and Ozai — trample, haste, firebending 4, flying and indestructible at six-plus unspent mana — closes the game alone. Shimmercreep’s life drain also wins without ever attacking.

title: Kindle the Archive
text:
Mulligan guide

Keep: 2–3 lands covering red plus one other color, a surveil source (Glarb, Gorehound, Risky Research) or early burn, and a path to Iroh by turn 5.
Trim: 5+ land hands, single-color hands, and hands with only the top end (Ozai, Sozin’s Comet, multiple Traumatic Critiques) and no early play.
The deck is happy to trade card quantity for quality: Traumatic Critique, Glarb, and the surveil lands all convert surplus cards into archive fuel.

title: Kindle the Archive
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Multiple Firebending instances stack. A creature with firebending 2 (Iroh) that gains firebending 4 from Fire Nation Palace triggers twice: 6 red mana per attack. Sozin’s Comet on top makes it 9.
Firebending mana lasts until end of combat — cast the flashback burn during the declare-attackers step while the mana is available. Iroh’s flashback works any time during your turn.
Iroh’s flashback is only during your turn, and each cast exiles the card after resolution — the loop is per-turn, not infinite. Multiple copies of a burn spell in the yard extend the chain.
Firebender Ascension copies attacking-creature triggered abilities — Azula’s spell-copy trigger and every Firebending mana trigger qualify. It does not copy static abilities.
Traumatic Critique’s loot is a feature: discarding burn into the archive sets up next turn’s flashback chain.
Glarb casts MV 4+ spells from the top — Iroh, Ozai, Squawkroaster, and Shimmercreep all qualify; surveil first to put the right card on top.
Ozai’s mana conversion means unspent Firebending red, treasure from Flick a Coin-style effects, and other colors all become red, letting one combat’s mana cast any mix of flashback spells.
Graveyard hate is the deck’s Achilles heel — versus heavy exile, pivot to the Vivid beatdown plan (Squawkroaster, Ozai) and stop over-investing in the archive.

title: Kindle the Archive
text:
Matchups

Aggro: early burn clears the board; Explosive Prodigy and Shimmercreep trade life-for-life favorably; Ozai becomes an indestructible wall at six unspent mana. Surveil toward removal first, engine second.
Control: the flashback loop is card-advantage-proof — every burn spell is a reusable threat, and counterspells only delay it. Glarb’s top-of-library casting dodges hand disruption. Fire Nation Palace’s firebending grant is instant-speed and uncounterable.
Midrange: race their threats with copied burn; Azula plus a stocked archive out-damages most midrange clocks. Squawkroaster beats blockers with double strike.
Graveyard hate (Rest in Peace-style): swap to plan B — Squawkroaster plus Self-Destruct and Ozai beatdown; keep surveil minimal and use the Vivid creatures as the primary threat.

The “combo turn” in this deck is a stacked combat step rather than an infinite loop. A representative turn:

Two nonland permanents enter (a Treasure plus a Spirit token, or two Treasures, or a Monument trigger plus a creature).

title: Gilded Reprise

Monument to Endurance drains 3 whenever you discard and choose that mode; with Charming Scoundrel, Seize the Spoils and Laughing Mad all discarding, that is 3 life a turn from an artifact that also makes Treasures.
Death to Our Enemies collects a plan counter on every noncreature spell and cashes four counters into 7 damage divided between one or two targets. Flashback spells trigger it twice on their own.
The Sackville-Bagginses turns every Treasure crack into 1 life lost, including Treasures spent on flashback costs.

Acceptable: four lands including one Restless land, plus Seize the Spoils and a payoff.

title: Gilded Reprise
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Celebration counts permanents, not cards. A Treasure token, a Spirit token, a cracked Monument trigger and a resolved creature all count. Two Treasures on the same turn is the cheapest way to switch it on.
Treasure tokens are artifacts that sacrifice for mana. The Sackville-Bagginses triggers on any token you sacrifice, so cashing a Treasure for the flashback half of Antiquities on the Loose both pays the spell and drains the opponent.
Flashback casts are cast from the graveyard, not from the hand. Antiquities on the Loose reads “if this spell was cast from anywhere other than your hand”, so the flashback half gives the Spirits their counters. It also triggers Death to Our Enemies, because the spell is a noncreature spell.
Goddric keeps the Dragon stats only that turn. The Celebration check happens continuously, so if you can make two permanents enter before combat, attack first and cast afterwards when the stats do not matter.
Magda, the Hoardmaster needs a crime. Targeting an opponent, something they control, or a card in their graveyard turns on the Treasure. Reckless Ransacking aimed at a blocker and Belligerent of the Ball are the usual ways to commit one.
Monument to Endurance modes cannot repeat in one turn. Choose the drain on turns you are racing and the Treasure on turns you are developing.
Exiling is relevant. Flashback exiles the card after the second cast, so plan the first cast; there is no third use.

Cast Web of Life and Destiny for {2}{G} or so (Convoke with whatever did not attack). From now on, every combat starts with a free creature from your top five.
Swing with the whole choir. If blocked, Reactor Raid or Tarrian’s Journal turns a dead body into cards, and the Tomb of Aclazotz casts the next creature from the graveyard.

title: Fertile Chorus
text:
Win condition 2: the rupture
Singularity Rupture ({3}{U}{B}{B}) destroys all creatures and then has any number of target players mill half their library, rounded down. Two casts from a 60-card deck remove 45 cards; with the natural mill from Lasyd Prowler and Midnight Tilling, the opponent’s library dies before their life total. The wipe also dumps your own creatures into the yard — where Bloodline Bidding (Convoke, choose Snake) returns Lasyd Prowler, Naga Fleshcrafter, Constrictor Sage and Omni-Changeling all at once for an immediate board.

title: Fertile Chorus
text:
Mulligan guide

Keep: two-plus lands including green, a two-drop, and either a mill source (Lasyd Prowler, Midnight Tilling) or a Renew creature.
Trim: five-plus land hands, all-one-color hands, and hands whose only plays are 5+ mana cards.
The deck mulligans well: the graveyard smooths draws, and Midnight Tilling finds whatever the mill reveals.

title: Fertile Chorus
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Renew exiles from the graveyard — it is a sorcery-speed activation, so plan it on your turn; it also shrinks the yard, which matters only for Lasyd Prowler’s Renew count (land cards only — lands stay).
Kheru Goldkeeper counts every card that leaves — one Renew activation exiles one card and creates one Treasure; two cards leaving creates two Treasures.
Bloodline Bidding’s type choice: Snakes cover Lasyd Prowler, Naga Fleshcrafter and Constrictor Sage; Omni-Changeling is every type, so any choice works.
The Tomb of Aclazotz casts creatures from the graveyard with a finality counter — they exile on death instead of returning, so use the Tomb for pressure, not for fuel.
Singularity Rupture hits your own board — that is the point: the wipe refills the yard for Bidding.
Web of Life and Destiny at combat — the free creature enters at the beginning of combat, so it cannot attack that turn but is untapped Convoke fuel for the next spell.
Reactor Raid needs a sacrifice to draw — sacrifice a tapped attacker after combat, or an artifact, to keep the yard stocked.

title: Fertile Chorus
text:
Matchups

Aggro: Mutant Town’s life gain and Qarsi Revenant’s lifelink buy turns; Vote Out and Constrictor Sage slow the swarm; the Tomb’s graveyard casting out-values any topdeck war.
Control: the deck’s threats are uncounterable-by-accident (Renew activates from the graveyard, the Tomb casts from the graveyard, manlands-style Town lands dodge sorcery-speed sweepers). Singularity Rupture mills them out even if they clear the board.
Graveyard hate: hard exile effects hurt. Plan B is real — the creatures are fine on their own, Omni-Changeling and Naga Fleshcrafter copy anything, and Web of Life does not touch the graveyard at all.

title: Deep-Down Thunder
text:
Curve and mana
23 lands: 2 Goblin-town, 1 Rogue’s Passage, 9 Swamp, 7 Mountain, 4 Forest. That is 11 black sources, 9 red sources and 4 green sources in a deck whose green cards are two copies of a five-mana enchantment and one five-mana legend, so the green splash is a late-game luxury rather than a requirement. Only two lands enter tapped and none of them cost life, so the deck can play an untapped land every turn and cast its hybrid cards with whatever it drew.
Nonland curve: one-drop x4, two-drops x12, three-drops x14, four-drops x2, five-drops x5. Average nonland CMC 2.78. Twenty-six creatures plus eleven noncreature cards, and nine of those eleven amass. The deck is deliberately top-light: the largest thing it casts costs five, so the Army does the heavy lifting and the curve keeps re-triggering The Great Goblin instead of tapping out for a single threat.

title: Deep-Down Thunder
text:
Early game
Turns one to three are about setting the board so that the first real amass turn is worth double. Lead with Tidings of War if you have it, because a one-mana amass 1 puts a 1/1 Goblin Army on the board and starts the ping counter at zero cost. Goblin-town Flunkies on turn two is the ideal follow-up: a hasty 1/1 that amasses 1 means three power swinging on turn two and 2 damage from The Great Goblin once he arrives.
The Great Goblin is the priority on turn three. Everything else in the deck is worth more after he is on the board, so do not trade a Goblin-town Flunkies into a block on turn two if it delays him. If you have no Great Goblin, Bothersome Noisemaker plus any amass spell is the fallback: the Noisemaker still builds the Army even without the payoff attached.

title: Deep-Down Thunder
text:
Mid game
Turns four to six are the engine turns. The rule that matters most is that The Great Goblin triggers once per counter-placing event, not once per counter, so amass 1 and amass 4 both deal 2 damage. That inverts the usual priority: many small amass events beat one big one. Cast Tidings of War before Rage into the Valley, and cast the Noisemaker before both, because his trigger is a separate event for every noncreature spell.
Sacrifice outlets are the second half of the mid game. Rhovanion Rampager’s attack trigger and Tom, Bert, and William’s one-mana ability both turn your own creatures into counters, and Fearsome Goblin Pair and Rhovanion Rampager both amass when they die, so sacrificing them is a net gain rather than a cost. Azog, Moria’s Ruin is the cleanest version of the trick: destroy your own Fearsome Goblin Pair, draw a card from Azog’s last clause, amass 1 from Azog and amass 4 from the Pair’s death trigger, which is two Great Goblin triggers, five counters and a card for three mana.

title: Deep-Down Thunder
text:
The combo turn

Land drop, then Goblin-town if you can afford to spend it: two black and a red, sacrifice, two +1/+1 counters on the Army and 2 damage from The Great Goblin.
Cast Goblin Plate Mail: amass 1 (2 damage), then it attaches itself to the Army, which is now a menacing plus-one-power threat. If Bothersome Noisemaker is out, that amass 1 is a second event and another 2 damage.
Cast Rage into the Valley: draw a card, lose 1 life, amass 2 (2 damage), plus the Noisemaker’s amass 1 (2 damage).
Flash back Tidings of War for three and a red: amass 3 (2 damage), plus the Noisemaker’s amass 1 (2 damage).
Attack with the Army and any hasty Goblin. Goblin Plate Mail gives menace, so the Army has to be double blocked; Dreaded Bat-Cloud is often a one-mana 4/2 flier that attacks in the same turn.

A worked example with The Great Goblin and Bothersome Noisemaker on board and three mana up: Goblin-town sacrifice (2 damage, two counters), then Rage into the Valley (2 damage from Rage, 2 damage from the Noisemaker, two more counters) is 8 damage and four counters on the Army in a single turn, and the Army attacks for at least four. That is a lethal swing from an empty-looking board.

title: Deep-Down Thunder
text:
Win condition 2
The ping damage is not a backup, it is the other half of the plan, but it can stall once the opponent stabilises behind blockers or gains life. That is what the Army is for. All the counters in the deck go onto one token, so the token is usually a 5/5 or better by turn five, and Rogue’s Passage’s four-mana activation makes it unblockable. Goblin Plate Mail’s menace does the same job cheaply against single blockers.
If the Army is answered, the deck rebuilds from the graveyard sideways: Part in Friendship puts a fresh creature onto the battlefield every time a nontoken creature dies, Tom, Bert, and William returns from the dead as an artifact and its sacrifice ability converts a large creature into drawn cards, and The Great Goblin’s second ability exiles a card from the top of your library on every Goblin death so the next wave is sitting in exile ready to be cast.

title: Deep-Down Thunder
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep two to four lands with at least one black source and one red source, plus at least one play that costs two or less. The ideal opener is Tidings of War or Goblin-town Flunkies, a second land, and The Great Goblin or Bothersome Noisemaker. Mulligan hands with fewer than two lands, hands with no red source (Tidings of War, Goblin-town Flunkies, Bothersome Noisemaker and Misty Mountains Raider are all red), hands with three or more five-drops and no action before turn three, and hands whose only black source is a Goblin-town that will enter tapped. Because only two lands in the deck enter tapped, there is no real reason to keep a slow hand.

title: Deep-Down Thunder
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

The Great Goblin triggers on “one or more counters”, so amass 4 is one trigger worth 2 damage, exactly like amass 1. Fire your smallest amass effects first if the opponent is at a life total the pings can finish.
The reminder text is the rules text: amass creates a 0/0 black Goblin Army token that becomes a Goblin, so The Great Goblin’s second ability (another Goblin, Orc or Army dying) applies to the Army itself. Losing the Army to a removal spell still draws you a card.
Azog, Moria’s Ruin gives the counters to the creature’s controller, not to you. Destroying an opposing creature hands the opponent an Army; destroying your own gives you the counters and a card, which is why Fearsome Goblin Pair is his best target.
Rhovanion Rampager’s death trigger amasses a number of counters equal to its power at the moment it died, not its base power, so pump it with the attack trigger before chumping.
Goblin-town sacrifices itself for two counters at sorcery speed, and the target has to be a Goblin or Orc, never a Bat or a Wolf. The Army is a Goblin, so the Army is always a legal target.
Flashback exiles Tidings of War, so the flashed-back copy is a one-shot. Cast the one-mana copy first and hold the three-mana one for the turn the ping damage matters.
Bothersome Noisemaker only cares about noncreature spells. Goblin Plate Mail, Rage into the Valley, Goblin-town’s ability and both halves of Tidings of War all trigger him; playing a creature does not.
Meager Meal puts a +1/+1 counter on a creature and gives a target player 2 life. Both halves are separate targets, so target yourself with the life gain or the opponent with a counter. The counter is another Great Goblin trigger.
Part in Friendship triggers only on nontoken creatures, so the Army token does not feed it. It also triggers only once each turn, so keep one nontoken Goblin in reserve rather than trading the whole board.
Dreaded Bat-Cloud’s discount checks whether a creature died this turn at all, yours or theirs. Goblin-town Flunkies attacking into a trade, a sacrificed Fearsome Goblin Pair, or an Azog trigger all turn it into a one-mana 4/2 flying deathtouch.
Tom, Bert, and William’s sacrifice ability draws cards equal to the sacrificed creature’s power. Sacrificing the Army to it is a real play when the Army is unblockable-size and you need to find the last burn spell.

title: Cold Case Haunting
text:
Overview
“Cold Case Haunting” fuses two Standard mechanics into one engine. Eerie (Duskmourn) rewards every enchantment that enters under your control; Clue (Murders at Karlov Manor and friends) rewards making, cracking, and sacrificing artifact tokens. The bridge cards do both at once: Case of the Filched Falcon is an enchantment that makes a Clue on entry, Curious Inquiry is an Aura that investigates on combat damage, and Teysa, Opulent Oligarch converts opponent life loss into Clues and Clues into flying Spirits.
The game plan is an enchantment snowball. Play eerie creatures early, then chain cheap enchantments (Cases, Auras, Rooms, enchantment creatures) so each entry triggers every eerie payoff. Clues smooth the draws, keep the chain going, and feed the alternate poison kill. Rooms are the premium fuel because a single Room can produce two or three eerie events: entering, making a Glimmer enchantment-creature token, and unlocking its second door.
The deck plays the full rolled color set WUBRG. Fetch lands and They Went This Way (itself a Clue maker) fix the five-color manabase; red arrives via Infernal Phantom, an eerie payoff that turns into reach.

title: Cold Case Haunting
text:
Approach

Game plan by phase

Setup (turns 1-3). Deploy eerie payoffs: Balemurk Leech, Entity Tracker, Gremlin Tamer, Teysa. Cast Case of the Filched Falcon for an early Clue and its eerie trigger. Curious Inquiry on a flier starts the Clue economy.
Engine (turns 4-5). Land Ghostly Dancers or Fear of Infinity. Start chaining enchantments: each one makes a 3/1 Spirit (Dancers), drains 1 per Leech, draws a card per Tracker, and makes a Gremlin per Tamer.
Combo turn. With two or more eerie payoffs in play, cast several enchantments in one turn. Grand Entryway counts twice on its own (entry plus its Glimmer token); unlocking Elegant Rotunda adds a third event plus +1/+1 counters. Crack Clues between spells to keep the chain fueled.
Finish. Drain plus a flying swarm closes the game. If the opponent races ahead on life, pivot to poison: Persuasive Interrogators plus five Clue sacrifices ends the game regardless of life totals.

title: Cold Case Haunting
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Prioritize an eerie creature over a lone enchantment: payoffs first, fuel second. Leech on turn 2 then a Falcon or Inquiry on turn 3 already drains for 1 and draws a card. Teysa rewards any damage Leech or the Falcon Bird deals. Hold fetch lands until you know which color the hand needs.


Mid game
Get a second eerie payoff down before chaining multiple enchantments in one turn. Fear of Infinity is best in the graveyard: every enchantment entry returns it to hand, so recasting it is another enchantment entry plus a 2/2 flying lifelink attacker. Ghostly Dancers doubles as recursion, pulling back a Falcon or Inquiry to cast again.


The combo turn
A typical kill turn with two Leeches, one Dancers, and one Tracker: cast Grand Entryway (drain 2, draw 1, Spirit, Glimmer), cast Case of the Filched Falcon (drain 2, draw 1, Spirit, Clue), unlock Elegant Rotunda (drain 2, draw 1, Spirit, counters), then crack the Clue to draw into more enchantments. Four to five entries in a turn is 8 to 10 damage from Leeches alone, plus a growing flying army. Cracked Clues also trigger Teysa Spirits and Interrogators poison.


Win condition 2: poison
Persuasive Interrogators turns the Clue economy into an alternative kill that ignores life totals and lifegain. Each Clue sacrificed (for {1} via the normal draw activation, or through Fountainport) deals 2 poison; five sacrifices wins. Keep Clues alive while Interrogators resolves rather than cracking them for cards.


Mulligan guide
Keep hands with two to three lands and an early play (Leech, Gremlin Tamer, Falcon, Inquiry, or Tracker). A hand with Ghostly Dancers or Teysa but no early eerie payoff is slow; mulligan hands that need three colors by turn 3 unless a fetch land is present. Seven-card hands with four or more lands and no spell are playable but lean to mulligan at five lands.


Key interactions and edge cases

Eerie triggers on any enchantment entering under your control, including tokens: Grand Entryway’s Glimmer tokens trigger eerie on their own entry.
A Room counts as a second eerie source when its last locked door is unlocked: casting the Room is one enchantment entry, unlocking the other door is a separate eerie event.
Fear of Infinity returns to hand only from the graveyard. If it is on the battlefield it stays there; it must die or be discarded first.
“When a Clue you control is put into a graveyard from the battlefield” (Teysa) includes cracking Clues for cards, not sacrificing via costs that exile them.
Case of the Filched Falcon solves once you control three artifacts; Clues and Treasure tokens count. The solved Falcon can animate a Clue token into a 4/4 flying Bird, which Rogue’s Passage then sends through unblocked.
No Witnesses destroys your own creatures too. Play it after your Clues and before committing a second wave, or when the board state favors resetting.
Infernal Phantom wants enchantment density: each entry makes it a bigger threat, and even a chump block turns into direct damage.



Matchups

Aggro swarms: No Witnesses resets the ground; Leech and Teysa keep the life total safe while Gremlin Tamer blocks. The flying spirits race well.
Control: Prioritize Entity Tracker and Clue draw to out-card the opponent; Grand Entryway rooms and enchantment recursion are resilient to sorcery-speed removal. Avoid overcommitting into a wipe.
Lifegain: pivot to the poison route; do not race the life total.
Big mana: pressure with the enchantment chain and finish with Rogue’s Passage on a solved Falcon Bird before the opponent’s haymakers resolve.

title: Spark Tithe
text:
Early game
Turns one and two are about putting a permanent that is also an engine onto the board. Repurposed Enforcer is the best turn-two play because it is a 3/2 that empowers for the whole team on the first attack; Way of the Pyromancer is the best turn-two play when you expect to need mana later, because it creates a Jace token with two loyalty and gives every planeswalker a red mana ability. title: Spark Tithe
text:
Mid game
Sanctum Lurker on turn three is the pivot. Before Lurker, Jace tokens are expendable; after Lurker they are permanent ability sources that cannot be killed by spending their own loyalty. The turn after Lurker lands, add Command the Stage: the sorcery makes a Cadet, grows every other Cadet, and then keeps coming back every upkeep because Lurker’s drain is noncombat damage.
The sacrifice engine comes online with Way of the Deathbringer. Each Jace token you control has its own loyalty ability activation, so with two tokens in play you can sacrifice two Cadets in a single turn for two Beasts, as long as the tokens have the two loyalty to pay.

title: Spark Tithe
text:
The combo turn
The engine turn is a loop of small, free conversions rather than a single storm turn:

Command the Stage is in the graveyard at the start of the turn; the upkeep trigger returns it to hand.
Cast it for {2}{R}: a Cadet enters, and every other Wizard token gets a +1/+1 counter (Mabel converts those entries into more counters).
Activate Way of the Deathbringer on the Jace token with the most loyalty: pay two loyalty, sacrifice the new Cadet, create a 4/4 green Beast with trample.
The sacrifice triggers Way of the Necromancer: one loyalty counter on every planeswalker, which refunds half the cost of the activation.
Activate Sanctum Lurker’s [+2] on a second token: 1 damage to each opponent and 1 life, which triggers Way of the Mentor for another loyalty counter on every planeswalker.
Attack with the Beast and the surviving Cadets, then repeat next turn: the sorcery comes back again because the drain was noncombat damage.

Two Beasts a turn from two tokens plus a recurring three-mana sorcery is the normal operating rate, and every sacrifice also pays Edgar a life and every life gain pays Way of the Mentor a loyalty counter.

title: Spark Tithe
text:
Win condition 2
The drain is the second finish and it does not care about blockers. Sanctum Lurker’s granted [+2] is available on every planeswalker you control, including every Jace token, and each activation is 1 damage to each opponent plus 1 life. In a long game the deck accumulates three or four tokens, which is three or four points of unavoidable damage per turn cycle that also grows the whole planeswalker suite through Way of the Mentor. Screeching Soulbreaker adds one more point per attack, so the drain is usually the closing two or three points behind a stalled ground board, dealt by permanents that cannot be killed by spending their own loyalty.
Hall of Echoes is the third conversion. {5} plus the land makes it a copy of the largest creature you control until end of turn: a 4/4 Beast, or a Cadet that has collected three Mabel counters. The legend rule does not apply to permanents you control that turn, so the copy attacks alongside the original and cannot be countered as a creature spell.

title: Spark Tithe
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep: any two-land hand with a two-drop; hands with Sanctum Lurker plus Command the Stage; hands with Way of the Deathbringer and at least one Way that makes a body (Pyromancer or Necromancer).
Mulligan: hands with no black source (the deck’s three best cards are black), one-land hands without a Way, and hands that are only removal. Five-land hands are acceptable when the spells are two-drops, because the deck has no four-drops and can use excess mana on Hall of Echoes.

title: Spark Tithe
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Jace tokens created by empower are not legendary, so multiple tokens coexist and each one activates its own loyalty ability once per turn. Two tokens means two Beast Forge activations.
Planeswalkers normally die as a state-based action at 0 loyalty. Sanctum Lurker replaces that, so a token that spent its last counters stays; without Lurker, budget the activation and do not spend the final two loyalty.
Empower creates the Jace token first if you do not control one, so a Way that resolves onto an empty board is a body plus an ability, never a blank.
Command the Stage only returns if an opponent was dealt noncombat damage last turn. Lurker’s drain and Soulbreaker’s attack trigger both qualify; combat damage does not.
Way of the Deathbringer is a may: you can activate with no creature to sacrifice, but the ability does nothing, so never do it.
Repurposed Enforcer counts creatures at the moment it attacks, so attack with the Cadets first and with Enforcer last.
Hall of Echoes taps for {C}. It cannot pay for Sanctum Lurker, Way of the Deathbringer or Command the Stage, so do not keep a hand where it is one of two lands.

title: Sunstar Vigil
text:
Overview
Sunstar Vigil fuses three build-around mechanics into one engine. Station (the Edge of Eternities mechanic) lets you tap a creature to put charge counters equal to its power on a Spacecraft or Planet, unlocking thresholds that turn your artifacts and lands into flying, lifelink, damage-dealing machines. Lifegain is the fuel: every life you gain powers Amalia’s explores, Exemplar of Light’s counters, and keeps you alive while your ships charge. Solved (the Case mechanic) provides the payoff layer: Case of the Shattered Pact solves off the five planets’ colors alone and turns any attacker into a flying double-striker, while Case of the Gorgon’s Kiss solves off your own milling and deaths into a 4/4 lifelink deathtouch creature.
Every card feeds the loop: high-power creatures (Vaultborn Tyrant, The Seriema) both gain life and charge Station; spacecraft draw cards and recur each other; the Planets are lands that become engines at 12+ charges, including the deck’s win-condition land, Adagia.

title: Sunstar Vigil

Game plan phases

Early (turns 1-3): Develop a Planet or triland, drop a cheap Spacecraft (Lumen-Class Frigate, Wurmwall Sweeper, Sledge-Class Seedship) or a Case. Case of the Shattered Pact tutors a basic to fix your five-color mana. The Seriema on turn 3 tutors Aurelia or Amalia, your two finishers.
Mid (turns 4-6): Resolve Vaultborn Tyrant (gain 3, draw a card, 6-power Station fuel) or Exemplar of Light. Start charging: tap your fatties as a sorcery to put counters on Spacecraft and Planets. Fell Gravship mills three (solving Gorgon’s Kiss) and returns a creature or Spacecraft to hand.
The combo turn: Charge Dawnsire to 10+ (one tap of Vaultborn plus The Seriema is 11), then attack: Dawnsire deals 100 damage to a blocker or planeswalker every combat. Amalia at 20 power destroys all other creatures, then attacks as a 20/20 with flying and double strike from the solved Pact. Aurelia adds a second combat phase, and Adagia at 12+ charges copies Dawnsire for double pings.

title: Sunstar Vigil
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Prioritize a 2-drop: Lumen-Class Frigate (it becomes an anthem at just 2 charges), Case of the Shattered Pact (fixes mana), or Wurmwall Sweeper (surveils toward your combo). The Seriema is the best turn-3 play: it finds Aurelia against race-y decks and Amalia when you need the wipe. Do not tap creatures to Station unless you are sure they will survive; the Seriema’s indestructible clause protects tapped legendaries, which makes charging with her safe.


Mid game and the combo turn
Chain lifegain triggers: Vaultborn Tyrant entering (gain 3, draw), Exemplar of Light growing on every lifegain event, Fell Gravship and Gorgon’s Kiss gaining life when they deal combat damage. Each trigger makes Amalia explore, growing her toward 20. When Amalia hits exactly 20 power, all other creatures are destroyed, and if the Pact is solved she attacks with flying and double strike for 40.
The Dawnsire line needs only 10 charges: tap Vaultborn Tyrant (6) and The Seriema (5) on a sorcery turn, then swing with anything, or animate Dawnsire with Case of the Filched Falcon for a 4/4 flying attacker that still pings 100. Aurelia’s extra combat phase untaps your team and triggers Dawnsire again; Adagia copying Dawnsire doubles both the pings and the 20/20 flyers.


Win condition #2 (spacecraft beatdown)
If Amalia is answered, the ships close the game: Sledge-Class Seedship cheats Vaultborn Tyrant into play on attack, robots from Wedgelight Rammer grow under Lumen’s anthem, and Kavaron’s haste anthem plus Aurelia’s extra combat turn any board into lethal. Dawnsire’s pings remove every blocker and opposing planeswalker first.


Mulligan guide
Keep: three or more lands with two colors, any 2-drop, The Seriema. Ship: one-landers, five-color hands with only tapped trilands and no 2-drop, hands with nothing but seven-drops.


Key interactions and edge cases

Station is a sorcery: you cannot charge in response to combat tricks.
Amalia’s wipe destroys all other creatures, including yours; plan to keep the spacecraft (they are artifacts) and the solved Gorgon’s Kiss (an enchantment) out of the blast radius.
The wipe puts many creature cards into graveyards, which solves Gorgon’s Kiss the same turn.
Vaultborn Tyrant’s death creates an artifact token copy; it is both Station fodder and a sacrifice for Susur Secundi.
Stroke of Midnight’s 1/1 Human token is extra sacrifice fodder; the token also gives you a creature to tap for Station.
Shattered Pact solves at end step once five colors are among permanents you control; the five Planets alone satisfy it.



Matchups

Aggro: Elspeth’s Smite exiles their attackers, Lumen’s anthem stalls the ground, and lifegain outpaces their burn. Solved Gorgon’s Kiss is a 4/4 lifelink wall.
Midrange: Out-grind with Vaultborn Tyrant draws and Susur Secundi’s power-based card draw; Dawnsire clears their best creatures every turn.
Control: Ward on Amalia taxes their counters, Planets are lands and dodge sweepers, and the solved Pact turns any surviving creature into a flying double-striker after a wipe.
Combo mirrors: Stroke of Midnight removes their enchantments and planeswalkers; Dawnsire’s 100-damage pings kill their combo creatures on sight.

title: Warpquake
text:
Overview
Warp lets you cast a card for its warp cost instead of its mana cost, exiles it at the beginning of the next end step, and then lets you cast it from exile on a later turn. That single line gives the deck two things at once: a permanent that enters the battlefield for far less than its printed price, and a card that is not spent when it leaves — it comes back as a real card in exile, ready to be cast again when the mana is there.
The deck converts those entries into damage. Three cards are paid for the same resource: Impact Tremors, Warleader’s Call and Weftstalker Ardent each deal 1 damage to every opponent when a creature you control enters. With all three on the battlefield a single creature entering is 3 damage; with Delney, Streetwise Lookout doubling Weftstalker Ardent’s trigger it is 4.
