title: Warpquake
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Lead with Impact Tremors whenever it is in the opening hand; it turns every later warp into damage and costs only two mana. On turn two the correct play is usually a warped one: Knight Luminary for two mana brings a Soldier, Weftstalker Ardent for one red mana is the cheapest ping in the deck, and Haliya for one white mana starts the lifegain count that draws cards later. Lightning Helix is for the creature that would otherwise eat your enchantments, not for the face. The warped permanent leaving at end of turn is not a loss: it goes to exile and stays castable.


Mid game
Turns three to five are about stacking payoffs. Warleader’s Call is the single most important card in the mid game because it both pings and pumps, which is what lets a board of 1/1 Soldiers actually attack. Tannuk, Steadfast Second is what makes the plan work on the turn it is played: the whole team has haste, so a warped Nova Hellkite or a Knight Luminary can attack immediately and then leave at end of turn with its damage already dealt. Delney is the other key piece, since doubling Weftstalker Ardent doubles the deck’s main clock.


The combo turn
The deck’s best turn is a two-mana warp that becomes four entries. With Impact Tremors, Warleader’s Call and Weftstalker Ardent on the battlefield, and Delney out, every creature that enters deals 4 damage to each opponent. Warp Knight Luminary for two mana: the Knight is one entry, and with Exalted Sunborn on the battlefield its Soldier is doubled into two more. Three entries is 12 damage to each opponent for two mana, and the same turn the Soldiers are 1/1s with Warleader’s Call’s +1/+1 on them. Recast the same Knight from exile later in the game for four mana and do it again; Possibility Technician turns each Kavu entry into an extra card off the top, so the loop refuels itself.


Win condition two
When the drain is not enough, the deck attacks. Nova Hellkite is a 4/5 flier with haste that also pings a creature on entry, Exalted Sunborn is a 4/5 flier with lifelink that doubles every token you make, and Warleader’s Call plus Memorial Team Leader make even the Soldier tokens into a real board. Rogue’s Passage is the finisher: four mana makes the largest body unblockable, which is usually the difference between a stalled board and lethal. Fountainport belongs to this plan too, since a free 1/1 each turn both adds to the attack and triggers all three drain payoffs.


Mulligan guide
Keep two or three lands with at least one Impact Tremors or Weftstalker Ardent, plus a cheap warp card to cast. Hands with two payoffs and no action are worse than they look, because the payoffs do nothing alone. Ship hands that need double white or double red on turn three without the matching basics, and ship hands whose only plays cost four or more unless Tannuk is among them, since Tannuk is what makes those cards castable early.


Key interactions and edge cases

Warp exiles the permanent at the beginning of the next end step, so a warped creature gets exactly one combat step and then leaves. Attack first, then let it go.
An exiled warped card can be cast again on a later turn, but that cast pays the printed cost, not the warp cost. Warp is a discount once per copy, not a permanent discount.
All-Fates Stalker exiles a creature until it leaves the battlefield, so warping it out returns the creature you removed. Cast it for four mana when you want the exile to stick.
Delney only doubles creatures with power 2 or less: Weftstalker Ardent, Rayblade Trooper and All-Fates Stalker qualify, while Haliya, Knight Luminary, Tannuk and Possibility Technician do not.
Haliya’s draw needs three or more life gained in the same turn. Three entries does it, and so does any entry plus Lightning Helix.
Rayblade Trooper only makes its Soldier when a nontoken creature with a +1/+1 counter dies. Warped creatures are exiled, not destroyed, so the trigger usually comes from a counter placed by Rayblade Trooper itself or by Weftblade Enhancer.
Tannuk, Steadfast Second is legendary. Warping a second copy while one is on the battlefield means one of them dies to the legend rule, so hold the second copy until the first is gone.
Possibility Technician needs a Kavu on the battlefield to cast the card it exiles. It is a Kavu itself, so it works alone, but if it is removed the exiled card is stranded until Tannuk or Memorial Team Leader arrives.
Exalted Sunborn doubles tokens, not entries: the two Soldiers it creates are two separate drain triggers, which is exactly why it is in the deck.



Matchups
Against aggro the deck is a favourite after sideboarding in spirit rather than in cards: Lightning Helix and All-Fates Stalker buy the turns, and Weftstalker Ardent plus Impact Tremors race small creature decks well because the damage does not require attacking. Against midrange the plan is to grind: every warped card is a second card later, and the drain payoffs do not care about blockers. Against control the deck wants Impact Tremors and Warleader’s Call down before the sweeper, since enchantments survive creature removal, and Delney makes the Soldier tokens unblockable against large blockers. Against combo there is no counterspell in the list, so the deck has to race with the drain plan and use Rogue’s Passage for the last points.

Curve and mana
The curve tops out at four. Twenty-two of thirty-six spells cost two or less, so the deck functions on three lands and starts drawing two cards a turn by turn four. Colored requirements are intentionally flat: the only double pip in the deck is The Water Crystal at {2}{U}{U}, and it is a four-drop you cast after your blue sources are online. Lead with fixing over action when you have both: a turn-one Llanowar Elves into a turn-two Vnwxt, Verbose Host is the best opening in the deck, because Vnwxt needs time to climb to max speed. Speed rises once on each of your turns when an opponent loses life, so the first point of damage matters more than it looks — a Raven Eagle attack, a Mischievous Mystic in the air, or a Warleader's Call trigger all advance the clock that doubles your draws.

Ninja Teen’s level 3 turns the graveyard into a hand: creature cards get sneak {3}{B}, so the creatures you sacrificed (or that died in combat) come back as attacking bodies, and each of those returns triggers the drain again.
Dark Leo & Shredder’s half-their-life clause needs five Ninjas. Splinter, Hamato Yoshi, Mechanized Ninja Cavalry, Mikey & Leo, Chaos and Order and Super Shredder are all Ninjas themselves, and Dark Leo’s tokens are Ninjas too, so five is reached with any two of them plus one token.
Balemurk Leech and Entity Tracker say “each opponent”, so in multiplayer the drain and the draw scale; the Room clause on their Eerie text is irrelevant here because the deck runs no Rooms.
Turtle Lair’s colour ability only pays for Ninja and Turtle spells. Use it on Splinter, Dark Leo, the Cavalry or Mikey and Leo, not on the enchantments.

Key interactions and edge cases

Prepared is one-shot per preparation. Casting the Soul Tether copy unprepares the creature. Only Woodwork Prodigy re-arms itself, and only during your upkeep, so a Prodigy killed at sorcery speed costs you the future tokens, not just the body.
Craterclaw counts artifacts as it resolves. Sacrificing a Heartwood to Marwyn in response lowers X, so make the draw decision before combat, not during it.

Solitary Cell is an artifact first. It exiles a permanent with mana value three or less until it leaves, so destroying your own Cell returns their permanent — and it counts for Craterclaw while it sits there.

title: Moon and Dale

Key interactions and edge cases

Thranduil, the Elvenking’s draw triggers on every other legendary Elf entering — including a second copy of himself, Elrond, Galion, Sindarin Liege, and The Queen of Dale (a legendary Human Noble, so it also draws).
Bard, King of Dale doubles only draws beyond the first card of your draw step, but it doubles every draw from Thranduil, Elrond, Ravenhill triggers, and the adventures. It also doubles all token creation — Sindarin Liege landfall tokens become two Elves.
Bard the Bowman triggers on your second draw each turn, so a burst of four cards still counts as one trigger; the counters accumulate from multiple turns and multiple legendary Elves.
Elrond’s draw triggers once per turn, on any creature-ability activation — Thranduil’s stolen Elf abilities (e.g. Woodland Weavemaster’s tap-for-mana if it is in the graveyard) count.

Mirkwood Meditator’s base 4/2 replacement only lasts until end of turn; it does not permanently shrink.

Stocking the Pantry on one is the best opening because it converts every later counter event into a card; Pawpatch Recruit on one is the fastest, because a 2/1 trampler that can make a token copy gives Skyknight Squire and Wildwood Scourge two triggers in one card.
Turn two is Bristly Bill whenever the mana allows it. Bristly Bill is the card that makes the fetch lands matter, and it is also the only way the deck doubles the whole board, so it is worth cracking Terramorphic Expanse or Evolving Wilds the same turn to put a counter somewhere immediately. Skyknight Squire on two is the alternative, and it snowballs by itself once the deck starts dropping creatures.
Take Up the Shield is the turn-two play to hold rather than cast: it is a counter, lifelink and indestructible for two mana, and it is nearly always better spent protecting the creature that is about to be pumped than on a 1/1 on turn two.

title: Tallywurm
text:
Mid game
Turns three to five are about stacking counter events in a single combat rather than deploying one threat at a time.
The highest-value sequence is to land Ouroboroid and then crack a fetch land before the beginning of the next combat. Ouroboroid’s trigger puts X counters on every creature (X equals its power, so one counter per creature on the first combat), the fetch land adds a landfall counter through Bristly Bill or Mossborn Hydra, Caradora makes each of those events one larger, and Wildwood Scourge adds a counter for each non-Hydra creature that received counters. A single combat step with those pieces in play adds four to six counters across the board at a cost of zero cards.
Broodguard Elite is the deck’s insurance policy. Cast for three or four mana it enters as a 3/3 or 4/4 with warp, and if it dies its counters move to another creature, so the investment is never wasted; warping it back later re-triggers the entry. Wildwood Scourge is the other card worth protecting, because every future counter event is worth an extra counter while it is in play.
Do not over-commit into a sweeper. The deck’s answer is Inspiring Call: hold it until the opponent taps out for a board wipe, cast it in response, draw four or five cards and keep every creature with a counter alive for the turn.

title: Tallywurm
text:
The combo turn
The engine turn needs three things: Ouroboroid in play, at least two other creatures with counters already on them, and a land drop or a fetch land still to use.

Start the turn with Ouroboroid and a board of counter carriers. Any Wildwood Scourge or Broodguard Elite counts double for the purposes of the next step.
Beginning of combat: Ouroboroid triggers for X, where X is its power. With Caradora in play every one of those placements becomes X plus one.
Crack a fetch land before the trigger resolves if the mana is open, so Bristly Bill or Mossborn Hydra adds its landfall counter to the same combat. Mossborn Hydra doubling its own counters is the single largest growth event in the deck.
Training Regimen adds one more counter and turns the whole board into tramplers, so the counters convert to damage in the same turn.
Attack with everything. Restless Prairie animates for {2}{G}{W} and pumps the rest of the team by +1/+1 when it attacks, which is the difference between a chump block and lethal.
If one blocker matters, Rogue’s Passage for four mana makes the biggest attacker unblockable, and Take Up the Shield gives it lifelink and indestructible so the swing is safe.

A realistic turn five with Ouroboroid, Caradora and Training Regimen in play is six to eight counters on the team plus trample, which is lethal against most boards that do not have a sweeper.

title: Tallywurm
text:
Win condition 2
The second path does not need Ouroboroid: it needs counters on creatures that cannot be blocked.
Skyknight Squire is the cheapest route. It gains a counter every time any other creature enters, so a turn of Pawpatch Recruit plus offspring token, a fetch land and a Broodguard Elite takes it past three counters and turns it into a 4/4 or larger flier. Mossborn Hydra is the other: a landfall doubling trigger on top of trample makes it a two-turn clock from three mana, and its counters keep doubling for free as the deck plays lands.
The lands are part of both paths. Restless Prairie attacking gives every other attacker +1/+1, so the Llama is a team pump on a land that survives sorcery-speed removal, and Rogue’s Passage makes whichever of these creatures is largest unblockable. That combination is the deck’s answer to a stalled board: pump the team with the manland, clear the last blocker with the Passage, and attack for the win with counters rather than with card advantage.

title: Tallywurm
text:
Key interactions and edge cases







Interaction
Ruling detail




Ouroboroid’s X is locked in as the trigger resolves
It puts X counters on each creature, X being its power at that moment. Its own counters arrive with the same instruction, so its power grows every combat and the next trigger is larger


Caradora, Heart of Alacria adds one per counter event
Any time one or more counters would be put on a creature you control, that many plus one are put on it instead. Ouroboroid’s mass placement counts as one event per creature, and so does a fetch land’s landfall trigger


Wildwood Scourge only counts non-Hydra recipients
It is a Hydra itself, so Ouroboroid’s counters on it do not trigger it, but every non-Hydra creature that receives counters does. A mass trigger across four non-Hydra creatures is four separate counters on the Scourge


Mossborn Hydra doubles only its own counters
Its landfall trigger is “double the number of +1/+1 counters on this creature”, so it does not interact with Caradora for the rest of the team. It does stack with Bristly Bill’s doubling on a later combat


Skyknight Squire counts three counters, not three triggers
As long as it has three or more counters total it has flying and is a Knight. Broodguard Elite’s exit trigger and Take Up the Shield both push it over the line without a single landfall trigger


Broodguard Elite passes counters when it leaves
The counters move to target creature you control, so using it as a chump blocker is a transfer rather than a loss. Its warp {X}{G} lets you recast it later, and the exit trigger fires again if it leaves a second time


Pawpatch Recruit’s second ability needs an opponent’s spell
Whenever a creature you control becomes the target of a spell or ability an opponent controls, put a +1/+1 counter on a different creature you control. Point their removal at the Recruit and the counter lands on Mossborn Hydra or Skyknight Squire instead


The offspring token arrives with the entry trigger
Paying the extra {2} creates the token copy as the Recruit enters, so Skyknight Squire and Wildwood Scourge see two entries, not one


Training Regimen triggers every combat, not every turn
A single +1/+1 counter per combat step on a creature you control, and every creature you control with a counter has trample for as long as the enchantment is in play


Inspiring Call is a draw spell first
It draws for each creature with a counter and only then grants indestructible, so cast it in response to a sweeper with the board already built. Board wipes that exile avoid it, and so do sacrifice effects


Take Up the Shield answers removal and wins races
The counter is permanent, the lifelink and indestructible are until end of turn. Cast it on the attacking creature in the turn you go for lethal to gain four or more life and survive the crack back


Stocking the Pantry tracks events, not counters
One or more counters is one supply counter, so Ouroboroid’s mass trigger adds one supply counter, not five. Each supply counter is two mana for a card at sorcery speed


Restless Prairie is a land until end of turn
Animating it does not stop it from being a land, so landfall triggers still fire if it enters after animation, and it keeps tapping for mana. It also counts for Training Regimen because it has counters only if something puts them on it


Rogue’s Passage ability timing
Four mana and a tap, at sorcery speed in practice because it is an activated ability of a land. Use it in the second main phase before attackers so the mana is not telegraphed, or in the mana you floated for a fetch


Fetches enter tapped but trigger landfall immediately
Terramorphic Expanse and Evolving Wilds sacrifice themselves and put the basic in tapped, and the basic entering is what triggers landfall. Promising Vein costs one mana for the same effect on a colourless land

Curve and mana
The nonland curve is 5 ones, 14 twos, 13 threes, 2 fours and 3 fives: nothing costs more than five, and the average is 2.57. That matters because Expend cares about total mana spent, not about a single expensive card. Three cheap spells spend four mana just as well as one four-drop, and each of them separately triggers Increment.

Early game (turns 1–3)

Turn 1: Ambitious Augmenter is the ideal play. It grows off any two-mana spell, and if it dies with counters it becomes a Fractal carrying those counters, which is a second body for free.
Turn 2: Wandertale Mentor is the best two-drop because it ramps: tap it for red or green and you reach four mana spent a full turn earlier. Bakersbane Duo and Bark-Knuckle Boxer are the aggressive alternatives.
Turn 3: Textbook Tabulator for surveil 2, or Muerra, Trash Tactician if you already have a couple of Raccoons. Muerra’s first-main mana makes the threshold trivial; keep her alive and the deck stops needing lands.
Do not spend removal here. Impossible Inferno and Beastie Beatdown are for the turn they double as threshold spells.

Mid game (turns 4–6)

Pick the spell that crosses four mana spent and cast it when your board is widest, not on curve. The expend 4 trigger is once per turn, so the payoff is proportional to how many Raccoons you have assembled.
Textbook Tabulator, Byway Barterer and Fear of Missing Out are your graveyard taps. Surveil and looting feel like card selection; they are actually Delirium enablers, so favour them over a slightly better body once the yard is one or two types short.
Track card types actively: creature, land, instant, sorcery, enchantment, artifact. Wildfire Wickerfolk and Fear of Missing Out each count as two types in the yard (artifact creature, enchantment creature), which is how a single loot can flip Delirium on.

The combo turn

Assemble at least one expend 4 payoff, ideally two or three, plus an Increment creature or two.
Keep four or more mana available with a spell in hand that costs four or more, or an X spell such as The Rollercrusher Ride.
Cast the expensive spell. Rule 700.14 gives exactly one expend 4 trigger this turn: Wandertale Mentor gains a counter, Bark-Knuckle Boxer turns indestructible, Byway Barterer loots a fresh hand and fills the yard, while Bakersbane Duo and Teapot Slinger pump and drain.
The same cast grows every Increment creature whose power or toughness is lower than the mana you spent, and Pensive Professor draws a card for each of its own counters.
With Delirium on, move to combat. Fear of Missing Out untaps your best attacker and grants an additional combat phase; Restless Ridgeline pumps and untaps another attacker. Two combat steps with trample and counters is the kill.

Teapot Slinger drains each opponent for 2 every time you expend 4. The Rollercrusher Ride states that while you have four or more card types in your graveyard, any noncombat damage a source you control would deal is doubled instead. Each Slinger ping becomes 4, and the Ride’s own entry trigger (X damage to each of up to X target creatures) doubles too. Against a stalled board, this is the win that does not need an attack step: hold two Slingers and a Ride, cross the threshold, and the table drains while the Ride clears blockers.

Keep: two or three lands with green in them, a turn-one or turn-two creature, and at least one graveyard tap (Textbook Tabulator, Byway Barterer, Fear of Missing Out) or a Muerra.
Keep aggressively if the hand has three mana, a Raccoon and any four-mana spell: that is the whole plan.
Trim: one-land hands; hands with no green source; hands of only expensive spells with no cheap Raccoons to convert the threshold into damage.

title: Compound Interest
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Expend 4 triggers once per turn. It is a threshold, not a counter that resets. Spending mana on activated abilities does not count; only mana spent to cast spells does. Sequence your biggest spell so the crossing mana is the one that pays for it.
Increment checks each spell separately and compares against current power or toughness, so a creature that already grew needs an even bigger spell next time. Small bodies stay live longest, which is why the one- and two-mana creatures are the engine.
Delirium counts types, not cards. One artifact creature and one enchantment creature plus a land and a spell already satisfy it.
Balustrade Wurm recurs for two plus green and green from the graveyard while Delirium is on, and comes back with a finality counter. It is the follow-up threat that beats sweepers.
Omnivorous Flytrap doubles at six card types, so if you can hold a seventh and eighth type (an instant and a sorcery) the counters explode.
Fear of Missing Out untaps any target creature, including the Dinosaur that Restless Ridgeline animated, so the pumped attacker can hit twice.
Terramorphic Expanse is a Delirium enabler first and fixing second — sacrificing it puts a land card in the graveyard, which is often the fourth type you needed.

title: Compound Interest
text:
Matchups

Aggro: the deck wins the long game, so trade early and lean on Bark-Knuckle Boxer’s indestructible trigger plus Bakersbane Duo’s Food life. Teapot Slinger’s drain buys the turns the threshold engine needs; do not race with a slower hand.
Control: Force them to answer your Raccoons one at a time before the threshold turn; Balustrade Wurm cannot be countered and recurs from the graveyard, which is your best answer to a sweeper. Keep The Rollercrusher Ride in hand until it can clear the board and cross the threshold in the same cast.
Graveyard hate: Delirium is upside, not dependency. Without it you still have a solid curve, expend 4 payoffs and the Ride’s entry damage; re-sequence toward the combat plan with Fear of Missing Out as a loot spell rather than a combo piece.
Fast creature decks: The Rollercrusher Ride for X equals three is a one-sided sweeper once Delirium is live (doubled damage), and Beastie Beatdown turns any grown Increment creature into a removal spell. The Ride is the card you are digging for.

Early game
Lead with a dual land or a basic, not a Raceway, unless you have nothing else to do with the colorless mana. Turn two is Manifest Dread when you are setting up depth, Deep-Cavern Bat when you want the hand information and the lifelink, or Souls of the Lost once the graveyard already holds two or three permanents. Sinkhole Surveyor is the best turn two when you expect a race, because attacking with it every turn is how speed climbs to 4.
The first attack is what matters most: speed only rises on turns the opponent actually loses life. A 1/3 flier attacking into nothing is one point of damage and one point of speed. Do not hold back attacks to protect creatures you are willing to trade; the deck’s plan is to run the clock in both directions at once.

title: Race the Reaper
text:
Mid game
Turns three to five are about stacking engines. Hauntwoods Shrieker turns every attack into another face down 2/2 and another permanent in the graveyard, which makes Threats Around Every Corner ramp a land on every combat and Aether Syphon’s milling start to matter. Growing Dread held up with flash is a blocker on demand that also deepens the graveyard, and Paranormal Analyst is the card that keeps the hand from running dry while the graveyard empties into the board.
The graveyard is a resource with two speeds: it grows with every manifest dread, and it shrinks with every Abhorrent Oculus and every Squirming Emergence. Spend it before you refill it. The usual sequence is manifest dread for several turns, cast Squirming Emergence to bring back the best permanent in the graveyard, then cast Abhorrent Oculus once the yard is deep enough to lose six cards and still keep three or four for the next Souls of the Lost.

title: Race the Reaper
text:
The combo turn
Max speed arrives on the third turn that an opponent loses life, and the deck can usually turn that corner by turn four or five with one flier plus the Raceway lands’ start your engines. The turn itself is simple: attack with everything that can profitably attack, keep Aether Syphon and Vnwxt on the board, and let the draws do the work. At max speed the arithmetic is brutal: Vnwxt doubles each draw, Aether Syphon mills two per draw, and if The Speed Demon is out the end step draws four cards, which is eight cards milled off each opponent plus eight cards in your hand.
Racers’ Scoreboard’s max speed clause stacks with that turn: every spell you cast costs one less, so a hand of four cards often contains two spells and the mana to spare. Endrider Catalyzer’s max speed tap for two red mana is the other half, and it is the only red card in the deck that matters after turn two.

title: Race the Reaper

The second win condition
When the mill plan is interrupted or the opponent is gaining life, the deck still kills with its graveyard. Souls of the Lost is frequently a five or six power creature for two mana, and Hauntwoods Shrieker’s free flip ability plus Growing Dread’s plus one counter turns a nameless face down 2/2 into a real threat without paying for it. Squirming Emergence returning The Speed Demon for three mana ends games from an empty board, and Amonkhet Raceway’s max speed haste means the creature that comes back swings in the same turn it arrives.

In a deck where Souls of the Lost and Squirming Emergence read that same graveyard, this is a real cost: cast it when the yard holds eight or more permanent cards, or after Squirming Emergence has already spent them for you.
Paranormal Analyst redirects the graveyard half of every manifest dread into your hand. That is a two for one every single time, and it is also the reason the descent count can stall: if you need a deep graveyard, do not lean on her, and if you need cards she is the best three drop in the deck.

Souls of the Lost’s additional cost can be paid with a spare face down 2/2 rather than a card from hand, which is the cheapest way to make it a six power creature, and it also puts a creature card into the graveyard for the next copy.
Speed rises only once per turn, no matter how much life the opponent loses. One attacker is enough to keep the clock moving, but you must attack every turn or the deck loses a turn of max speed.
The Speed Demon’s end step costs you real life: at max speed it draws four and loses four. Deep-Cavern Bat’s lifelink and the opponent’s own damage output decide whether that is a clock or a suicide note, so hold the Demon until you are above ten life or the opponent is nearly dead.

title: Storyforge
text:
Curve and mana
The deck curves out at 1-2 and stops there on purpose: 4 one-drops, 23 two-drops, 3 three-drops and 6 four-drops. Red is the primary colour (Dáin Ironfoot, Dwarven Mauler, Leyline Axe, Erode is white), white supplies the legendary Dwarf core, and green is a three-card splash for Elvish Archivist and Sandstorm Salvager off Gathering Place, Training Compound and the two Forests. Fifteen sources produce white, twelve produce red, and seven produce green — enough for a splash that only wants to see one green card a game.

title: Storyforge
text:
Early game
Open on Dwarven Mauler or a two-drop legend rather than on an Equipment: the storied count is what turns the deck on, and the legends are themselves artifacts-or-legendaries. Iron Hills Blacksmith is the best turn two — it enters with an Axe, attacks for two with double strike, and gives you a free artifact for the Storied check. Kíli the Resourceful on two is the value line: hold the first Dwarf or Equipment of the turn and it draws you a card.

title: Storyforge
text:
Mid game
Turn three to five is where the deck separates from a vanilla tribal deck. Dáin’s Company re-fills the hand and finds the missing piece, Giott and Kíli make every subsequent permanent a cantrip, and Elvish Archivist grows into the biggest creature on the board if the artifact half of the deck shows up. Keep one Equipment unattached if you are about to cast Thorin, Mountain-king — it attaches everything on entry, so every extra Equipment is extra damage.

title: Storyforge
text:
The combo turn
The killing turn is assembled from three pieces that are each fine on their own:

An Equipment on a Dwarf — Dwarven Mattock (+2/+2, ward) or Leyline Axe (double strike and trample).
Dáin Ironfoot, whose attack trigger gives every equipped attacking creature double strike.
Dwalin, Weaponmaster, whose attack trigger puts a hone counter on each Equipment ({+1}/{+0} per counter).

With Mattock on a Dwarven Mauler and Dáin Ironfoot attacking, a single 2/1 becomes a 5/4 double striker for eight damage, and Dwalin’s hone counters scale every Equipment you control, including the Axe tokens the Blacksmith and Dáin hand you. Kíli’s Storied ability makes the first equip of that turn free, so the whole package costs nothing extra to assemble and Fíli’s +1/+1 is applied on top of it.

title: Storyforge
text:
Win condition 2
When the combat route is bottled up, the deck wins off tokens. The Lonely Mountain activates for {4}{R} minus {1} for each Equipment you control — with three Equipment that is {1}{R} for a 2/2 Dwarf, every turn, forever. Fíli the Pathfinder makes a 2/2 token off every nontoken Dwarf entry, Sandstorm Salvager makes a 3/3 Golem artifact token and then puts +1/+1 counters and trample on the whole token team, and Warleader’s Call turns each of those entries into a point of damage to each opponent. Leyline Axe and Dwarven Mattock sit on whichever token lives, so the tokens are not simply chump blockers.

title: Storyforge
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep any hand with two or three lands, one one-drop or Blacksmith, and one Equipment. A hand with Leyline Axe plus The Lonely Mountain is a keep even on four lands: the Axe begins on the battlefield, which turns on the untapped Mountain and puts you one permanent away from Storied before you cast anything. Ship hands that are all four-drops, and ship hands with three or more colourless lands (Gathering Place and Training Compound only produce coloured mana once you control a basic land).

title: Storyforge
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Leyline Axe starts on the battlefield when it is in your opening hand. That is a free Storied piece and it leaves The Lonely Mountain untapped on turn one.
Dwarven Mauler discounts equip abilities that target it — it does not make them free, but it makes Leyline Axe’s and Mattock’s {3} equips cost {1}.
Dáin Ironfoot’s Axe token counts toward Storied and is the cheapest equip in the deck at {2}, which Dwarven Mauler reduces to nothing.
Kíli the Resourceful triggers only once per turn: sequence a Dwarf first, then an Equipment, so the single draw lands when you want it.
Giott, King of the Dwarves triggers on your own entry as well as on each Dwarf and Equipment, so he is a three-card dig engine by himself once the board is assembled.
Thorin, Mountain-king’s trigger deals damage equal to the attached creature’s power to a target creature, so it is removal, not reach: point it at the biggest blocker before combat.
Elvish Archivist has two separate once-per-turn triggers — artifacts give counters, enchantments draw cards. Warleader’s Call entering is a card, and each subsequent Equipment is two counters.
Gathering Place and Training Compound produce coloured mana only if the land entered this turn or you control a basic land. Play them behind a basic whenever possible; otherwise they are a {C} source for that turn.
Erode is unconditional, but the opponent fetches a basic land. Use it on the creature that actually kills you, not on the first thing that attacks.
Sandstorm Salvager’s Golem is an artifact creature token: it counts for Storied, it is a legal target for its own pump ability, and it carries Equipment.

title: Loyalty Lattice
text:
Game plan in three phases

Seed the lattice (turns 1 to 3). One untapped basic, then the cheapest empower effects. Way of the Necromancer on turn two creates a Jace token and puts two counters on it; Theorist's Proxy is a flashed-in 0/3 that empowers Jace 3 and protects the token at instant speed; Ajani Resolute on turn one is a zero ability that gains a life every turn and grows itself off that life. From the moment you control a planeswalker, the Annex lands stop entering tapped, so this phase is also the mana-fixing phase.
Build the stack (turns 4 to 6). Sanctum Lurker turns every planeswalker into a pinger and makes them immortal at zero loyalty. Jace's Machinations is the biggest single loyalty swing in the deck — empower Jace 8, plus the ability to activate Jace loyalty abilities on any player’s turn at instant speed. Mindseeker Oculus, Protege's Awakening and Way of the Mind Sculptor each add four, six and five more counters. Way of the Mentor and Way of the Healer are the multipliers: Mentor converts every point of life you gain (and the Lurker gains life on every activation) into a counter on every planeswalker, while Healer gives every planeswalker “[-2]: Create a 2/2 colorless Wizard Soldier token named Cadet. Surveil 1.”
Convert (turn six plus). With a Jace token carrying twenty-five or more counters, with Jace, Reality Sculptor on the battlefield, activate its zero ability and exile the opponent’s library down to one card. From there the opponent draws their last card and loses on the following draw step. If the Sculptor is not there yet, the Lurker board is already winning: each planeswalker pings for one and gains a life every turn, Cadets and Illusions attack, and The Theorist, Jace Beleren draws you an extra card on each opponent’s draw step while you find the kill.

title: Loyalty Lattice
text:
Curve and mana
36 nonland cards and 24 lands, average nonland mana value 2.97 — two ones, eleven twos, thirteen threes, six fours and four fives. The deck wants a turn-one play almost always and a turn-two empower effect in most games, then spends the mid game on four- and five-mana engines.
The mana base is blue with white and black support: eighteen blue sources, eleven white and ten black. Blue is that deep on purpose. It pays for a heavy blue top end (The Theorist and Jace, Reality Sculptor both cost two blue, and the Sculptor’s plus ability counts Islands), and it is the colour that the Annex cycle and Shipwreck Marsh share.
The six Annex and Commons lands all enter untapped once you control a planeswalker, so the first empower spell of the game is also the moment the mana base comes online. Run the basics first: turn one should be an untapped basic or a Deserted Beach, never a tapped Annex. After the first Jace lands, all six duals are free.

title: Loyalty Lattice
text:
Early game (turns 1 to 3)

Turn 1: Liliana the Faultless is the best one-drop — a 1/1 that gains a life every time a creature or planeswalker enters, which is the deck’s entire game plan arriving early. Ajani Resolute is the other option: a two-mana planeswalker that gains a life every turn and grows itself.
Turn 2: Way of the Necromancer is the cheapest way to put a Jace token (and two counters) on the battlefield, and it turns every future trade into a loyalty counter on every planeswalker. Theorist's Proxy at flash speed is the safe version: hold up two mana, and if the opponent does nothing relevant, empower Jace 3 at end of turn.
Turn 3: Sanctum Lurker is the priority. It makes the board of planeswalkers permanent and turns each of them into a pinger. Mindseeker Oculus (empower Jace 4) and Fatehold Charm (draw a card, empower Jace 2) are the backup plays.
Every one of those spells also untaps your Annex lands for the rest of the game. Treat the first empower spell of the game as the mana-fixing play, not just the engine play.

title: Loyalty Lattice
text:
Mid game (turns 4 to 6)

Jace's Machinations is the turn the clock starts. Eight counters in one instant, plus instant-speed loyalty activation for the rest of the turn — with Sanctum Lurker down that means a ping and a life point for every planeswalker even on the opponent’s turn.
Way of the Mentor doubles the value of every ping, every Ajani activation and every Liliana trigger. Cast it before the next batch of empower spells, not after.
The Theorist, Jace Beleren is the card-advantage engine: it draws on each opponent’s draw step, so holding mana for Theorist's Proxy or a charm costs you nothing in the long run.
Hold Vraska's Final Mercy for the mode you actually need. Two life for “destroy target creature or planeswalker” is a bargain against a resolved threat; two life for empower Jace 6 is a bargain when you are two counters short of the combo.
Jace, Reality Sculptor’s minus three is a real defensive play: every creature that attacks you or a planeswalker you control gets minus five minus zero until your next turn. It buys the extra turn the deck needs.

title: Loyalty Lattice
text:
The combo turn

Have Jace, Reality Sculptor on the battlefield and a Jace token (or any Jace) with a stack of loyalty counters. Sanctum Lurker is strongly preferred, because it keeps every planeswalker alive at zero loyalty and adds the ping ability.
Count the loyalty among all Jaces you control. Common contributions: Jace's Machinations eight, Protege's Awakening six, Way of the Mind Sculptor five, Way of the Mentor five, Mindseeker Oculus four, Theorist's Proxy three, Way of the Necromancer two, Vraska's Final Mercy six, Fatehold Charm two, Theorist's Sanctum two per activation, and the Sculptor’s own plus ability for one per Island.
Two or three empower spells plus a Sanctum activation is normally enough. When the total reaches twenty-five, activate Jace, Reality Sculptor’s zero ability: exile all but the bottom card of each opponent’s library.
The opponent is not decked immediately — they still have one card. They draw it, then lose on their next draw step. In the meantime the Lurker board keeps pinging and gaining life, so there is no window where they can race back.
If the combo is disrupted, you have not lost anything. The empower spells left a board of planeswalkers, the Ways keep growing them, and Way of the Healer keeps making 2/2 Cadets every turn.

title: Loyalty Lattice
text:
Win condition 2: the Lurker board
Sanctum Lurker turns every planeswalker — the token from an empower spell, The Theorist, Jace Reality Sculptor, Ajani Resolute — into a permanent that deals one damage to each opponent and gains you a life for two loyalty counters. In a normal game the deck fields between three and six planeswalkers, so that is three to six damage a turn from permanents the opponent cannot kill by attacking them to zero loyalty. Way of the Mentor adds a counter to every one of them on each of those life gains, Way of the Necromancer adds another counter every time a Cadet or Illusion chump-blocks, and Way of the Healer makes every planeswalker a Cadet factory at minus two. The result is a board that grows while it drains; The Theorist, Jace Beleren’s ultimate then converts the hand into +1/+1 counters on every creature for a lethal swing.

title: Loyalty Lattice
text:
Mulligan guide

Keep: two or three lands with at least one untapped basic, plus a cheap empower effect (Way of the Necromancer, Theorist's Proxy, Mindseeker Oculus) and one payoff or multiplier (Sanctum Lurker, Way of the Mentor, Jace's Machinations).
Keep on six: one basic land plus Liliana the Faultless or Ajani Resolute and two more lands. A turn-one lifegain engine is a functional start.
Trim: hands with four or more lands but nothing to cast under three mana; hands that are all defence; one-land hands with no one-drop.
Do not go to five looking for Jace's Machinations. The deck’s floor is cheap empower spells, and the Ways and Lurkers are the cards that make them matter.

title: Loyalty Lattice
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

A planeswalker at zero loyalty is not dead here. Sanctum Lurker stops your planeswalkers from being put into graveyards for having zero loyalty. Costs that remove loyalty cannot be paid below zero, but a cost that adds counters — the Lurker’s granted plus-two, Jace, Reality Sculptor’s plus one — is always payable, so a zero-loyalty planeswalker keeps working.
Empower targets a Jace token, not a Jace card. “Put counters on a Jace token you control; if you do not control one, first create a blue Jace planeswalker token.” The Theorist, Jace Beleren is a Jace for the loyalty-count and for beholding, but the counters from empower land on the token.
Way of the Mentor and Sanctum Lurker are the engine pair. The Lurker’s ping gains a life on every activation, and Mentor converts every life gain into a counter on each planeswalker. Ajani Resolute’s zero ability and Liliana the Faultless’s enters-trigger do the same job on their own.
Way of the Necromancer wants bodies, not bombs. It only triggers when a creature dies, so Cadets, Illusions and Cat Soldiers are the fuel — chump-blocking is often a loyalty counter on every planeswalker.
Behold a Jace is a cost, not a sacrifice. Theorist’s Sanctum either chooses a Jace you control or reveals a Jace card from your hand; the permanent stays. Casting the Sanctum with a Jace in hand makes it an untapped Island.
Jace’s Machinations lifts timing, not the once-per-turn rule. Each planeswalker still activates one loyalty ability per turn, but with the instant it can activate on the opponent’s turn as well.
The last-card rule. Jace, Reality Sculptor leaves the opponent exactly one library card. That player draws it and then loses on the following draw. If they have a way to skip draws or shuffle back in, keep the Lurker board attacking; the ping-plus-Cadets plan does not care.
Vraska’s Final Mercy always costs two life, whichever mode you pick. Do not fire it at three life against a deck with reach.

title: Loyalty Lattice
text:
Matchups

Aggro: the deck’s early bodies are 1/1s and 0/3s, so the opening turns are about survival, not tempo. Ajani Resolute and Liliana the Faultless gain the life back, Jace, Reality Sculptor’s minus three makes attacking into the board miserable, and once Sanctum Lurker arrives pressure stops mattering — the board pings back every turn and cannot be killed.
Midrange: this is the best matchup. The deck out-grows whatever the opponent plays, because the Ways add counters every turn and the empower spells never spend a card on the engine itself. Save Vraska's Final Mercy for the one threat that actually blocks the combo.
Control: the value sits on enchantments and planeswalkers rather than on spells, so counterspells trade down. Theorist's Proxy can be sacrificed to make the next spell uncounterable, and Way of the Mentor and Way of the Necromancer are the survivals after a sweeper because they keep the rebuilt board growing.
Combo and graveyard decks: the deck has no graveyard interaction beyond Fatehold Charm and Vraska’s Final Mercy, so racing with the Lurker board plus the Jace deck-out is the plan. The Theorist, Jace Beleren’s draw step trigger means the deck finds its kill quickly against decks that do not pressure life totals.
Artifact and enchantment removal: Way of the Healer and Way of the Necromancer are the expendable pieces; Way of the Mentor and Sanctum Lurker are the ones worth protecting with Theorist's Proxy’s sacrifice ability or by simply doubling up.

Reality Fracture is Standard-legal but still carries no arena_id in the data, so the import list becomes playable on Arena once the set is enabled there.

title: Steel and Saga
text:
Curve and mana
Twenty-four lands: twelve basics (5 Plains, 5 Mountain, 2 Island) plus twelve nonbasics (3 The Lonely Mountain, 2 Iron Hills, 1 Raucous Carnival, 2 Rabanastre Royal City, 2 Cori Mountain Monastery, 1 Sharlayan, 1 Hidden Grotto). The base is white-red: the two-drop cluster (Thorin, Kíli, Dáin Lord of the Iron Hills, Blacksmith, Dwalin, Dáin’s Company, Mattock) needs {W} and {R} on turns two and three, and there are enough red and white sources for double-color four-drops by turn four. Blue is a three-card splash (2 Opt, 2 hybrid Patient Instructor) kept honest by 2 Islands, Sharlayan and Cori Mountain Monastery. The curve is engine-shaped: three one-drops (2 Opt, 1 Burst Lightning), twenty-one two-drop plays, five three-drops (3 Dáin Ironfoot, 2 Patient Instructor), three four-drops (Fíli the Pathfinder), and a four-card five-plus cluster (2 Balin, 2 Esgaroth Garrison). The Lonely Mountain smooths the top end — late lands become 2/2 Dwarves instead of dead draws.

title: Steel and Saga
text:
Early game
Lead with Iron Hills Blacksmith (Axe token) so the story is two artifacts deep on turn one. Thorin Oakenshield, Kíli the Resourceful, or Dáin’s Company come next — with two legends plus the Axe the story endures, and from that moment Thorin taxes every spell aimed at your board and Kíli draws on each new Dwarf or Equipment. Against fast decks, Dáin, Lord of the Iron Hills slows every attack. Do not over-commit into sweepers before Balin arrives; the deck rebuilds faster than control clears.

title: Steel and Saga
text:
Mid game
Resolve Fíli the Pathfinder and start the token machine: every Dwarf cast adds a 2/2 token, and Kíli turns the busiest turn into extra cards. Dáin Ironfoot’s Axe and Dwalin’s hone counters turn one equipped creature into a 4/5+ double-striker, while Dáin’s Company keeps the chain fed. The Lonely Mountain becomes active: each Equipment out discounts the Dwarf tokens it creates.

title: Steel and Saga
text:
The combo turn
With the story enduring, Balin on the battlefield, and a hand of four or more, the kill is any Dwarf entry — cast one or activate The Lonely Mountain:

The Dwarf enters: Balin’s trigger and (if Fíli is out) a 2/2 Dwarf token both go on the stack; Kíli adds a card for the turn’s first Dwarf/Equipment entry.
First Balin trigger resolves: discard your hand (say five cards), draw five, and deal 5 damage to each opponent.
Fíli’s token enters: Balin triggers again, discarding the fresh hand (six with Kíli’s draw), drawing six, dealing 6.

One Dwarf cast with a five-card hand is 11 damage and a new grip; two Dwarves or a Lonely Mountain activation on top is lethal. You may decline any Balin trigger — against a low-value hand of lands, let it pass rather than wheel into nothing.

title: Steel and Saga
text:
Win condition 2
The equipped beatdown. Dáin Ironfoot’s Axe plus Dwarven Mattock on a storied board makes a 5/5-plus creature with double strike when Dáin attacks, ward from Thorin and Mattock, and Dwalin’s hone counters still climbing. Esgaroth Garrison’s power tracks your creature count, so the Fíli token swarm plus Garrison is a second wide clock. Iron Hills pumps the chosen Dwarf by +2/+2 when the last points are needed.

title: Steel and Saga
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep any hand with two or three lands and a two-drop (Thorin, Kíli, Blacksmith, Dáin’s Company, Dwalin). Hands that reach three artifacts/legendaries by turn three are ideal. Ship one-landers, hands with Balin and no early plays, and hands without both colors. Against aggressive decks, prioritize Dáin, Lord of the Iron Hills and Patient Instructor; against control, keep Kíli and the tutors and lean on the ward stack.

title: Steel and Saga
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Storied is a state, not a trigger: once you control three or more artifacts, legendaries, and/or Sagas you have an enduring story for the rest of the game — Axe tokens count as artifacts, so Blacksmith and Dáin Ironfoot fuel it alone.
Balin triggers on tokens too. Fíli’s 2/2 tokens, The Lonely Mountain’s tokens, and any clone-style Dwarf all wheel and burn.
Each Balin trigger resolves separately: the second trigger discards the hand drawn by the first, so damage compounds — order your triggers so Kíli’s draw lands between them.
Thorin’s storied ward and Dwarven Mattock’s ward are separate abilities: an equipped creature has two ward {1} triggers, and the opponent pays 1 for each.
The Lonely Mountain enters tapped unless you control an Equipment — Axe tokens and Mattock keep it untapped. Its token ability is sorcery-speed.
Dáin Ironfoot’s double strike applies to each equipped attacking creature when he attacks — equip the Mattock before combat and swing with two double-strikers.
Smaug’s Fury is first strike, so it is wasted on Dwalin (already first strike); it shines on an unequipped Dáin Ironfoot or a blocker.
Iron Hills is a land first: do not sacrifice it for counters unless the mana is no longer needed.
Patient Instructor and Esgaroth Garrison recruit at sorcery speed on entry: the Soldier tokens are not Dwarves, so they do not trigger Balin or Kíli, but they grow Garrison and chump-block.

title: Steel and Saga
text:
Matchups

Aggro (fliers, lifegain, cats): Dáin, Lord of the Iron Hills taxes every attack, Thorin wards the blockers, and Patient Instructor stalls the ground; Balin wheels find Burst Lightning and Smaug’s Fury, and the Fíli token swarm races.
Midrange (landfall, counters): the trigger engine out-grows a mid board — Dáin Ironfoot double strike closes fast and The Lonely Mountain spends the late mana; Garrison’s power tracks the widening board.
Control: the ward stack (Thorin plus Mattock) makes spot removal and counterspells cost double, Kíli and Dáin’s Company restock after sweepers, and Balin punishes any tapped-out turn. Play toward the wheel rather than the voltron.
Combo and big mana: this deck is the aggressor — storied comes online before most engines, and a turn-five Balin wheel usually ends the game before the opponent’s payoff lands.

title: Cinderhoard
text:
Curve and mana
The deck curves 2 / 7 / 11 / 6 / 5 / 3 / 2 across one through seven mana with an average nonland cost of 3.6, and the Treasure tokens pay the top of that curve early. Counting only lands and applying the Treasures as wildcards, the base offers roughly sixteen red sources, thirteen blue and seven black — red is the deepest because Smaug the Magnificent, Desert Were-Worm and Desolation of Smaug all ask for double red, while black is the shallowest and is covered by the four Treasure-makers plus Giant’s Boulder’s any-colour activation.
Twenty-four lands is deliberate. The deck has no one-mana accelerant, so hitting land three on time matters, and The Lonely Mountain’s token ability wants to be activated only after the fourth land is down. The Lonely Mountain also enters tapped unless you control an Equipment, so curve it behind Thrór’s Map, Orcrist or Giant’s Boulder rather than leading with it on a slow hand.

title: Cinderhoard
text:
Early game
The first two turns are about not falling behind. Giant’s Boulder is the best one-drop: it scries two on entry, which fixes a stumble, and it later taps for any colour, which lets the deck cast Smaug, Wicked Worm off a hand that only drew Mountains. Thrór’s Map does the same job with a guaranteed land; cast it before the first Smaug so that the four-drop never misses its fourth land.
Against aggro, hold Pinecone Strike and Bilbo’s Deadly Slice rather than developing. A Smaug the Magnificent that survives to attack is worth more than a two-drop, so trade removal for their best attacker and land the dragon on turn four.

title: Cinderhoard
text:
Mid game
Turn four is Smaug the Magnificent, almost every game. He attacks the turn he is cast, so the first attack is already two or three damage from the Treasures made by Dori, Grey Dog and the Misty Mountains chapter. From there the upkeep trigger compounds: each turn adds a Treasure, which raises the attack damage by one and moves The Misty Mountains Cold one step closer to a 6/6 Dragon.
Fateful Discovery is the card that makes the middle turns unfair. Every Treasure the deck makes is an extra card, so a turn that produces three artifacts draws three cards. Because Smaug, Wicked Worm also draws off Treasure mana, the deck can spend a turn making Treasures and still come out ahead in cards.
Desolation of Smaug is the reset button for the middle game. It deals three damage to every non-Dragon creature — the deck’s own Dragons are immune — and then pays four mana toward the next Dragon spell. Cast it with a Dragon in hand and it becomes a two-for-one plus a mana refund.

title: Cinderhoard
text:
The combo turn
The kill usually arrives in one of three forms, all fed by the same Treasure bank.

Smaug burn. With six or more Treasures out, Smaug the Magnificent attacks for six or more to any target, and the upkeep trigger adds another Treasure for next turn. Two Smaugs on the board attack for double the hoard.
Misty Mountains Dragon. The Misty Mountains Cold needs four Treasures when a chapter resolves; once it has them the Saga sacrifices itself and leaves a 6/6 flying Dragon token behind, and the Saga’s own chapters supply two of the four Treasures it needs.
Were-Worm extra combat. Attack with twelve or more total power and Desert Were-Worm untaps every attacker for a second combat phase. A 6/6 Dragon token plus a Smaug is already twelve.

A representative turn: Smaug the Magnificent and a 6/6 Misty Mountains Dragon token attack for eleven, Desert Were-Worm’s trigger untaps them, and the second combat step attacks for eleven more — twenty-two through the air with two fliers.

title: Cinderhoard
text:
Win condition 2
When the opponent stabilises the ground, the deck wins from the library instead. Last Light of Durin’s Day puts a quest counter on itself every time a Mountain enters; six counters sacrifice it and put a Dragon from hand or library directly onto the battlefield. With five Mountains, The Lonely Mountain and Thrór’s Map fetching a seventh, the quest is realistically complete by turn six or seven, and the payoff is Smaug, the Great Calamity or Desert Were-Worm for free.
The second route to the same finish is the token hoard. The Lonely Mountain makes a 2/2 Dwarf token for four mana, one cheaper for each Equipment, and every token draws a card under Fateful Discovery. Those Dwarves then provide the twelve power Desert Were-Worm needs for the extra combat, so the mana sink and the finisher are the same plan.

title: Cinderhoard
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep two or three lands, one two-drop and one card that makes Treasures. A hand with Smaug the Magnificent, a Treasure-maker and four lands is a clear keep — the deck’s whole plan is to bank Treasures, and four lands casts the dragon and leaves room to activate The Lonely Mountain later. Ship one-land hands, and ship hands with no Treasure source at all; without Treasures the deck is a pile of expensive Dragons that arrive late.

title: Cinderhoard
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Smaug the Magnificent makes his Treasure at the beginning of your upkeep, so the attack on that same turn already counts it — the first swing after a fresh Smaug is one damage larger than it looks.
Smaug’s attack trigger can target any target, including creatures for removal or opposing planeswalkers, not just the player.
Smaug, Wicked Worm counts artifacts your opponents control when it enters, so it is worst against a creature deck and best after an opposing Treasure or Equipment has hit the board.
The Misty Mountains Cold checks for four Treasures when a chapter resolves; if you already have four, the very first chapter sacrifices the Saga and makes the Dragon immediately, so it can be a three-mana 6/6 flier.
Last Light of Durin’s Day counts Mountains, not lands — only The Lonely Mountain and Mountain trigger it, so Islands and Swamps never advance the quest.
Desert Were-Worm is a 0/5 that only becomes lethal with Mountains; leave it back as a blocker when your Mountain count is low and attack with it only once the team’s power clears twelve.
Desolation of Smaug spares Dragons, so it is a one-sided sweeper while your own fliers are on the board, and its four mana can pay for Smaug, the Great Calamity in the same turn.
Pinecone Strike can choose both modes, so it destroys an opposing Treasure or Equipment and deals three to a creature in the same spell.
The Sackville-Bagginses can sacrifice a Treasure or a Dwarf token to itself, drawing a card and replacing the token while draining an opponent.
Fateful Discovery triggers on Treasure tokens as well as artifacts, so an Orcrist combat step that makes three Treasures draws three cards.
The Lonely Mountain enters tapped unless you control an Equipment, so cast it behind Thrór’s Map, Orcrist or Giant’s Boulder when the turn’s mana is tight.

title: Swarm Calculus
text:
Game plan in three phases

Deploy the arithmetic (turns 1–4): Ambitious Augmenter or Cuboid Colony on curve, then EPF Point Squad and Raphael to establish the Alliance tax. Cast 3+ mana spells to start Increment growth — every spell makes every Increment creature bigger.
Compound (turns 4–6): land Berta (mana per counter) and Fractal Tender (3/3 Fractal every end step). Tokens enter, Raphael and Slash ping, Mutanimals spreads counters, Delney doubles the small entries. Pensive Professor and Topiary Lecturer convert the counter pile into cards and mana.
Cash out: either burn the opponent out with a multi-entry turn (Fountainport Fish at instant speed + Neutrinos flickers + Slash attack tokens) or move a 10+ counter stack onto a Fractal with Tester of the Tangential and send it through Rogue’s Passage.

title: Swarm Calculus
text:
Curve and mana
26 lands: 4 utility/token lands (2 Fountainport, 1 Rogue’s Passage), 5 manlands (3 Restless Prairie, 2 Restless Ridgeline), 3 Secluded Courtyard, 2 Frontier Bivouac, 9 Verge/fixing lands (2 Sandstorm, 2 Hushwood, 2 Sunbillow, 1 Riverpyre, 1 Floodfarm), and 6 basics (2 Forest, 1 Island, 1 Plains, 1 Mountain). The Verge lands need a basic to enter untapped, so fetch basics early; Frontier Bivouac and Secluded Courtyard smooth the three-color Increment spells.
The nonland curve is 3 one-drops, 10 twos, 9 threes, 7 fours, 4 fives — average mana value about 2.9. The deck is low to the ground but every 3+ mana spell is an Increment trigger, so the midgame naturally accelerates: Berta and Topiary turn the counter pile into mana for a Fractal Tender turn.

title: Swarm Calculus
text:
Early game (turns 1–3)

Turn 1: Ambitious Augmenter — a 1/1 that will grow with every spell and pays into a Fractal when it dies.
Turn 2: Cuboid Colony (flash, flying, trample — hold it up as a surprise blocker and Increment grower) or Raphael, Tough Turtle to start taxing entries.
Turn 3: EPF Point Squad (grows on every entry) or Delney if you have tokens coming. Get Lost any problematic permanent.
Prioritize lands that enter untapped; play Fountainport early to build toward its activated abilities.

title: Swarm Calculus
text:
Mid game (turns 4–6)

Land Berta and Fractal Tender. Every spell now does quadruple duty: Increment counters, Berta mana, a Fractal at end step, and Alliance pings from that Fractal.
Attack with manlands to trigger Prairies anthem and Ridgelines pump; Slash’s attack makes a Mutant that pings again.
The Neutrinos: attack, exile a Raphael or EPF, return it tapped and attacking — that entry re-fires every Alliance trigger and re-triggers its own ETB.

title: Swarm Calculus
text:
The combo turn

Build a counter stack on Tester of the Tangential (Increment makes it grow with each spell; it is 1/3, so any 2+ mana spell adds a counter; a 4-mana spell adds two).
At combat, activate Tester, pay X equal to the stack, and move every counter onto a Fractal (from Fractal Tender or Berta) or Slash.
Activate Rogue’s Passage ({4}, {T}) on that creature — it can’t be blocked this turn.
Swing for lethal. With Delney out, the small creatures’ abilities double all the way down, and Venom-style deathtouch or Prairie anthems make the wide attack nearly unblockable too.

title: Swarm Calculus
section: Win condition 2: the ETB burn loop
text:
Win condition 2: the ETB burn loop
Raphael (1) plus Slash (2) plus a source of entries equals 3 damage per creature that enters. Sources of entries on a single turn: Mutanimals tokens, Slash attack tokens, Fractal Tender’s end-step Fractal, Berta’s X-Fractals, Fountainport Fish at instant speed (pay 1 life each), Cuboid Colony flashed on the opponent’s turn, and Neutrinos flickers. With Delney on the battlefield, each small entry triggers everything twice — a four-entry turn becomes 24 damage. Fountainport’s sacrifice-draw keeps the hand full while the Fish keep pinging.

title: Swarm Calculus
text:
Mulligan guide

Keep: 2–3 lands with two or more colors, a two-drop, and at least one Alliance or Increment piece. Ambitious Augmenter plus any 3-drop is a strong open.
Trim: 5+ land hands; hands with only 4- and 5-drops; single-color hands (the deck needs green for the one-drops and red for Raphael).
The deck wants density, not specific cards — almost every creature is both engine and payoff, so mulligan on mana and curve, not on particular names.

title: Swarm Calculus
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Delney doubles entry abilities of creatures with power 2 or less. That includes every Alliance trigger (they are abilities of the entering creature’s triggers… in practice: when a 2/2 Mutant or 1/1 Fish enters, all Alliance abilities trigger an additional time). Creatures with power 3+ (Mutanimals, Slash, Neutrinos, Fractal Tender) are not doubled.
Increment checks mana spent, not mana value. A Get Lost cast for {1}{W} is a 2-mana spell; kicked or extra-cost spells count more. Counters are added by any spell you cast, so instant-speed Fountainport activations do not grow Increment creatures — only spells do.
Ambitious Augmenter’s death trigger puts its counters onto a 0/0 Fractal — a great way to move a counter stack in a pinch, and that Fractal entering triggers Alliance.
Tester of the Tangential moves counters at the beginning of combat — activate before declaring attackers, and remember the {X} is paid from your mana pool, so Berta’s floating mana pays for it.
Fountainport’s Fish token costs 1 life — in a burn race, prefer Mutanimals and Fractal Tender as the entry sources.
The Neutrinos’ flicker returns the creature tapped and attacking — it deals combat damage that same combat, so flickering Raphael or a big EPF is both triggers and damage.
Secluded Courtyard — name Wizard: Ambitious Augmenter, Berta, Fractal Tender, Pensive Professor, Tester, and Topiary are all Wizards.

title: Swarm Calculus
text:
Matchups

Aggro: Cuboid Colony’s flash flying blocker and deathtouch-adjacent pressure buy time; Get Lost removes the biggest threat; race with Slash pings — the burn loop outdamages most combat plans.
Control: manlands are uncounterable and keep the Alliance clock running through sweepers; Delney’s unblockability clause (power 2 or less can’t be blocked by 3+) is irrelevant here, but Increment growth on uncounterable manlands is not; rebuild fast with Fountainport draws.
Midrange: the counter spread from Mutanimals and EPF outgrows most ground armies; Tester + Rogue’s Passage punches through the biggest blocker.
Board wipes: everything except the manlands dies, but Ambitious Augmenter dies into a Fractal, Slash’s tokens already pings, and the manlands survive to keep attacking.

title: Songsteel
text:
Curve and mana
24 lands: 4 The Lonely Mountain, 4 Mystic Monastery, 2 Temple of Epiphany, 9 Plains, 5 Mountain. White sources 13, red sources 15, blue sources 6. Six of the lands enter tapped, which is why the deck wants nothing cheaper than two mana: turn one is a tapped dual or a basic, and every real play starts on turn two.
Nonland curve: 2-drop x22, 3-drop x6, 4-drop x5, 5-drop x2, 6-drop x1. Average nonland CMC 2.72. The deck is nineteen-percent six-plus drops by design — the swarm is cheap, the payoffs are legendaries, and Dwarven Provisioner turns surplus mana into +1/+1.

title: Songsteel
text:
Early game
The deck has no one-drop, so turn one is a land and nothing else. Turn two is the identity decision. Iron Hills Blacksmith is the best aggressive start: a 1/1 double strike plus an Axe token gives you two of the three Storied requirements before turn three. Thorin Oakenshield is the best defensive start: 3/2 trample blocks well and makes the board expensive to attack into once the story turns on.
Sequence Kíli the Resourceful after another Dwarf when possible — his draw fires on the first Dwarf or Equipment that enters each turn, so leading with him wastes the trigger on himself. Óin the Brave and Dáin, Lord of the Iron Hills exist to turn the story on early and to make the opponent’s attack step awkward.

title: Songsteel
text:
Mid game
Turn three to five is where the deck separates. Fíli the Pathfinder converts every subsequent nontoken Dwarf into two permanents — the Dwarf plus a 2/2 red token — and once the story is active, both get +1/+1 from his static ability. Play the cheap Dwarf first and Fíli second: that way Kíli’s once-per-turn draw and Fíli’s token come from the same turn.
The Axe count matters more than it looks. Every Equipment is a Storied requirement, a Dwalin hone counter target, a discount on The Lonely Mountain’s token ability, and an extra double-striking attacker once Dáin Ironfoot is on the board. Iron Hills Stalwart is in the list mainly to move an Axe from a dead Dwarf onto a live one.

title: Songsteel
text:
The combo turn

Story check. Three or more artifacts, legendaries, and/or Sagas: typically Fíli, Kíli or Óin, and an Axe or The Black Arrow. Once achieved, it lasts the rest of the game.
Assemble Equipment. Dáin Ironfoot or Iron Hills Blacksmith makes an Axe; The Black Arrow and Dwarven Provisioner fill the curve. Kíli makes the first equip free.
Anthem up. An Unexpected Party naming Dwarf gives every Dwarf +2/+2; Dwarven Provisioner’s activated ability adds another +1/+1 for four mana.
Attack with Dáin Ironfoot. Each equipped attacking creature gains double strike until end of turn. A 2/2 token with an Axe and +2/+2 is a 5/5 double strike, so ten damage per token that connects.

A typical kill from an empty board: Fíli the Pathfinder, two Dwarves, and Dáin Ironfoot over two turns is four bodies; add two Axes and An Unexpected Party and the attack step is 20-plus damage across double-striking attackers.

title: Songsteel
text:
Win condition 2
Balin, Loremaster is a burn spell disguised as a 4/4. Whenever Balin or another Dwarf enters, you may discard your hand, draw that many cards, and, if you have an enduring story, Balin deals that much damage to each opponent. With five cards in hand, that is five damage to each opponent and a fresh five-card hand. Bifur, Melodic Rider makes every Dwarf triggered ability trigger an additional time, and the second drain resolves after the first redraw, so it drains for the new hand size too. Balin plus Bifur plus two cheap Dwarves is often ten to sixteen points without an attack step, and each entry refills your hand, so the loop does not run out of cards.
The land backs this up. The Lonely Mountain needs four red minus one per Equipment, so with three Equipment out the token costs {1}{R}, and the token is a Dwarf: it triggers Fíli and Balin and becomes another drain trigger the following turn. That is the slow, inevitable half of the deck.

title: Songsteel
text:
Mulligan guide
Keep two to four lands with at least two Dwarves. Because the deck has twenty-two two-drops, almost any two lands plus any two Dwarves is keepable; the ideal opener is a white source, a red source, Iron Hills Blacksmith or Thorin Oakenshield, and a second Dwarf for turn three. Mulligan hands with fewer than two lands, hands with six or more lands and no Dwarf, and hands whose only blue source is Bilbo Baggins — the splash is a bonus, never a plan. With six tapped lands in the mana base, treat a hand of one tapped dual plus one basic as a functional two-land hand only if it casts a two-drop on turn two.

title: Songsteel
text:
Key interactions and edge cases

Storied is a state check on permanents you control, not a spell count: Equipment tokens, legendary creatures, and Sagas all count, and an enduring story persists for the rest of the game even if you lose the board. An Unexpected Party is an enchantment — it does not help turn the story on.
Kíli the Resourceful draws only once each turn, and his free-equip clause applies only to the first equip ability you activate each turn. Play the permanent you want to draw off first.
Equip is sorcery speed, and Dáin Ironfoot’s double strike trigger happens when he attacks, so attach every Axe and The Black Arrow before combat — re-equipping mid-combat does not retroactively grant double strike.
Dwalin, Weaponmaster’s hone counters sit on the Equipment, not the creature, so the bonus moves with the Axe if you re-equip it.
Balin, Loremaster’s discard is optional and resolves as one effect: you discard the hand you have, then draw that many. Discarding a land-heavy hand is a deliberate gamble on the redraw.
Bifur, Melodic Rider doubles triggered abilities of Dwarves only — Fíli’s token, Kíli’s draw, Dáin Ironfoot’s Axe, Balin’s drain, and his own +1/+1 counter trigger, but not Fíli’s static anthem or Thorin’s ward.
The Black Arrow has flash and equip {1}: cast it on the opponent’s turn to ping a one-toughness attacker or a key utility creature, and its anti-Dragon clause is a clean answer to Smaug decks.
The Lonely Mountain enters tapped unless you control an Equipment, so keep an Axe or The Black Arrow around before playing it if you want the untapped red source on curve; Iron Hills Stalwart’s enter trigger can move an Equipment to blank a removal spell or re-attach after a wipe.
Óin the Brave’s loot costs one mana and taps him, and his discard is a real cost when a Balin drain is coming — loot before casting Dwarves, not after.

title: Crypt Curriculum
text:
Gameplay strategy

Early game
Open on Eye of Jace and Yuriko. Eye of Jace is the perfect one-drop here: it surveils every upkeep on its own, so the graveyard count climbs whether or not you draw anything else. Yuriko’s surveil 2 mode is almost always the right choice on turn one; the minus-X mode is a real removal spell later, when the graveyard count is what decides a block. Proctor of Potential is the two-drop that makes the engine stick: it surveils on every creature entering, so a hand with two or three cheap bodies turns into six or seven cards in the graveyard by turn four.


Mid game
From turn three the deck stops paying for its graveyard and starts spending it. Seasoned Cryomancer is the turn-three play that keeps the plan moving: draw two, discard two, then tap the opponent’s best attackers and put stun counters on them, which is how this deck survives aggro without removal. Denzilore Fatehold at instant speed is the real payoff, and once it is on the battlefield every surveil trigger is a team-wide pump, so Eye of Jace’s upkeep, Proctor of Potential’s entry trigger and the Restless Reef attack all become combat math the opponent cannot profitably block.


The combo turn
The deck’s best turn is a self-mill loop into a reanimation. Surveil once to satisfy Proctor of Potential, then pay two mana to return it to the battlefield from the graveyard. It enters, which surveils again, which pays for the next Proctor, and each of those entries is another +1/+1 counter on the team with Denzilore Fatehold out. Two Proctors in the graveyard plus five mana is two surveil triggers, two counters on the whole board, and two extra cards filtered into the yard, all in one turn, and the same loop turns on threshold for Proft Sinister Mastermind and the seven-card clause on Eye of Jace. Use the loop before combat; the counters land on the attackers you are about to use.


Win condition two
The second win is a drain, not a combat step. Every copy of Eye of Jace that reaches an upkeep with seven or more cards in the graveyard sacrifices itself for 2 damage to each opponent and 2 life for you, so four copies are eight damage to the face spread over four turns and eight points of life buffer. Dark Matter Manipulator turns the same graveyard count into a body: it is a one-drop that grows by +2/+0 for every seven cards in the graveyard, so a game that goes long turns a one-mana 1/2 into a lethal attacker. When the drain plan is not quite enough, Uldaros Theorix rebuys a creature and a spell out of the graveyard and casts them for free, and Denzilore Fatehold is the usual creature half of that.


Mulligan guide
Keep two or three lands with at least one blue source and one engine card, ideally Eye of Jace or Yuriko. Hands with a surveil engine plus a payoff are keeps even without a plan for turn two, because the deck’s engine pays out on its own triggers. Be careful with hands that have no black or white source at all: Proft Sinister Mastermind, Denzilore Fatehold and Proctor of Potential are all locked behind a second colour. Ship hands of five lands, hands with Uldaros Theorix and no early plays, and hands with Restless Reef as the only blue source, because it always enters tapped.


Key interactions and edge cases

Eye of Jace sacrifices itself when the trigger resolves, so it is a one-shot. Do not treat it as a permanent; four copies are four separate drains, and they stage over the game.
Denzilore Fatehold triggers on each scry or surveil, not each card. A single Surveil 2 that puts two cards into the graveyard is still one +1/+1 counter on each creature.
Proctor of Potential’s recursion needs you to have scried or surveilled this turn, and the returned body carries a finality counter, so it is exiled instead of dying. Return it in the turn you are attacking, not as a blocker.
Proft Sinister Mastermind cannot be cast at all until the graveyard holds seven or more cards. Treat it as a turn-four-plus card, and note that its discard ability is a real removal spell on any turn the seven-card clause is live.
Seasoned Cryomancer’s tap-and-stun clause only triggers if you discard at least one nonland card. When the hand is all lands, the discard is a blank; that is the correct time to mill into a spell with Sphinx’s Approach instead.
Sphinx’s Approach can be cast from the graveyard only in the sense that it can be milled into value for threshold. With three copies, the exile-five-copies clause can never turn on; the spell is here as an instant-speed draw-two that a mill-heavy turn makes cheap in card terms.
Dark Matter Manipulator counts every seven cards in the graveyard, both players included, and it counts card types only for Tarmogoyf-style effects, not here: it is a flat +2/+0 per seven cards, so it is a 3/2 at seven cards, a 5/2 at fourteen.
Uldaros Theorix casts copies of permanents as tokens. Exiling a creature and a sorcery from the graveyard and casting both is legitimate as long as the total mana value is six or less.



Matchups
Against aggro, the plan is to race with Drain and to blank attackers with Seasoned Cryomancer’s stun counters and Surveillance Phantasm’s 2/3 flying body; this is the deck’s tightest matchup, because there is no removal spell in the list. Against midrange it is a favourite: Denzilore Fatehold grows the board faster than most decks can trade, and the Proctor loop converts spare mana into counters. Against control, keep Eye of Jace for the drain and hold Sphinx of False Conclusions for flash blocks, and expect to win slowly through the drain plus the Recursion from Liliana the Repentant and Uldaros Theorix after a wipe. Against combo, the deck has no interaction beyond tapping attackers down, so it must count on Denzilore Fatehold plus fliers to close before the opponent goes off.
